docs.title: ReplayGain and loudness
docs.text: Why can two tracks have the same peak level but sound different in volume? Peak amplitude and perceived loudness describe different things. ReplayGain stores measured playback adjustments as metadata; a supporting player can use them when playing the audio. Editing those fields is different from measuring the recording or changing the encoded audio samples.

docs.title: The four common fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_GAIN Gain adjustment measured for this track. REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_GAIN Gain adjustment measured for the album as a group. REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_PEAK Peak amplitude recorded for this track. REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_PEAK Peak amplitude recorded for the album.

Track mode levels individual songs. Album mode uses a common adjustment to retain the loudness differences within an album. Negative gain means reduce level; positive gain means increase it. Peak metadata can help a player avoid clipping after gain, subject to its settings. See the ReplayGain specification for the measurement and playback model.

A stored gain is not a volume percentage, a peak reading, or the track's bitrate. Changing the number by hand does not run a loudness analysis. Whether playback uses track gain, album gain, additional preamp gain or no ReplayGain depends on the player. OpenTag's field display is not a playback meter.

docs.title: Read the stored text before changing it
docs.text:
The following values are invented metadata for a practice copy. They are not measurements of the guide's example album and should not be copied to real tracks as a normalization recipe.

Field Practice value REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_GAIN -4.25 dB REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_GAIN -3.00 dB REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_PEAK 0.950000 REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_PEAK 0.990000

OpenTag can inspect these stored fields in Extended tags. A custom column or export can read their placeholders, for example %replaygain_track_gain%. Unknown text fields use the tag family's supported custom-field path, so storage and player interpretation can differ by format. ID3v1 has no general custom-field space for this set. Do not assume that an arbitrary similarly named field is an alias for another loudness scheme.

For a deliberate metadata correction, Keep changes stages Extended tags edits and Save tags writes them. Actions and converters have their own write timing. Reopen/read back the saved file before deciding that a player's lack of volume change is a failed tag save. It may be ignoring the field or using a different playback mode. Use an audio-analysis tool that supports your target workflow to calculate gains from the recording; this guide's OpenTag workflows edit the stored metadata.

docs.title: Preservation during MPEG saves has conditions
docs.text:
An MP3 can have ReplayGain data in an APEv2 tag while OpenTag displays its ID3v2 tag. A normal save may remove the APE tag according to Mpeg preferences. In that path, when ID3v2 is being written, OpenTag has a specific safeguard: it copies nonempty REPLAYGAIN_ and MP3GAIN_ fields from the removed, undisplayed APE tag if the full displayed values and existing ID3v2 tag do not already contain that field name. Existing values take precedence; this is not a conflict-merging or recalculation operation.

These written cases use APE Read off, ID3v2 Read/Write on, APE Write off and APE Remove on. Each practice file starts with ID3v2 TITLE = Paper Boats; saving ARTIST = Juniper Vale triggers the normal field-save path.

APE track gain Existing ID3v2 track gain Saved ID3v2 track gain -4.25 dB Absent -4.25 dB -4.25 dB -1.50 dB -1.50 dB Absent Absent Absent

Do not generalize that safeguard to Remove tag, an explicit field removal action, a save without an ID3v2 target, or every container format. A broad keep-list action can erase loudness fields that are not listed. MP3GAIN_UNDO is another tool's restoration information, not a ReplayGain track gain or OpenTag's Edit → Undo history. Preserve it when needed.

docs.title: What this means in OpenTag
docs.text:
Before cleaning tags, inspect the actual tag families and stored field names, and retain original files. Keep track and album measurements together where your workflow needs both. If the audio was replaced, edited or transcoded, consider whether the old measurements still describe that recording rather than copying numbers blindly. After an operation, verify the written fields and the receiving player's settings separately.

Removing gain metadata does not itself reverse audio changes made by a different program. OpenTag session undo can restore recorded file operations while available; it does not reconstruct missing analysis or another tool's lost recovery information.

docs.title: Sort fields and compilations
docs.text: Why does a player file The Lanterns under T, and why does a guest appearance split an album into several artists? Display credits, ordering hints and album grouping are separate metadata choices. Preserve the credit people should read, then add the information the receiving player needs.

docs.title: A sort name is an extra value
docs.text:
ARTIST is the displayed track credit. ARTISTSORT offers an alternate ordering name without replacing that credit. Similarly, ALBUMARTIST can identify the album-level credit while ALBUMARTISTSORT supplies its sorting form. A player may support these fields, ignore them, or apply its own article rules. Test the actual player before retagging a library.

This invented practice record keeps the visible artist intact:

Field Stored value ARTIST The Lanterns ARTISTSORT Lanterns, The ALBUMARTIST The Lanterns ALBUMARTISTSORT Lanterns, The ALBUM Harbour Lights ALBUMSORT 2024 - Harbour Lights TITLE Paper Boats

The alternate album text is an ordering convention chosen for this example; it does not change ALBUM, the release year, or the audio. There is no universal rule that every name beginning with “The” should be rewritten. Names in other languages and intentional artist spellings need a deliberate policy. Keep accents and punctuation unless the target system requires a different sorting form.

The remaining common counterparts are TITLESORT for TITLE and COMPOSERSORT for COMPOSER. These are separate fields, not switches that transform their associated display values. See the native mapping table for their storage in each tag family; an ID3 or MP4 name is not a promise that another format or player has the same native facility.

docs.title: File-list sorting is a separate decision
docs.text:
OpenTag's default Artist column displays the artist values and sorts that column's evaluated display value. It does not automatically substitute ARTISTSORT. A custom column can display the original credit while using a different SORT BY (EMPTY = VALUE) expression.

For the practice record above:

Purpose Format string Result Display credit %artist% The Lanterns Use the alternate key when present $if2(%artistsort%,%artist%) Lanterns, The Album ordering key $if2(%albumsort%,%album%) 2024 - Harbour Lights

$if2 uses the second expression when the first has no value. Removing ARTISTSORT therefore makes the second example fall back to The Lanterns. Evaluating these expressions, or clicking a column heading, does not write a sort field into the audio file. Configure columns through the column guide. For a list of several artists, choose an explicit join if the ordering key should include all of them; a plain placeholder reads the first value.

docs.title: Album artist and compilation answer different questions
docs.text:
Imagine a collection called Harbour Sessions: one track credits Juniper Vale, another Mira Solberg. Their ARTIST values should stay different. Giving both ALBUMARTIST = Various Artists can supply a common album credit where a player uses album artist for grouping. Keep the album name and disc/track numbers consistent too. Grouping behavior still belongs to the player; the text Various Artists is not a special OpenTag command.

COMPILATION is a separate flag. It neither fills ALBUMARTIST nor changes track credits. In OpenTag's constrained ID3v2 and MP4 mappings, enable it with 1, or remove the field to disable it:

Requested field value Result in the ID3v2 practice file 1 1 0 Error; existing 1 remains true Error; existing 1 remains Remove field Absent

An absent flag and a text value of 0 are different write requests. Native APEv2/Vorbis text fields do not acquire these ID3/MP4 constraints merely because they have the same name. Inspect the structured-field rules and saved result for the actual file format.

docs.title: What this means in OpenTag
docs.text: Use Extended tags to inspect or add fields that are not in the tag panel. Keep changes stages its text edits; finish with Save tags. A Tag → Tag converter or action that writes these values has its own immediate write path. Try a copied album first, read the saved values back, and refresh the consuming player's library if necessary. Session Edit → Undo is useful for recorded operations; retain originals for recovery beyond that session.

docs.title: Tag formats and why readers can disagree
docs.text: A tag format is the structure used to store metadata. It is distinct from the audio codec and container. An MP3 stream can carry ID3 and APE blocks; AAC audio inside MP4 uses MP4 metadata, while a raw .aac stream follows a different supported tag path.

docs.title: Choose a format by the file, not by its name alone
docs.text:
Changing an extension does not transcode audio or install another tag format. OpenTag checks file contents and uses the supported writer for that format. The format reference lists exact current read/write/remove capabilities and exceptional layouts.

Metadata family Where it is relevant Important distinction ID3v1 Legacy MPEG and supported APE-family paths Small fixed fields; no arbitrary custom fields or embedded artwork ID3v2 MPEG and supported ID3 paths such as AIFF, WAV, DSF/DFF Richer frames, revisions and text encodings; limits still vary by field/container APEv2 Monkey's Audio, Musepack, WavPack and other supported APE paths; can coexist on MPEG Separate block, including custom fields and supported artwork Vorbis-style comments FLAC and Ogg-family formats such as Vorbis/Opus/Speex Native named entries; repeated values and picture storage follow the format MP4 items/atoms MP4/M4A/M4B and related files carrying AAC/ALAC or other streams Native items such as title, track pairs and artwork; not an ID3 tag added by renaming ASF attributes Windows Media / ASF Native attributes and pictures, with stream-specific limits Matroska tags/attachments Matroska and WebM Scoped tags, supported chapters and image attachments; target levels matter RIFF INFO Supported WAV metadata Different capacity from ID3v2, which a WAV can also contain

This table is an orientation, not a promise that every field or image type works identically in each family. In particular, AIFF's supported editing path is ID3v2 here; do not infer other editors' native chunk behavior.

docs.title: One MP3 can contain conflicting blocks
docs.text:
Suppose one copied practice MP3 physically contains:

Block TITLE ALBUM ID3v1 Old Short Title Absent ID3v2 Paper Boats Harbour Lights APEv2 Archive Title Absent

OpenTag's Mpeg reading policy chooses an enabled block in priority order: APE, then ID3v2, then ID3v1. It does not merge an album from one block into a title selected from another. The following Read switches produce these results for that same physical file after pending edits are resolved and the file is read again:

Read ID3v1 Read ID3v2 Read APE TITLE shown ALBUM shown On On On Archive Title Absent On On Off Paper Boats Harbour Lights On Off Off Old Short Title Absent Off Off On Archive Title Absent

Seeing a blank album with APE enabled does not establish that the ID3v2 album was erased. Inspect present/read tag information and the Read options before “repairing” a value that another block already contains. A different player can choose another block or keep a library cache; investigate the actual file and reader settings separately.

docs.title: Read, Write and Remove are independent decisions
docs.text:
Read chooses the displayed metadata. Write selects supported tag types to receive saved data. Remove chooses types for File → Remove tag…; saving also removes a selected type when it is not being written.

For example, disabling Write APEv2 while leaving Remove APE enabled can strip an APE tag during an ordinary save. Saving can synchronize several written types from the displayed values; conflicting hidden blocks are not guaranteed to retain independent versions of every field. Keep original files before changing policies on a mixed collection.

These Mpeg options also serve supported raw AAC and TTA paths. The Ape, Mpc family uses APE ahead of ID3v1 and has its own write/remove choices. Other containers use their own supported native structures. The Tags options and its child pages provide the actual controls, defaults and restrictions.

docs.title: Revision, encoding and logical field names
docs.text:
The MPEG ID3v2 default is ID3v2.3 UTF-16. ID3v2.4 UTF-8 is another Unicode representation; ID3v2.3 ISO-8859-1 is a legacy choice that can lose characters outside its repertoire. Choose compatibility from the actual consumer's requirements and test a copy, rather than assuming the oldest or newest spelling is universally best.

A logical field can map to different native identifiers. TITLE maps to ID3v2 TIT2, for example. Native field names can also remain visible in APEv2 or Vorbis Comments; DATE is not automatically the same displayed field as an MP3's YEAR. Custom mappings can change that relationship. Use the mapping reference before rewriting a field merely because two formats name related information differently.

docs.title: Know what a successful write establishes
docs.text:
Writers have field, artwork, numeric and structural limits. An unusual container can be readable but refused for writing; opaque or unsupported data can follow preservation rules rather than appearing in the editor. A successful core operation on one fixture is not a complete player or native-device compatibility guarantee for every file in that family.

Inspect the operation result, saved read-back and intended consumer. Keep backups, including original metadata blocks when their differences matter.

docs.title: Text encodings and codepages
docs.text: Why can the same title appear as Café in one file and CafÃ© in another? The intended characters and the bytes used to store them are different layers. An encoding tells a reader how to turn bytes back into characters.

docs.title: Characters are not bytes
docs.text:
Unicode identifies characters independently of a file format. For example, é is U+00E9. UTF-8 and UTF-16 are different ways to encode that character:

Encoding example Bytes for é What must be known when reading UTF-8 C3 A9 Interpret the bytes as UTF-8 UTF-16 little-endian E9 00 Interpret 16-bit units in little-endian order ISO-8859-1 E9 Use that restricted single-byte character set

UTF-8 and UTF-16 can represent the Unicode character repertoire. A legacy codepage represents a smaller repertoire and assigns particular meanings to its byte values. Windows-1252 and ISO-8859-1 overlap for many characters but are not identical encodings.

A byte-order mark (BOM) can identify a Unicode encoding at the start of a text file: EF BB BF for UTF-8, FF FE for UTF-16 little-endian, and FE FF for UTF-16 big-endian. It is an encoding marker, not an extra title character the reader should display.

docs.title: How garbled text is created
docs.text:
Consider the UTF-8 bytes for the final character in Café:

Intended character:       é
UTF-8 bytes:              C3 A9
Wrong Windows-1252 read:  Ã©

The wrong decoding produces real Unicode characters Ã and ©. Saving those characters correctly as UTF-8 preserves the wrong text; it does not magically recover é. This kind of garbling is often called mojibake.

The direction of the mistake matters. Different legacy encodings can interpret the same bytes differently, so selecting an encoding by the language name alone can produce another plausible but wrong result.

docs.title: Tag format and text encoding are separate choices
docs.text:
An MP3 file can contain ID3 tags. The ID3 revision and selected text encoding determine how its text frames are written. OpenTag's MPEG options offer these combinations:

ID3v2 write choice Text encoding ID3v2.3 UTF-16 Unicode UTF-16 ID3v2.3 ISO-8859-1 Restricted Latin-1 ID3v2.4 UTF-8 Unicode UTF-8

The initial default is ID3v2.3 UTF-16. The Latin-1 choice cannot preserve characters outside U+0000–U+00FF; OpenTag's conversion replaces those with ?. Keep originals before choosing a restricted encoding for compatibility.

This is metadata encoding. It does not change MP3 audio encoding, bitrate or sound quality. Other tag formats have their own text-storage rules; an ID3 option does not change how every audio format stores text.

docs.title: Reading external text files
docs.text:
Text import uses a decoding rule for the source file, separate from the tag encoding used when the imported values are saved. For OpenTag's structured text import, Import Text File action and export-template reader:

  1. A supported Unicode BOM selects that decoding.
  2. Without a BOM, valid UTF-8 is read as UTF-8.
  3. Otherwise a supplied ANSI/legacy fallback is used; without one, the reader falls back to Windows-1252.

A fallback is not a command to reinterpret a file already accepted as valid UTF-8. Save new text files as UTF-8. For UTF-16 text input, include its BOM so the reader can identify the byte order. Invalid sequences can report an error rather than being silently replaced.

docs.title: Repair and character-loss operations differ
docs.text:
The Convert Codepage action can recover some known mistakes by turning the existing characters back into legacy bytes and decoding those bytes with the chosen encoding. For example, choosing UTF-8 for CafÃ© recovers Café when those characters still preserve the original bytes.

By contrast, $ansi limits text to characters available in the current ANSI codepage. With Windows-1252 context:

Expression Result $ansi(Café) Café $ansi(猫) ? $upper($ansi(Café)) CAFÉ

On a UTF-8 system context, $ansi preserves Unicode text. It is not an automatic mojibake repair. A ? or replacement character introduced by an earlier lossy conversion usually means the original information is already missing; another codepage cannot infer the lost name.

docs.title: What this means in OpenTag
docs.text:
Start by checking whether the text is wrong in the saved tag or only in one player's display. If the tag contains correct Unicode, a destructive repair action can make it worse. If the stored text is garbled, preserve the original and test one diagnosed conversion on a copy.

Choose a Unicode tag encoding when the target player supports it. For older players, verify the specific revision and encoding they need using a practice file. Check accented characters, non-Latin names and artwork after saving rather than treating an encoding label as a compatibility test.

docs.title: Track and disc numbers are metadata, not list positions
docs.text: TRACK=3/8 conventionally describes track 3 of 8, while DISCNUMBER=2/3 describes disc 2 of 3. Each is one text value in OpenTag's editing model. It is not a list containing two separate values, a fraction to calculate, or proof of how many files are currently selected.

docs.title: Separate the number from its display
docs.text:
For this practice snapshot, the title is Paper Boats. The operation is currently processing its fifth file:

Kind Name Values Metadata TITLE ["Paper Boats"] Metadata TRACK ["3/8"] Metadata DISCNUMBER ["2/3"] Information _COUNTER ["5"] Format string Calculated text %track% 3/8 $num(%track%,2) 03 $num(%discnumber%,1) 2 $num(%discnumber%,1)-$num(%track%,2) - %title% 2-03 - Paper Boats $num(%_counter%,2) 05

$num reads a numeric prefix and pads it; it does not preserve /8 or save the total somewhere else. The fourth expression calculates a useful filename stem without changing the stored track/disc fields. Applying a naming converter is a separate step.

%_counter% follows the current operation's file order. It is not the saved track number: here the counter is 5 while TRACK begins with 3. Using it on a filtered subset can generate a different sequence from an album's existing numbers.

docs.title: Padding is a representation choice
docs.text:
3, 03 and 003 can denote the same current track. Padding is useful in names sorted as text, but some native formats store numbers as integers and do not preserve those zeros. Use $num(%track%,2) when building padded filenames even if saved MP4 track metadata reads back as 3/8.

A two-digit minimum does not truncate track 100. Conversely, a nonnumeric value such as B2 is not converted into a vinyl-side numbering system by $num; its numeric prefix is absent. Preview mixed conventions before renumbering them.

docs.title: Totals and native storage differ by format
docs.text:
In ID3v2, TRACK and DISCNUMBER map to TRCK and TPOS. MP4 stores a current number and total in native trkn and disk pairs. Its mapped total fields are TOTALTRACKS and TOTALDISCS; a read can expose both TRACK=3/8 and TOTALTRACKS=8. Conflicting simultaneously supplied totals are rejected, and native MP4 components use unsigned 16-bit integers.

TRACKTOTAL and DISCTOTAL are not universal automatic aliases for those MP4 fields in this baseline. A similarly named custom field can coexist without configuring a player's native total. Other formats may expose native names such as TRACKNUMBER; inspect the actual file and mappings before assuming a blank %track% means no stored number exists.

See read or split track totals before separating a slash value. A slash-splitting pattern alone does not validate numbers or check that current track is within the total. A partial selection also does not establish a whole album's correct total.

docs.title: Order files before assigning new numbers
docs.text:
Sorting changes the file list's view; it does not by itself rewrite TRACK. Auto-numbering uses the selected files' current list order, shows a preview and stages numbers as pending edits. Save tags then writes them. Changing its inputs or selection invalidates the reviewed sequence.

Folder/field counter changes detect transitions between adjacent selected files. Interleaving discs can create repeated resets rather than one global group per album. In the per-folder shortcut, a saved total is the final assigned number in that run; starting at 5 with three files gives total 7. The regular wizard's entered fixed total is a different mode.

A disc counter and a track counter have separate controls. Enabling a disc field does not infer disc boundaries from audio, and a directory transition can restart tracks without writing DISCNUMBER. Review Auto-numbering before staging a batch.

docs.title: Check copies and saved results
docs.text:
Use a small copied selection while learning, then inspect the actual pending values and save outcome. A number shown in a preview or filename does not prove the native tag was changed. Actions and applied converters can write immediately, unlike staged numbering; follow each command's commit step.

Use Edit → Undo … for recorded saved changes in the current desktop session, and retain original files when old ordering/totals must remain recoverable beyond it.

docs.title: What tags are
docs.text: Tags are descriptive data stored with an audio file: a title, artist, album, track number or embedded picture. The audio stream, the file's path and a player's library records are separate things. Understanding that separation makes an unexpected display easier to diagnose.

docs.title: One recording, several descriptions
docs.text:
Imagine a copied file named 07 - Old Label.mp3 whose stored title is Paper Boats. Those names can disagree without the audio being different. A player might show the tag title, a filename fallback or its own cached library information. Check which source it is using before changing every copy of the file.

OpenTag's tag fields describe the file; changing TITLE does not automatically rename it. A file-list filename edit or a rename converter changes its path without automatically changing the title. An export creates another output; it does not turn the report text into saved tags.

docs.title: Fields hold values
docs.text:
A field name identifies the kind of information. A value is its content. ARTIST and ALBUMARTIST are different fields, not two spellings of the same credit. A field can have several values, such as two artists, rather than one string containing punctuation.

This practice snapshot distinguishes stored metadata from information computed for the current file:

Kind Name Values Metadata TITLE ["Paper Boats"] Metadata ARTIST ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] Metadata ALBUM ["Harbour Lights"] Metadata TRACK ["3/8"] Information _FILENAME_EXT ["07 - Old Label.mp3"]

The brackets illustrate lists, not characters to type into the tag panel. TRACK=3/8 here is one value describing track and total. Two ARTIST values carry separate credits. A semicolon inside one value remains punctuation unless an operation explicitly splits it.

docs.title: Reading a value is not writing it
docs.text:
Format strings read fields and calculate text. For the snapshot above:

Format string Calculated text %title% Paper Boats %artist% Juniper Vale $meta_sep(artist,' & ') Juniper Vale & Mira Solberg %_filename_ext% 07 - Old Label.mp3 $num(%track%,2) - %title% 03 - Paper Boats

A bare placeholder reads the first value; $meta_sep intentionally joins the artist list for this display. Calculating 03 - Paper Boats does not rename the file. A converter or action has to use that result as a naming target and be applied before a path changes.

Information placeholders such as %_filename_ext%, %_codec% and %_bitrate% come from the file or operation. Typing a tag field named CODEC does not transcode the audio. Use the documented naming targets when a path change is intended, rather than treating all displayed information as writable tag fields.

docs.title: The field name and native storage are different
docs.text:
TITLE is a logical name. A mapping connects it to native storage: for example, ID3v2 TIT2 or an MP4 title item. A filename extension is not a universal tag format. One MP3 can contain several tag blocks with different values, and different readers can prioritize them differently.

Tag formats explains those choices. The field reference explains meanings and mappings. A successful text calculation does not prove that every destination format can store multiple values, long Unicode text, artwork or custom fields.

docs.title: Pending edits and saved files
docs.text:
In the tag panel, typing stages edits for the selection. Save tags writes the selected pending changes. Extended tags… can show several values explicitly. Actions and applied converters have their own immediate-write behavior; they do not all wait for Save tags.

A player's old library display does not establish that a save failed, and an updated OpenTag display alone does not establish a completed disk write. Inspect the operation result, read the file back, and check the receiving player's import/cache behavior when displays disagree.

Work on copies while learning. Native-format and source-access limitations still apply; retained backups matter beyond the current desktop undo session.

docs.title: Converters
docs.text: Converters move information between tags, filenames and structured text. Choose the route from the information you already trust to the result you want. A preview shows the proposed result before you commit it.

docs.title: Choose a converter
docs.text:
Trusted source Goal Converter Shortcut Existing tags Rename or move the files Tag → Filename Alt+1 File or folder names Fill tag fields Filename → Tag Alt+2 Parts of the existing names Rearrange filenames without first tagging Filename → Filename Alt+3 One text record per audio file Fill several fields Text File → Tag Alt+4 Existing tag values Calculate or copy one field Tag → Tag Alt+5 Current file-list order Assign track and disc numbers Auto-numbering Cmd+K / Ctrl+K

Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac. Save or discard pending edits and select the files before opening a converter.

docs.title: Read a template versus write a pattern
docs.text:
These two uses of %title% look similar but point in opposite directions:

Context Meaning of %title% Example A format string building output Read the existing title %artist% - %title% → Juniper Vale - Paper Boats A pattern importing information Capture text into the title field %track% - %title% reads 03 - Paper Boats

Output formats can evaluate functions such as $num(%track%,2). Import patterns describe exact separators and destination names; they do not execute scripting functions. Filename → Filename uses numbered parts %1 through %9 instead of tag-field names in its matching pattern.

docs.title: Preview, apply and save
docs.text:
1. Work on copied practice files first.
  2. Enter the format or pattern and choose Preview when provided. Tag → Tag refreshes its preview automatically as you type.
  3. Check multiple rows, including unusual names and missing fields.
  4. Apply the reviewed conversion. If the input or selection changes, refresh the preview before applying.

The five converters with arrows save or rename when applied. There is no second Save tags step. Auto-numbering is different: Stage numbers creates pending edits, and Save tags writes them afterward.

A preview is not a backup or proof that every later disk write will succeed. Inspect operation errors and the actual files afterward. Use Edit → Undo for recorded changes in the current desktop session, and keep original copies for recovery beyond that session.

docs.title: Auto-numbering
docs.text: Use Auto-numbering to assign track and optional disc numbers in the current file-list order. Preview the sequence, stage it as pending edits, then save. The wizard does not infer an album's intended order from audio.

docs.title: Number one album
docs.text:
1. Keep copies, save pending edits and arrange the files in their intended playing order. Select only the tracks to number.
  2. Choose Convert → Auto-numbering… (Cmd+K / Ctrl+K).
  3. Set Begin at track to 1 and Minimum digits to 2.
  4. For this trial, leave total count, disc numbers and counter changes off.
  5. Choose Preview. Expect 01, 02, 03 and so on in file-list order.
  6. Choose Stage numbers. Inspect the pending values in the main window.
  7. Choose File → Save tags (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S) to write them.

Until the last step, the staged numbers are pending edits. Discard them if the sequence is wrong rather than saving and trying to reconstruct the original numbers.

docs.title: Track and disc settings
docs.text:
Setting Effect Initial value Begin at track First track number and restart value 1 Minimum digits under Track numbers Pad track numbers to this width 2 Save total track count Add /total to every track value Off Total tracks The total to store when enabled Number of selected files Disc numbers Also write DISCNUMBER Off Begin at disc First disc number and disc reset value 1 Minimum digits under Disc numbers Pad disc numbers 1 Save total disc count Add /total to every disc value Off Total discs The total to store when enabled 1

These are initial defaults. Most options are remembered after a staged run, so check them when reopening the wizard. Total tracks starts with the current selection count each time.

Begin at track Minimum digits Total enabled/value First three results 1 2 Off 01, 02, 03 5 3 Off 005, 006, 007 1 2 On, 8 01/8, 02/8, 03/8

In the regular wizard, totals are the numbers entered, not an automatic count of each group. For different per-disc totals, number each disc separately or use the per-folder shortcut described below. A minimum width does not truncate larger numbers: width 2 still allows track 100.

Some tag formats store track/disc components as integers and may not retain leading zeros after saving. For consistently padded filenames, use $num(%track%,2) in a filename format.

docs.title: Restart tracks in each folder
docs.text:
For local files, Cmd+Shift+K / Ctrl+Shift+K opens a per-folder run. It enables directory changes and track resets, while leaving disc-number writing off. Arrange the selection so each folder's tracks are together. When Save total track count is enabled in this shortcut mode, each run uses its own final assigned track number. Starting at 1, a 12-track folder and an 8-track folder receive totals 12 and 8, rather than both 20. Starting at 5 with three tracks instead ends at 7, so its total is 7. A selected subset or another configured reset can shorten a run; select all intended tracks and check every boundary in the preview.

For the same track resets in the regular wizard, enable Next disc on change of directory and Reset track counter on next disc while leaving Disc numbers off. That regular mode keeps the entered total; it does not enable the shortcut’s per-run totals. An internal disc boundary can restart tracks without writing a disc field.

These small examples use the per-folder shortcut with total count enabled:

Begin at track Folder Selected tracks First result Last result 1 Harbour 3 01/3 03/3 1 Low Tide 2 01/2 02/2 5 Bonus 3 05/7 07/7

The first two folders can share one run starting at 1; the Bonus example is a separate run starting at 5. The entered Total tracks box is disabled in this shortcut mode because the run determines it.

Directory grouping requires known local folders. For provider documents without those paths, the directory control is unavailable; use a reliable tag-field grouping or process each album separately.

docs.title: Number a multi-disc collection
docs.text:
The wizard compares each file with the previous file in list order:

Counter-change setting When it acts Next disc on change of directory Parent folder changes Next disc on change of field The chosen field's values change Reset track counter on next disc A next-disc boundary restarts tracks at Begin at track Reset disc counter on change of field Reset discs to Begin at disc and tracks to Begin at track

For two album folders, each with two disc subfolders:

  1. Sort by album, disc and intended track order.
  2. Enable Disc numbers and begin both counters at 1.
  3. Set Next disc on change of field to DISCNUMBER, using the existing disc tags to identify the boundaries.
  4. Enable Reset track counter on next disc.
  5. Set Reset disc counter on change of field to ALBUM.
  6. Preview the first and last rows of every disc before staging.

A disc reset takes priority if both a next-disc and reset condition occur at the same boundary. A field's missing value also participates in these comparisons; clean inconsistent album/disc tags first.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Grouping detects transitions, not all equal values across the selection. Interleaved albums cause repeated resets; keep groups together.
  • Disc settings do not change tracks unless their configured boundary or reset rule acts. Preview instead of assuming enabling discs groups files.
  • Preview shows at most 100 rows, although the plan covers the selection. Use smaller selections when the unshown boundaries need inspection.
  • Start and total values must be positive whole numbers. Minimum digits must be 1–10; counter overflow reports an error.
  • Keep original copies and inspect Edit → Undo for recorded changes after saving. Staging alone is not proof that tags were written.

docs.title: Filename → Filename
docs.text: Use Filename → Filename to rearrange parts of existing names without reading or changing tags. Mark the parts in the old pattern with %1 through %9, then reuse those parts in the new pattern.

docs.title: Swap an artist and title
docs.text:
Start with Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.mp3 and make Paper Boats - Juniper Vale.mp3:

  1. Save pending edits and select copied practice files.
  2. Choose Convert → Filename → Filename… (Alt+3; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).
  3. Set Old filename pattern to %1 - %2.
  4. Set New filename pattern to %2 - %1.
  5. Choose Preview and inspect the source and destination rows.
  6. Choose Rename … files to apply that reviewed plan.

The old pattern captures %1 = Juniper Vale and %2 = Paper Boats. The new pattern outputs them in reverse order. The audio extension is retained; it need not appear in either pattern.

docs.title: Keep, drop and transform parts
docs.text:
Input filename Old filename pattern New filename pattern Result 003 Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.mp3 %1 %2 - %3 %2 - %3 Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.mp3 Juniper Vale__Paper Boats.flac %1__%2 %1 - %2 Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.flac Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.mp3 %1 - %2 $upper(%1) - %2 JUNIPER VALE - Paper Boats.mp3 03 - Paper Boats.mp3 %1 - %2 $num(%1,3). %2 003. Paper Boats.mp3

The old pattern is a matching pattern: literal punctuation must match exactly. It accepts only numbered parts, with no closing percent sign after the number. %artist% is not an old-pattern capture.

The new pattern is an output format. It can use scripting functions and existing tag placeholders alongside the numbered parts. A part omitted from the new pattern is discarded from the name. Reusing a part there is allowed, for example %2 - %2.

docs.title: Read and create folders
docs.text:
Backslashes in the old pattern mark folder boundaries. For example:

Setting Value Input path Music/Juniper Vale - Harbour Lights/03 Paper Boats.mp3 Old filename pattern %1 - %2\%3 %4 New filename pattern %1 - %2 - %3 - %4

The four parts are Juniper Vale, Harbour Lights, 03 and Paper Boats. The output name is Juniper Vale - Harbour Lights - 03 - Paper Boats.mp3. The path's earlier Music component is outside this relative match.

Backslashes in the new pattern create destination folders. A relative destination is based on the source file's containing folder, not the earlier root omitted from the matching pattern. Use an absolute destination when moving several source folders into one new layout. Preview the full paths before applying.

docs.title: Combine folder captures, functions and literal brackets
docs.text:
Suppose this incoming file needs a new archive layout:

D:\Incoming\Juniper Vale - Harbour Lights\03 Paper Boats (2024_DEMO).mp3

Set Old filename pattern to:

%1 - %2\%3 %4 (%5_DEMO)

The pattern captures five parts: %1 is Juniper Vale, %2 is Harbour Lights, %3 is 03, %4 is Paper Boats, and %5 is 2024. _DEMO is fixed text describing the source naming convention, so it does not become part of the year capture.

Set New filename pattern to:

D:\Archive\$upper(%1) - %2 '['%5']'\$num(%3,2). %4 (Demo)

The expected destination is:

D:\Archive\JUNIPER VALE - Harbour Lights [2024]\03. Paper Boats (Demo).mp3

Work through it before applying:

  1. D:\Archive\ gives the absolute destination root. On macOS or Linux, choose the intended absolute root there instead.
  2. $upper(%1) capitalizes the captured artist, without changing a tag.
  3. %2 retains the captured album. '['%5']' writes actual square brackets around the captured year; unquoted brackets would mark an optional section.
  4. The next backslash starts the filename inside that new album folder.
  5. $num(%3,2) pads the captured track number, and %4 retains the title.
  6. (Demo) adds a normalized suffix, and the converter keeps .mp3.

Preview the full destination. Unlike a relative output, this layout does not nest a new album folder inside the incoming album folder. Check that the chosen archive root is writable and the destination is not occupied.

docs.title: Working folder and replacement characters
docs.text: The new-name format can use %_workingdir% and %_workingpath% from the app’s working folder. They are separate from each source file’s own folder. Slashes inside captured tag values use the replacement configured under Options → Files, rather than always becoming underscores. Literal backslashes in the new pattern still create destination folders.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• %10, an undefined numbered part, or a repeated number in the old pattern is rejected. Use each old-pattern number once, from %1 to %9.
  • Adjacent captures such as %1%2 have no separator and are ambiguous.
  • Files whose old names do not match are listed as No match, not changed. Matching files can still be renamed together in one undo step. Check each planned path and reported error before assuming every file was renamed.
  • Preview plans expire and are tied to the inputs, selection and source files. If the plan is stale or a file changed, run Preview again.
  • Avoid duplicate destinations and existing files with those names. Keep copies and inspect Edit → Undo for recorded renames.

docs.title: Filename → Tag
docs.text: Use Filename → Tag when the names contain reliable metadata but the tag fields are missing or wrong. A pattern captures pieces of each name into fields. It can read parent folders as well as the filename.

docs.title: Extract a track number and title
docs.text:
1. Save pending edits and select copied files named like 03 - Paper Boats.mp3.
  2. Choose Convert → Filename → Tag… (Alt+2; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).

  3. In Filename pattern, enter:

    %track% - %title%

  4. Choose Preview. Check for TRACK = 03 and TITLE = Paper Boats.

  5. Choose Apply to … files to save the matched files immediately.

The converter replaces fields named in the pattern and retains other fields. It does not rename the audio file. Files that do not match stay unchanged; the preview marks them No match, not changed.

docs.title: Match separators exactly
docs.text:
%track% names a destination field. - is literal text separating it from %title%; its spaces and punctuation must occur in the filename.

Filename Pattern Fields captured 03 - Paper Boats.mp3 %track% - %title% TRACK = 03; TITLE = Paper Boats Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.flac %artist% - %title% ARTIST = Juniper Vale; TITLE = Paper Boats 03_Paper Boats_demo.mp3 %track%_%title%_%dummy% TRACK = 03; TITLE = Paper Boats 03. Paper Boats.mp3 %track% - %title% No match

The entire candidate name must match. %dummy% consumes unwanted text without writing a field. Captures are not trimmed, so put fixed surrounding spaces in the pattern rather than capturing them into a field.

The normal pattern omits the audio extension. OpenTag removes the extension from the name before matching unless the pattern ends in that same literal extension. Thus %track% - %title%.mp3 also works for the MP3 example, but is less useful for a selection mixing formats.

docs.title: Read parent folders
docs.text:
For a layout such as:

Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights (2024)/03 - Paper Boats.mp3

use backslashes in the pattern, including on macOS and Linux:

%artist%\%album% (%year%)\%track% - %title%

The result includes ARTIST = Juniper Vale, ALBUM = Harbour Lights, YEAR = 2024, TRACK = 03 and TITLE = Paper Boats. Without an absolute root, the pattern reads the required trailing levels of the path; the earlier Music folder is not needed. A leading backslash or drive specification makes that root part of the match too.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• %artist%%title% is rejected because adjacent captures have no separator. Use a real delimiter from the names.
  • A delimiter repeated inside an artist or title can make the split ambiguous for your intended meaning. Check those rows in the preview.
  • This is a capture pattern, not a scripting expression or regex. For later cleanup, apply a separate field-formatting step.
  • Read-only underscore placeholders are not destinations here. Use ordinary field names and %dummy%.
  • Applying saves immediately. Keep copies and inspect operation errors and Edit → Undo for recorded changes.

docs.title: Tag → Filename
docs.text: Use Tag → Filename to give files consistent names from their tags. The same converter can build folders and move the files into them. Check that the source fields are correct before using them to construct paths.

docs.title: Rename a few tracks
docs.text:
1. Keep copies, save pending edits and select practice files.
  2. Choose Convert → Tag → Filename… (Alt+1; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).

  3. Enter this Format string:

    $num(%track%,2) - %title%

  4. Choose Preview. For track 3/8 and title Paper Boats, expect 03 - Paper Boats.mp3 for an MP3 file.

  5. Check every destination, then choose Apply to … files.

The source tags remain unchanged. The rename happens when applied; there is no separate Save tags step. The audio extension is retained, so usually leave it out of the expression. An expression already ending in that extension does not receive another copy.

docs.title: Understand the expression
docs.text:
Part Meaning %track% Read the track value, such as 3/8 $num(%track%,2) Keep its leading number and pad to at least two digits: 03 - Insert the literal separator, including the two spaces %title% Read the title

$num reads a number; it does not preserve a vinyl side such as B2. Preview those cases before using a numeric format on a mixed collection.

With artist Juniper Vale, album Harbour Lights, year 2024, track 3/8 and title Paper Boats:

Format string Result for an MP3 file %artist% - %title% Juniper Vale - Paper Boats.mp3 $num(%track%,3). %title% 003. Paper Boats.mp3 %album%\$num(%track%,2) - %title% Harbour Lights\03 - Paper Boats.mp3 %artist%\%album% (%year%)\$num(%track%,2) - %title% Juniper Vale\Harbour Lights (2024)\03 - Paper Boats.mp3

The backslashes in the last two rows separate folders on every platform.

docs.title: Build folders deliberately
docs.text:
A relative folder format creates the destination beneath the audio file's current folder. Use an absolute destination when reorganizing files from different locations into one collection. For example, on Windows:

D:\Music\%artist%\%album%\$num(%track%,2) - %title%

On macOS or Linux, use the intended absolute root, for example /Music/%artist%/%album%/$num(%track%,2) - %title%. Choose a writable location appropriate to the machine; the example root need not exist there.

Literal separators in the expression create folders. Separators originating inside tag values are treated as characters in a component and use the configured folder-separator replacement. Other forbidden filename characters are sanitized. See filename-mode rules.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• A missing title can produce an incomplete but valid name. Check the preview rather than assuming missing fields make the whole conversion fail.
  • Two files can produce the same destination when track or disc information is omitted. Include enough information to make each path unique.
  • Changing the selection or format invalidates the preview. Run it again. A changed file or occupied destination can still prevent applying a plan.
  • Moving a file may remove it from the list depending on Keep moved files. Inspect the destination folder before assuming the file disappeared.
  • Keep originals and inspect Edit → Undo for recorded renames.

docs.title: Tag → Tag
docs.text: Use Tag → Tag to copy or calculate one destination field from existing tags. Its preview refreshes as you change the field or format string, making it useful for learning an expression before saving it in an action.

docs.title: Fill missing album artists
docs.text:
1. Keep copies, save pending edits and select practice files.
  2. Choose Convert → Tag → Tag… (Alt+5; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).
  3. Enter ALBUMARTIST in Field.

  4. Enter this Format string:

    $if2(%albumartist%,%artist%)

  5. Wait for the preview to finish. An existing album artist should remain; a missing one should receive the artist value.

  6. Choose Apply to … files to write the reviewed values immediately.

$if2 chooses the first nonempty argument. With ARTIST = Juniper Vale, the result is Juniper Vale only when ALBUMARTIST is empty. Entering %artist% alone would replace existing album artists as well.

docs.title: Expressions to try
docs.text:
Destination field Format string Input Result ALBUMARTIST %artist% ARTIST = Juniper Vale Juniper Vale YEAR $left(%year%,4) YEAR = 2024-05-01 2024 TITLE $trim(%title%) TITLE = Paper Boats Paper Boats COMMENT Library copy Any existing comment Library copy TRACK $num(%track%,2) TRACK = 3/8 03

For ordinary metadata fields, two consecutive backslashes (\\) in the evaluated output separate values, as in Format Value. With that delimiter, each component is trimmed and empty components are dropped; if no values remain, the field is removed. The preview shows the surviving values joined with \\, or Field will be removed if none remain. Without the delimiter, a nonempty output is one value whose surrounding whitespace is kept.

A bare placeholder reads only the first existing value. For example, $meta_sep(artist,\\) writes the existing artists as separate values, while $meta_sep(artist,' & ') writes one joined value. Read the multivalue rules before replacing artist or composer lists. Filename/directory targets use the naming rules below instead of splitting metadata values.

An empty result removes the destination field. The preview labels that outcome Field will be removed. '' produces an apostrophe, not empty text; see quoting.

docs.title: Rename from the same dialog
docs.text:
The two special destinations are _FILENAME and _DIRECTORY:

Field Format string Effect _FILENAME $num(%track%,2) - %title% Build a filename and retain the audio extension _DIRECTORY %album% Rename the containing folder from the album

These destinations use filename evaluation: literal separators can create folders, while separators from field values use the configured replacement. An empty generated name disables applying the conversion.

A folder rename affects the folder itself, potentially including files outside the selection. Practice with a copied folder, and use Tag → Filename when reviewing a full file-and-folder layout is the goal.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Applying saves immediately, unlike editing the tag panel.
  • Changing the expression or field invalidates the previous result until the automatic preview finishes. Review the final version before applying.
  • At most the first 100 preview rows are displayed, even when more files are selected. Split a large unfamiliar collection into smaller batches.
  • _TAG, _ALL and technical information placeholders are not destination fields. Choose an ordinary tag field or one of the two naming targets.
  • Keep copies and inspect operation errors and Edit → Undo for recorded changes in the current desktop session.

docs.title: Text File → Tag
docs.text: Use Text File → Tag to import one structured text record per selected audio file. A mask assigns parts of each record to tag fields. Match by list order for a controlled selection, or include a filename/path key to connect records to files explicitly.

docs.title: Import two pasted records
docs.text:
1. Keep copies, save pending edits and select two practice files in the order Paper Boats, then North Pier.
  2. Choose Convert → Text File → Tag… (Alt+4; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).

  3. Set Text source to Pasted text and enter in Records to import:

    Paper Boats;Juniper Vale;3
North Pier;Juniper Vale;4

  4. Set Import mask to:

    %title%;%artist%;%track%

  5. Choose Preview and inspect every destination file, source line and captured field. The first selected file should receive track 3, and the second track 4.

  6. Choose Save tags to … files to write the reviewed values immediately.

Each named field is replaced with its captured value; fields absent from the mask are retained. The mask's semicolons are literal separators. It is not a spreadsheet CSV parser: quoting a cell does not automatically protect delimiters inside that cell.

docs.title: Read a text file
docs.text:
Set Text source to Text file, then choose Choose file… or enter a path in Source file. The path can itself be a format string:

%_folderpath%tracks.txt

It is evaluated from the first selected audio file. One source file is read for the whole selection; this expression does not independently read tracks.txt in every selected album folder. Process one album at a time when each folder has its own text listing.

UTF-8 and BOM-marked Unicode are detected first. Legacy encoding fallback (optional) selects how to decode older non-UTF-8 files, for example windows-1251 or windows-1252. It is used only when the source is not valid UTF-8. Check non-ASCII characters in the preview before applying.

docs.title: Match records by filename
docs.text:
When the records might be in a different order from the file list, add %_filename_ext% to the mask. For selected files 03.mp3 and 04.mp3, this text intentionally lists track 4 first:

04.mp3;North Pier;4
03.mp3;Paper Boats;3

Use:

%_filename_ext%;%title%;%track%

04.mp3 is matched to that selected filename regardless of its position. The key includes the extension but no folders. Two selected files with the same filename are ambiguous; use absolute paths instead.

For example, a record /Music/Harbour Lights/03.mp3;Paper Boats matches with:

%_path%;%title%

%_path% requires an absolute path. Backslashes and forward slashes are normalized for path-key matching. Match filename and path keys case-sensitively is checked initially; uncheck it only when the intended matching rule ignores case. It controls keys, not the literal punctuation of the mask or the capitalization of imported values.

docs.title: Import part of an album listing
docs.text:
With only 03.mp3 and 05.mp3 selected, use the same filename-key mask with this whole-album excerpt:

03.mp3;Paper Boats;3
04.mp3;North Pier;4

The row for unselected 04.mp3 is skipped. 03.mp3 receives title Paper Boats and track 3; selected 05.mp3 has no row and keeps its tags. The preview lists it as No match, not changed. A positional mask without a filename key cannot make this association.

docs.title: Shape the records
docs.text:
• Use %dummy% to skip an unwanted part: %dummy%;%title%;%artist%.
  • Repeat a field name to create multiple values: %title%;%artist%;%artist% captures two artist values.
  • Include a real separator between captures. %artist%%title% is rejected.
  • Match each complete line. Extra prefix/suffix text must be represented by literals or a %dummy% capture.
  • Captured whitespace is preserved. Put fixed padding in the mask or clean it in a later field-formatting step.

A positional import requires exactly one record per selected file, in the intended order. A keyed import can contain rows for files outside the selection; those rows are skipped. Selected files with no matching row keep their tags and appear as No match, not changed. This lets you select a few tracks from a whole-album text listing without deleting its other rows. If no row names a selected file, the plan reports that no changes are planned.

Both modes reject malformed records, duplicate selection paths and repeated matches for the same selected file before importing tags. A final line ending is allowed; an extra blank record is still a record, not an ignored comment. Inspect both matched and unmatched rows before applying a partial plan.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• This converter imports one record into several fields. To put an entire multiline file into one lyrics or comment field, use the Import Text File action instead.
  • Mask placeholders for technical properties cannot be written. The only supported underscore placeholders are the two matching keys, with at most one key in a mask.
  • Editing inputs, changing the selection or changing a source after preview requires a new preview. Check errors instead of repeatedly applying a stale plan.
  • Applying saves immediately. Keep originals and inspect Edit → Undo for recorded changes in the current desktop session.

docs.title: Fill missing album artists from a reviewed track credit
docs.text:
Uses Filter and Tag → Tag / Format Value

Works on Copied ordinary local files with a reviewed primary artist

Time About 5 minutes

Undo Recorded applied changes in the current desktop session; keep originals

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Your album has ARTIST, but no ALBUMARTIST. A player may group that album using Album Artist. Copying each track's artist is suitable only when that is the intended album-level credit. A compilation with a different artist per track usually needs one deliberately chosen common album artist instead.

This recipe uses the first Artist value as that primary credit. It does not decide who the album artist ought to be. Existing Album Artist values are excluded from the main selection.

The tables use JSON lists to show distinct values, including empty strings. Absent means no field. They describe core metadata snapshots; native formats can normalize empty values differently when saved.

ID ARTIST before ALBUMARTIST before Pass main filter? ALBUMARTIST after applying to matching rows A ["Juniper Vale"] Absent Yes ["Juniper Vale"] B ["Juniper Vale"] ["Harbour Collective"] No ["Harbour Collective"] C ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] Absent Yes ["Juniper Vale"] D Absent Absent No Absent E [""] Absent Yes Absent F ["Juniper Vale"] [""] No [""] G [" "] Absent Yes [" "] H ["","Mira Solberg"] Absent Yes Absent

E, G and H pass a presence test but do not supply a useful primary credit. Stop at the preview and fix or exclude those files. C intentionally uses only the first artist; preserve a joint credit with the list-aware variation below instead.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Work on a copied album. Save or discard pending edits before opening the converter. Inspect its track artists and decide whether one primary artist per file is the right album-level policy. For a compilation, enter the common reviewed Album Artist through the tag panel and save instead.

  2. Choose Edit → Unselect all, show the filter and enter:

    ALBUMARTIST MISSING AND ARTIST PRESENT

    Wait for filtering, or press Enter when auto-apply is disabled. MISSING means no values; a present empty string is not missing. Filtering can inspect pending metadata, which is another reason to resolve edits first. 3. Select only the intended visible practice rows. A filter does not clear earlier hidden selections. Exclude empty or whitespace-only artists and credits that should not become an album artist. 4. Choose Convert → Tag → Tag…, enter ALBUMARTIST in Field, and use:

    $if2(%albumartist%,%artist%)

  3. Inspect the preview. %artist% is the first Artist value. An empty result is a reason to stop and investigate, not a request to guess a name.

  4. Apply only the reviewed practice selection. This converter writes immediately; it does not leave the result waiting for Save tags. Reload and inspect the saved fields before processing the rest of the album.

The same format string can be a Format Value action with Field ALBUMARTIST. A quick action's Apply action also writes immediately; it is not the converter's preview. Test the definition on a copy before putting it into a larger group.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The filter chooses files with no Album Artist values and at least one Artist value. PRESENT does not require useful nonempty text; E and G demonstrate why a preview and a human credit decision are still required.

$if2 returns its first nonempty argument. It reads Album Artist first and uses Artist when that first text is empty. Ordinary placeholders read the first value, so this is a primary-credit rule, not a copy-every-artist rule. If the first Artist value is empty, a later nonempty Artist is not chosen automatically, as H shows. Spaces are nonempty text. The single-value Format Value result is not implicitly trimmed.

The filter is what protects existing lists here. Running the scalar formula on every file could reduce a multi-value Album Artist to its first value. Do not treat $if2 as an exact whole-field/list preservation operation.

docs.title: Preserve all credited Artist values
docs.text:
If the album genuinely has a joint credit, keep the same reviewed missing-field selection but preview this expression:

$meta_sep(ARTIST,$char(92)$char(92))

$meta_sep joins every Artist value with two backslashes. Format Value splits that result into separate metadata values, trims each part, and drops empty parts when the separator is present. Without it, a nonempty single result retains its spaces. It is not a universal lossless copy of arbitrary text containing literal double-backslash pairs.

ARTIST values Resulting ALBUMARTIST values ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] [" Juniper Vale ","", " Mira Solberg "] ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] [""] Absent [" "] [" "]

docs.title: Include blank-looking existing fields
docs.text: A field containing "" or spaces is present. Inspect its full value list in Extended tags before changing the filter or clearing it. A test for an empty value can also match a list that has useful other values. Review those lists rather than applying a broader query to the whole library.

docs.title: Recover from the wrong credit
docs.text: Read Edit → Undo …'s operation label and count in the current desktop session. History is not a permanent backup and may cover a larger batch than the current selection. Inspect any pending edits afterward; saving them can replace the restored values. Keep copies for recovery beyond that session.

docs.title: Your library in a spreadsheet
docs.text: Uses: File → Export and a CSV import in your spreadsheet · Works on: selected files in the current file list · Time: about 5 minutes for a sample · Undo: audio is unchanged; keep earlier reports because export can replace them

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
You want a table of your music to inspect missing titles, share an album list or compare tags outside OpenTag. Export creates a text report from the selected files. It does not scan a whole collection automatically, even when the Library cache is enabled.

In OpenTag In a carefully imported spreadsheet Title Paper, "folded" Boats One title cell containing that comma and those quotes Track 03 Text 03, retaining the leading zero Artist Juniper Vale Its own Artist column

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Save pending edits so the report represents your saved metadata. Select a small practice set first. Check the selection count and file-list order.
  2. Choose File → Export…, then select CSV (spreadsheet).
  3. Set Export file name to a new destination ending in .csv. Choose a separate report location and filename; do not point it at audio, lyrics sidecars or a report you still need.
  4. Leave Append data off and Create one output file per off for this first single table. Choose Export. It also saves the current export configuration and preferences.
  5. In your spreadsheet, use its text/CSV import facility to open the report. Choose UTF-8, a comma delimiter and double quote as text qualifier. Exact dialog labels depend on the spreadsheet and platform.
  6. Import columns whose spelling matters as Text, including Track, Disc, Year and identifiers. Inspect the preview before loading the table.
  7. Check the first and last selected files, a quoted title, an accented name and a track with a leading zero. Save your working spreadsheet as a separate file if you will add calculations or notes.

The bundled export has Path, Title, Artist, Album, Album artist, Track, Disc, Year, Genre and Length columns. It uses UTF-8, CRLF record endings and the current file-list input order. Write BOM is a separate setting under Options → Export; enable it if your receiving program needs a BOM to recognize Unicode when opening the file directly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
CSV protects a comma inside a cell by surrounding the cell with double quotes. A quote inside that cell becomes two quotes. For example:

Field value Text written for that CSV cell Paper Boats "Paper Boats" Paper, "folded" Boats "Paper, ""folded"" Boats" 03 "03"

Quotes describe the table structure; they do not force the spreadsheet's data type. Automatic conversion can still turn 03 into 3, 2/8 into a date, or a long numeric identifier into a rounded number. Reimport as Text if needed. Formatting a converted cell afterward may not recover its original spelling. Treat arbitrary imported metadata as text when you do not intend it to become spreadsheet formulas.

A multiline field can span physical text-file lines inside one quoted cell. The number of lines in a text editor can therefore exceed the number of table records. Use the spreadsheet's actual import preview to inspect the table rather than splitting the file at every comma or line break.

docs.title: Make a three-column table with a stable file key
docs.text:
The built-in report already includes Path. Keep a file key in a smaller report too, especially if you will sort the spreadsheet. Duplicate an export configuration and replace the copy's Export template with:

$filename(csv,utf-8)"Path","Title","Track"$char(13)$char(10)$loop(1)"$replace(%_path%,","")","$replace(%title%,","")","$replace(%track%,","")"$char(13)$char(10)$loopend()

For /Music/01.flac, title Paper, "folded" Boats, track 03, followed by /Music/02.flac, title Café at Low Tide, track 04, it writes:

"Path","Title","Track"
"/Music/01.flac","Paper, ""folded"" Boats","03"
"/Music/02.flac","Café at Low Tide","04"

These example paths illustrate the template; real output uses the actual audio paths on your platform. $loop(1) repeats the row in input order. The literal header outside the loop appears once. $char(13)$char(10) adds each CRLF record ending, and $replace doubles quotes in every cell. Keep that escaping for every added arbitrary field, including Track.

docs.title: Use a semicolon delimiter
docs.text: In the three-column template, replace the literal commas between quoted cells in both header and body with semicolons. Keep the commas inside $replace(...); those separate scripting arguments, not CSV columns. Choose semicolon in the spreadsheet's import dialog too. Regional defaults do not automatically change OpenTag's comma-based built-in template.

docs.title: Repeat the report later
docs.text: Use a new report name when you want a dated snapshot. Keep Append data off for a complete replacement table: appending a whole CSV template writes another header and repeats the selected records. Export does not deduplicate tracks or merge spreadsheet changes. See the export controls before using partitioned reports for several albums.

docs.title: Can I edit the spreadsheet and import it back?
docs.text:
Editing or saving this report does not update the audio files. Keep a separate original report, retain file keys and preserve text types while planning changes. There is no automatic two-way link.

Text File → Tag can import deliberately prepared one-record-per-file text using an explicit mask and filename/path keys. It does not decode general spreadsheet CSV quoting, doubled quotes or multiline cells. Do not feed the exported CSV back unchanged and assume a round trip. Prepare a simpler unambiguous listing, try copied files, and inspect every previewed association with the tracklist recipe.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Result Next step One huge column Choose the actual comma or semicolon delimiter during import Shifted columns around a title Check quote escaping and the text qualifier; do not split at every comma 03 became 3 Reimport as Text from the original CSV Garbled accents Select UTF-8; use Write BOM if direct opening needs it Missing files Check which rows were selected at export time; the cache is not a collection-wide export source Repeated headers Start a new output or replace it with Append data off Audio unchanged after spreadsheet edits Export is a report; a separate reviewed import must write tags

Export creates or replaces an external file immediately. Edit → Undo for tag edits is not a general recovery mechanism for a replaced CSV. Keep older reports you need before writing their paths again.

docs.title: Read disc numbers from CD1 and CD2 folders
docs.text: Use a consistent folder convention to fill DISCNUMBER, while leaving unrelated folders' existing disc values alone. This recipe accepts CD1, CD02, CD-03 and similar names with positive decimal numbers. It reads the containing folder's name; it does not rename that folder or number tracks.

docs.title: Inspect the folder and current value
docs.text:
Use copied local files with at most one existing numeric DISCNUMBER value. Exclude text containing two consecutive backslashes: Format Value interprets those as value separators even when its fallback keeps existing text. The practice cases start at DISCNUMBER=7 so that a nonmatch visibly keeps it:

Containing folder name DISCNUMBER before DISCNUMBER after CD1 7 1 cd002 7 2 CD-03 7 3 Extras 7 7 CD0 7 7 CD2 bonus 7 7

%_directory% is the immediate folder name, not its parent or the whole path. If tracks are inside CD1/FLAC, it reads FLAC; this recipe will not look upward for the disc folder. Inspect the actual layout first.

docs.title: Preview a guarded expression
docs.text:
1. Save pending edits and select one copied file from CD1.
  2. Open Convert → Tag → Tag… and set Field to DISCNUMBER.
  3. Enter the expression below and wait for the preview.
  4. Compare matched and unmatched practice folders before applying to a batch.
  5. Choose Apply to … files only when the reviewed values are wanted.
$if($stricmp($regexp(%_directory%,'\ACD[ _-]*0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$1'),%_directory%),%discnumber%,$num($regexp(%_directory%,'\ACD[ _-]*0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$1'),1))

The same expression can be saved as a Format Value action with Field DISCNUMBER. A saved group is only a workflow; applying it writes the selected files immediately. The converter also writes when applied, rather than leaving its successful result waiting for Save tags.

docs.title: Build the expression in understandable pieces
docs.text:
The extraction inside the expression is:

$regexp(%_directory%,'\ACD[ _-]*0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$1')
Folder name Extraction result before the guard cd002 2 CD-03 3 Extras Extras CD0 CD0
  • \A and \z restrict the match to the whole folder name.
  • CD ignores case in this function's default mode.
  • [ _-]* allows spaces, underscores or hyphens before the number.
  • 0* consumes leading zeros. ([1-9][0-9]*) captures a positive number; an all-zero disc or a suffix such as bonus does not fit.
  • $1 returns only the captured digits.

Do not apply that extraction alone to every file: $regexp returns its original input when there is no match, so Extras would become the disc value. The final expression compares extraction with the original folder. Equality means this particular pattern did not remove the CD prefix, so $if keeps the old %discnumber%. A successful digits-only capture differs from the original CD… name; $num(…,1) then produces an unpadded number.

This guard works because every successful capture necessarily changes this pattern's input. It is not a general test for an arbitrary regex match.

docs.title: Other source layouts
docs.text:
For a strictly reviewed CD… selection, Guess Values can use Source %_directory% and Guessing pattern CD%discnumber%. That pattern is literal and case-sensitive and does not validate digits: CDfoo captures foo. It also retains captured spacing. Prefer the guarded expression when a mixed folder selection should leave nonmatches unchanged.

For deeper folder structures, review Filename → Tag and its folder-level patterns instead of making this expression assume an unseen parent layout. A file's name and its containing folder are different sources.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• An existing list of disc values is not preserved by a bare %discnumber%: the fallback reads its first value. Use the stated single-value scope.
  • This does not calculate a total disc count. Native formats have their own number/total representation; inspect field storage.
  • A positive numeric shape does not establish the album's actual disc count or the intended playing order.
  • Use Edit → Undo … for a recorded conversion/action in the current desktop session. Keep copied files for recovery beyond that session.

docs.title: Embed each folder's folder.jpg
docs.text: Copy an album-folder image into its audio files so the picture can travel with them. A picture already displayed as Folder image / Not embedded in the file is still an external file; seeing it in the tag panel does not mean it is inside the audio.

docs.title: Prepare one album copy
docs.text:
Put the intended image in the copied album folder as folder.jpg. Check that it opens as a real supported image, and select a few copied audio files with a writable artwork-capable tag, such as MP3 with ID3v2 enabled. Keep the separate high-resolution image and original audio files.

Start with the exact filename rather than a broad wildcard. When several album folders are selected, each needs its own image in the expected place. This action does not find online artwork or choose an image by album title.

docs.title: Run the import once
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits and select the practice audio files.
  2. Choose Actions → Actions (Quick)…, then Import Cover from File.
  3. Enter the settings below. The filename expression includes the extension.
  4. Choose Apply action and inspect the operation result.
  5. Select each practice file separately and inspect its embedded cover set.
Setting Value Image filename format %_folderpath%folder.jpg Import cover as Front Cover Delete existing covers Off

%_folderpath% already ends with the file's native folder separator. Appending folder.jpg reads that folder's image; it does not introduce a second separator. A relative folder.jpg also resolves beside each audio file. An absolute filename chosen with Browse instead reads the same image for every selected file.

The action writes immediately. There is no later Save tags step for the completed import. Saving an equivalent group with Save groups only stores the workflow; applying the checked group runs it.

docs.title: Understand adding versus replacing
docs.text:
With deletion off, existing artwork stays and a new front-cover picture is added. A repeated import can add another picture. It is not an automatic “replace the old front cover” operation.

Existing embedded pictures Delete existing covers Source image Pictures after successful import, or retained after refusal 0 Off Valid 1 1 Off Valid 2 2 Off Valid 3 2 On Valid 1 2 On Invalid image 2

These are practice MP3 cases with supported picture roles/descriptions. The deletion-on row removes all existing pictures, including booklet and back images, before adding the new front. Use Manage covers to replace one selected image while keeping the others instead.

A missing or invalid image is refused before that removal step, but a later write failure still needs inspection. Read all file errors and keep backups; a multi-file run is not one atomic write. Ordinary action warnings do not stop later actions/groups, so a following adjustment may still act on a file's old artwork if its import warned.

docs.title: Use a wildcard only when needed
docs.text:
For an explicit local naming convention, %_folderpath%front*.png can select the first importable matching image in natural, case-insensitive name order.

For example, this folder's candidates are considered as follows:

Candidate What it contains Result for front*.png front1.png Plain text, not an image Skipped Front2.PNG Valid PNG Chosen front3.png A folder Skipped front10.png Valid PNG Later valid candidate

The action does not compare image quality or recognize which picture is the correct front. A broad * can select unwanted artwork. Filename matching uses the final component; folder components are literal existing paths, not a recursive search pattern. See Import Cover for accepted formats and path-placeholder behavior.

docs.title: Verify and recover
docs.text:
The audio format must support embedded pictures; ID3v1 alone cannot store them. Some formats cannot preserve every role or description. Check format capabilities and the saved result instead of assuming a folder image proves a successful embed.

Use Edit → Undo … for a recorded import in the current desktop session. Undo is not a replacement for retaining the original files. These action paths require local files; provider-document action groups are unavailable in the current baseline.
