docs.title: Lower-case, dash-separated filenames
docs.text: Uses: Filename → Filename · Works on: copied local files with useful existing names · Time: about 5 minutes for a small batch · Undo: recorded renames in the current desktop session; keep originals

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
You want a consistent lowercase filename stem with hyphens instead of spaces or underscores. Keep the mixed-case title in the tag: a filename policy does not need to become a metadata policy. This can be useful for an established transfer or naming convention, but it does not certify compatibility with a particular website, USB device or filesystem.

Existing filename Expected destination 03 Paper Boats.mp3 03-paper-boats.mp3 04_Lanterns On The Water.flac 04-lanterns-on-the-water.flac 05 Café At Low Tide.MP3 05-café-at-low-tide.MP3 06 Paper Boats.mp3 06-paper--boats.mp3

The converter retains the original audio extension, including its spelling. The third example lowers the stem while keeping .MP3. Accents remain; this is not an ASCII-only or accent-removal recipe. The last row deliberately shows that replacing individual spaces can produce repeated hyphens.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Keep the originals elsewhere and select a few copied local audio files. Save or discard pending tag edits before renaming. If a filter is active, inspect the intended selection, including any previously selected hidden rows.
  2. Choose Convert → Filename → Filename….

  3. Set Old filename pattern to:

    %1

  4. Set New filename pattern to:

    $lower($replace(%1, ,-,_,-))

  5. Choose Preview. Compare every full destination with the table and your actual folder contents. The single space after the first comma is the search text; it must remain a real space in the expression.

  6. Choose Rename … files only for the reviewed small plan. Inspect the operation result, the actual destination names and the unchanged tag fields.

Paths change when the rename runs. There is no subsequent Save tags step for these names. Editing an input or changing the selection requires another preview; an expired plan or changed file can also require it. A preview is not a reservation of the destination.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The old pattern %1 captures the current basename without the audio extension. It is a numbered capture, with no trailing percent sign: %1% is not the same syntax. It does not read TITLE or ARTIST.

Read the new pattern from the inside out:

Part Meaning %1 Reuse the captured basename $replace(%1, ,-,_,-) Replace each ordinary space with -, then each underscore with - $lower(...) Lowercase the resulting text

Commas separate function arguments. The first pair has a space as its search string and a hyphen as its replacement. The second pair does the same for _. Existing hyphens, punctuation and non-ASCII letters are not removed by those replacements. Tabs are not ordinary spaces either.

This route works from names even if the title tags are empty. It does not lowercase tags or rename the parent album folder. To derive names from reviewed tags instead, use the variation below and its different converter.

docs.title: Collapse runs of spaces, underscores and hyphens
docs.text:
If repeated hyphens are unwanted, keep Old filename pattern %1 and use:

$lower($regexp(%1,'[ _-]+',-))

For 06 Paper Boats.mp3, this produces 06-paper-boats.mp3. [ _-]+ matches one or more ordinary spaces, underscores or hyphens; putting the hyphen last makes it literal in that character class. This also collapses an intentionally doubled hyphen. It does not trim a leading/trailing separator or normalize all Unicode whitespace.

docs.title: Derive a name from saved tags
docs.text:
When TRACK = 3/8 and TITLE = Paper Boats, use Tag → Filename… instead, with:

$num(%track%,2)-$lower($replace(%title%, ,-,_,-))

For an MP3 this gives 03-paper-boats.mp3. This route reads the tags, not the captured old basename. Check missing titles, nonnumeric tracks and multi-value fields before applying it. $num reads a leading number; it does not preserve a vinyl-side label such as B2.

docs.title: Keep the original spelling when case is significant
docs.text: Remove the outer $lower(...) and use only the replacement expression. That is a different naming policy, useful when deliberate capitals matter. Do not rename a larger set merely because lowercase looked acceptable in one example. A case-only spelling change can behave differently on different volumes; check the actual operation result and the name your file manager shows.

docs.title: Before using the result elsewhere
docs.text:
Two different names can collapse to one destination after lowercasing or separator replacement. Include an established distinguishing track/disc part and compare the complete paths. Do not delete another file to make a refused rename succeed. If the only intended change is capitalization, try one copy first on the actual destination volume rather than treating it as proof for every platform.

A lowercase name can still be too long or contain characters a receiving system dislikes. Follow the portable-name recipe for a more explicit character and length policy. Test the resulting copies on the receiving device; a successful rename is not a playback test.

Use Edit → Undo and its operation label for recorded renames in the current desktop session. Keep original copies for recovery after quitting.

docs.title: Keep multi-disc albums distinct when renaming
docs.text:
Uses: Tag → Filename, DISCNUMBER, TRACK and $num.

Works on: A copied local album with checked disc and track numbers.

Time: About 10 minutes for a two-disc practice selection.

Undo: Apply changes paths immediately; use recorded session Edit → Undo where available and keep untouched originals.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Disc 1 and disc 2 both start with track 1. They may even both contain a title such as Intro. A filename made from track and title alone can therefore produce the same target twice. Keep the disc number in the folder or filename instead of changing the original track numbering to hide that information.

Start with copied files in one practice folder. Save or deliberately discard pending edits. Inspect ALBUM, DISCNUMBER, TRACK and TITLE in Extended tags; the converter reads tags, not a guessed disc number from the filename.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Select the copied album. Confirm the intended selection, including any rows hidden by a filter.
  2. Choose Convert → Tag → Filename… (Alt+1; Alt is ⌥ Option on macOS).

  3. Enter:

    %album%\CD$num(%discnumber%,2)\$num(%track%,2) - %title%

  4. Choose Preview. In the following table, all inputs use ALBUM = Harbour Lights. Destinations are relative to each source file's current containing folder, with / showing folder levels. The absent-disc row demonstrates a result to correct before applying, not an inferred disc.

    Scroll the table sideways on a narrow screen to read the complete destinations.

    Disc number Track Title Source name Relative destination 1/2 1/8 Intro old.mp3 Harbour Lights/CD01/01 - Intro.mp3 2/2 1/9 Intro old.mp3 Harbour Lights/CD02/01 - Intro.mp3 12 10 Last Harbour old.flac Harbour Lights/CD12/10 - Last Harbour.flac Absent 1 Intro old.mp3 Harbour Lights/CD00/01 - Intro.mp3

  5. Confirm actual disc metadata, folder roots and every complete destination. If a disc value is missing or wrong, leave the preview and correct/save that metadata deliberately. Then run Preview again.

  6. Apply only the checked small plan with Apply to … files. Inspect both disc folders and operation errors. Paths change immediately; Save tags is not an additional rename confirmation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
%album% supplies the album folder. The literal CD and the padded leading disc number create CD01, CD02, and so on. The next backslash starts the filename within that disc folder. Track padding starts again from the actual track tag of each file; the converter does not renumber the album.

A stored slash value such as 2/2 is one text value: $num reads its leading 2 and does not include the total. An absent/nonnumeric disc also yields numeric zero, producing CD00. Width 2 is a minimum, not a two-digit limit. No total is inferred from how many files are currently selected.

The two Intro examples now have distinct written destinations because their disc folders differ. This illustrates the naming rule; it is not a universal collision or overwrite guarantee. Review existing files, actual filesystem behavior and any error reports before trusting a larger reorganization.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
If disc folders should be omitted for files whose disc field is absent, choose this explicit conditional after reviewing that policy:

%album%\$if(%discnumber%,CD$num(%discnumber%,2)\,)$num(%track%,2) - %title%

For TRACK = 1, TITLE = Intro and no disc field, the relative result is

Harbour Lights/01 - Intro.mp3. With disc 2/2, it is

Harbour Lights/CD02/01 - Intro.mp3. The backslash belongs inside the selected branch; the empty branch contributes no extra disc folder. A present text value 0 still takes the present branch and creates CD00; this is a presence condition, not a test that the number is valid.

To keep one album folder while preserving disc identity in each filename:

%album%\$num(%discnumber%,2)-$num(%track%,2) - %title%

For the second practice row, expect Harbour Lights/02-01 - Intro.mp3. This changes the path convention, not the saved DISCNUMBER or TRACK. If you prefer artist folders too, build that outer level after following the artist/album recipe.

docs.title: Recovery and common mistakes
docs.text:
A relative path is anchored at each input's containing folder. Files already in separate disc folders do not automatically converge on one album root; a relative expression can create another nested album beneath each disc. Use an intentionally chosen absolute root when consolidation is the goal.

Do not include the source extension unnecessarily: the host retains it. Moving only audio files does not promise to move folder images, cue sheets, playlists or other sidecars. Depending on Keep moved files, a moved track can leave the list while still existing at the shown destination.

Changing the expression or selection requires a new preview. Applying can report partial outcomes; inspect which files moved. Use Edit → Undo for recorded renames in the same desktop session, verify the original paths, and keep copies for recovery if a later file occupies an old name.

docs.title: Keep filenames portable
docs.text: Uses: Tag → Filename with $validate, $replace and trimming · Works on: copied local files with reviewed track/title fields · Time: about 10 minutes for a small album · Undo: recorded renames in this desktop session; retain originals

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A title can contain punctuation that is useful in metadata but unsuitable for a filename on another system. Choose a naming policy for the copy you will transfer while preserving the title tag. This recipe replaces a defined character set and trims trailing dots/spaces; it does not establish that every generated path is valid on every filesystem or device.

The examples use TRACK = 3/8, and show MP3 destinations. · marks a significant ordinary space in the input column; type actual spaces.

TITLE Expected destination Paper: Boats? 03 - Paper- Boats-.mp3 Harbour/Live 03 - Harbour-Live.mp3 Harbour\Live 03 - Harbour-Live.mp3 Low Tide...·· 03 - Low Tide.mp3 Café at Low Tide 03 - Café at Low Tide.mp3

The first row keeps two resulting hyphens: this rule changes characters, not the title's meaning or punctuation style. Accents are retained.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Work on copied files and keep the originals elsewhere. Check TRACK and TITLE in Extended tags…; use meaningful values before deriving names. Save or discard pending edits, then select only the intended copies.
  2. Choose Convert → Tag → Filename….

  3. Put this in Format string, without adding the audio extension:

    $num(%track%,2) - $trimright($replace($validate(%title%,-),'\',-),' .')

  4. Choose Preview. Compare complete destination paths, not only the text of the title. Inspect the actual destination folder for existing files and compare the selected rows for repeated resulting names.

  5. Apply only the reviewed small plan with Apply to … files. Read all errors and inspect the resulting filenames and unchanged title tags.

The rename applies immediately. A later Save tags does not confirm or finish it. If the selection or expression changes, preview again; a stale plan or changed source can also prevent applying it. Leave a refused plan and inspect the cause rather than forcing a different file out of the way.

docs.title: Understand the expression in pieces
docs.text:
Read the nested title expression from the inside out:

Part What it does $validate(%title%,-) Replace each of / ? * " < > and the vertical-bar and colon characters with - $replace(...,'\',-) Also replace literal backslashes with -; apostrophes quote that search text $trimright(...,' .') Remove trailing ordinary spaces and periods; the quoted argument is a set of characters $num(%track%,2) Read the leading track number and pad it to at least two digits - Put a visible separator between that number and the cleaned title

$validate has a specific replacement set. It does not replace a backslash, shorten names, reserve a destination, recognize device names, or decide whether two paths refer to the same file. Its replacement may contain several characters; each offending character receives the whole replacement.

Filename evaluation has further handling of tag-derived separators, forbidden characters and control characters. The explicit replacements above state the desired appearance before those rules are applied. The Files options govern the default replacement for separators inside tag values when you do not replace them explicitly. That default is different from separators you deliberately write between expression components to create folders.

docs.title: Use a different visible replacement
docs.text: Changing only the two replacement arguments from - to _ makes the policy use underscores. Change both $validate and the explicit backslash replacement if the result should treat those characters consistently. Choosing an empty replacement removes the characters and can join words: A/B becomes AB under $validate(%title%,) in ordinary text evaluation. Choose the intended result before renaming.

docs.title: Shorten a title component deliberately
docs.text:
For a known transfer convention, this variation limits the cleaned title part to at most 80 Unicode scalar values and trims its resulting end:

$num(%track%,2) - $trimright($left($replace($validate(%title%,-),'\',-),80),' .')

The track prefix and retained extension add more characters. 80 is an example policy, not a filesystem limit or a guarantee about the full path. A long parent folder still contributes to that path. Unicode scalar counts are not encoded byte counts; combining marks can count separately from the letters they decorate. Shortening can also erase the part that made two titles distinct. Inspect every complete destination afterward.

docs.title: Preserve folder boundaries you intended
docs.text:
The recipe outputs one filename in each source file's containing folder. If you add literal folders, keep the component-cleaning expression inside the filename or folder component it is meant to clean. For example, %album%\ written before the recipe's number/title output deliberately creates an album folder beneath each source folder. It does not gather separate source folders into one common root automatically.

Do not apply $validate to an entire intended path and expect its slashes to keep creating folders: slashes are in that function's replacement set. Use explicit path components and a reviewed root. See format strings in filenames before extending a one-folder recipe.

docs.title: Limits to check in the real destination
docs.text:
Question What this recipe establishes Are the listed punctuation characters replaced? Yes, according to the expression and actual field text Is every title complete and meaningful? No; inspect missing/empty/whitespace-only metadata and truncation Are generated names distinct? No; different source text can collapse to the same cleaned result Is the full path within a destination's limits? No; folder length, encoding and receiving system rules also matter Will reserved names, trailing characters and case behavior all be accepted? No; this is a component transformation, not a platform filesystem validator Will the receiving player accept the file? No; naming is separate from format, codec, artwork and player support

For example, A/B and A:B both clean to A-B. A distinguishing track or disc can help, but it does not make every possible input unique. Keep case sensitivity, existing destinations and actual folder roots in the review instead of treating character replacement as collision prevention.

Use Edit → Undo for recorded renames in the current desktop session; read its label and keep the originals beyond the session. Verify one copied album on the actual receiving system before repeating the chosen policy.

docs.title: Zero-padded track numbers in filenames
docs.text: Uses Tag → Filename, $num Works on any files with a TRACK tag Time 2 minutes Undo Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Your file names start with the track number, but some have one digit and some two, and a few also have the total. File managers and car stereos sort them in the wrong order:

Before After 1 Low Tide.mp3 01 Low Tide.mp3 10 Bonus Light.mp3 10 Bonus Light.mp3 2 Lanterns on the Water.mp3 02 Lanterns on the Water.mp3 3-12 Paper Boats.mp3 03 Paper Boats.mp3

Sorted as text, 10 comes before 2. With two digits everywhere, it doesn't.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
Try this on a copy of a few files first. Check the results before applying it to your library; use Edit → Undo in the same session to reverse the recorded changes. Keep the originals as a backup.

  1. Select the files (Cmd+A / Ctrl+A selects all of them).
  2. Choose Convert → Tag → Filename… (Alt+1; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).

  3. Enter this format string:

    $num(%track%,2) %title%

  4. Click Preview, check the new names, then click Apply.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
%track% is the track number as stored in the tag. It can be 2, 02 or 2/12, because many programs store the total after a slash.

$num(x,2) reads the number at the start of x and writes it with at least two digits:

TRACK tag $num(%track%,2) 2 02 02 02 2/12 02 10 10 112 112 (never cut short)

Everything after the first non-digit is ignored, which is how /12 disappears. %title% adds the title, and OpenTag keeps the extension.

Check for files without a track number first

A file without a TRACK tag, or with a vinyl-style track like B2, gets 00. To find such files before renaming, type this into the filter (F3 shows it):

track MATCHES ^[^0-9] OR track MISSING

Number them with Auto-numbering or by hand, then come back.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
Three digits for long compilations or audiobooks

$num(%track%,3) %title%

Disc number in front, only when there is one

[$num(%discnumber%,1)-]$num(%track%,2) %title%

gives 2-05 Salt & Cedar.mp3 on disc 2, and 05 Salt & Cedar.mp3 on an album without disc numbers. The optional section […] disappears when DISCNUMBER is empty.

A separator after the number

$num(%track%,2) - %artist% - %title%

Pad the number in the tag too

To store 02 in the tag itself, use Convert → Tag → Tag… (Alt+5) with the field TRACK and the format string $num(%track%,2). Most players don't need it, but some car stereos sort by the tag text.

docs.title: Shrink oversized covers without enlarging small ones
docs.text: Reduce the longer side of large embedded images to at most 600 pixels while keeping their proportions. This recipe changes the pictures inside selected audio files; it leaves a separate folder.jpg untouched.

docs.title: Choose the scope before applying
docs.text:
Adjust Cover as an action affects all embedded pictures in each selected file, including back covers and booklet images. If only selected front pictures should change, use Manage covers…, select those rows and choose Adjust… there instead; its changes wait for that dialog's OK.

Keep original copies before shrinking or converting images. Resampling can remove detail, and a small source cannot regain detail by being enlarged. A player that requires a square or JPEG image needs a different explicit choice, not an assumption that every resize produces one.

docs.title: Apply a maximum-size proportional resize
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits and select a few copied practice files.
  2. Choose Actions → Actions (Quick)…, then Adjust Cover.
  3. Use these settings and inspect their scope once more.
  4. Choose Apply action and inspect dimensions and file errors afterward.
Setting Value Image format Original Quality High (90 for JPEG) Resize cover On Size in pixels 600 Size policy Maximum size Scaling Scale proportionally

Quality applies when encoding JPEG. It does not select dimensions or control PNG compression. With Original format, an already small image keeps its format and bytes when no resize is needed.

Original width Original height Result width Result height 1600 1000 600 375 800 1200 400 600 1200 1200 600 600 400 400 400 400

For a 1600 × 1000 picture, 600/1600 is the scale, so the other side becomes 1000 × 600/1600 = 375. The longer side controls the maximum. The 400 × 400 picture is already within it and is not enlarged.

Picture type and description remain associated with adjusted artwork. An action can resize several pictures in one file; inspect all of them rather than only the image currently displayed first.

docs.title: Distinguish maximum, minimum and square policies
docs.text:
These examples all use Size in pixels 600, but change the other controls:

Original width Original height Size policy Scaling Result width Result height 1200 800 Maximum size Scale proportionally 600 400 1200 800 Minimum size Scale proportionally 900 600 1200 800 Maximum size Scale to square 600 600 1200 800 Maximum size Crop to square 600 600 400 200 Maximum size Crop to square 400 200 400 200 Minimum size Crop to square 600 600

Minimum size matches the shorter side and can enlarge an image. Scale to square stretches it; Crop to square keeps proportions while discarding excess around the center. Under Maximum size, an already-small image stays unchanged even when a square scaling choice is selected. Check the result instead of using that combination to force every small cover square.

docs.title: Choose encoding deliberately
docs.text:
Original keeps a supported writable original format. Select JPEG or PNG when a new encoding is intended or the original format cannot be written. JPEG does not preserve transparency; inspect its appearance before replacing transparent originals. PNG can preserve it. Changing a filename extension alone does not convert image bytes.

A JPEG whose format and dimensions remain the same is left byte-for-byte unchanged, even if Quality was changed. Quality alone is therefore not a “recompress all JPEGs” command. When conversion or resizing occurs, file size still depends on content, dimensions and encoding; a quality number is not a guaranteed byte budget.

docs.title: Save timing and recovery
docs.text:
The action writes when run. Save groups stores a reusable setup without running it; applying its checked group does the work. In Manage covers…, Adjust stages replacement images and OK commits the plan. A direct cover window Adjust cover… has its own immediate operation.

Inspect errors and saved artwork on the intended player. A successful core resize is not proof that a particular device accepts that size, format or picture role. Use Edit → Undo … for recorded writes in the current desktop session and keep original images/audio for recovery beyond it.

docs.title: Split an Artist - Title credit stored in TITLE
docs.text: Extract an artist and track title when TITLE contains a predictable credit such as Juniper Vale - Paper Boats. Use Guess Values for the extraction, then trim the two captured fields. This changes metadata; it does not rename the audio file.

docs.title: Prepare a small practice selection
docs.text:
Use copied files with one TITLE value per file and at most one existing ARTIST value. Inspect the existing artist: extraction will replace it when the source matches. The separator in this recipe is one space, a hyphen, and one space: -.

For the expected results below, · marks an ordinary space inside quoted values. It is a display marker, not text to type.

TITLE before ARTIST before ARTIST after TITLE after Juniper Vale - Paper Boats Old credit Juniper Vale Paper Boats ··AC/DC - North Pier·· Old credit AC/DC North Pier Paper Boats Juniper Vale Juniper Vale Paper Boats ··Paper Boats·· ··Juniper Vale·· Juniper Vale Paper Boats Kofi - Tide - Quiet Harbour Old credit Kofi Tide - Quiet Harbour

The final row shows the ambiguity: the parser uses the first delimiter that permits a full match, not knowledge of artist names. If Kofi - Tide is the intended artist, this pattern is wrong for that file. Choose another source, edit that file manually, or use a separately tested pattern for that layout.

docs.title: Run extraction on one copy
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits and select the first practice file.
  2. Open Actions → Actions (Quick)… and choose Guess Values.
  3. Enter %title% in Source format string.
  4. Enter %artist% - %title% in Guessing pattern.
  5. Choose Apply action and inspect both fields in Extended tags….

The source expression reads the old title before either destination changes. The %artist% and %title% tokens in the guessing pattern name destinations; they do not fetch existing values. The expected first result is ARTIST=Juniper Vale, TITLE=Paper Boats.

This applies immediately. There is no full Guess-Values dry-run preview in this recipe. Test a copied file and compare results before expanding the selection. Use Edit → Undo … for a recorded write when needed.

docs.title: Add trimming in a reusable group
docs.text:
Once the source layout is confirmed, create an Actions… group named Practice split title credit. Add the following rows in Edit actions…:

Step Action Field / source Pattern / format / separator Replacement / option 1 Guess Values %title% %artist% - %title% Not used 2 Format Value ARTIST $trim(%artist%) Not used 3 Format Value TITLE $trim(%title%) Not used

For row 1, the third column is Source format string and the fourth is Guessing pattern. For the Format Value rows they are Field and Format string. Keep the actions and group, Save groups, then apply only the checked practice group to the intended copies.

Captures preserve their surrounding spaces, so trimming happens after the split. Trimming first would affect only the outside of the combined source; it would not necessarily clean each captured artist/title independently. A source using a different separator, such as Artist – Title with an en dash, does not match this literal hyphen pattern.

The third and fourth example rows are important: Guess Values makes no field changes when the source does not fully match, but the later Format Value rows still run. Thus the complete group can trim fields on a nonmatching file. Restrict the selection to the intended layout if those extra trims are unwanted. A warning from another action also does not stop later actions in the group; inspect every reported file result.

docs.title: Preview a trim without writing it
docs.text:
For a single stored title or artist, Convert → Tag → Tag… can preview $trim(%title%) or $trim(%artist%) with the corresponding destination. Wait for the result, then Cancel if this is only an experiment. This previews the individual expression on the current tags, not the whole ordered group or the tags as they would look after a future Guess Values row.

A bare placeholder reads only the first value. Do not run this group on files with multiple title or artist values when the other values must be preserved, even if the Guess Values row would not match. After extraction, use Tag → Filename as a separate reviewed rename if filenames should also change.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Do not paste a regex such as (.+) - (.+) into Guessing pattern. Guess Values uses named placeholders and literal separators, not capture groups.
  • Omitting the separator between %artist% and %title% is ambiguous and rejected. The pattern needs text that defines where one capture ends.
  • The first action overwrites a matching file's artist. Keep a file backup when the previous credit matters; an extra metadata field is not a complete backup of the original file.
  • Actions write immediately; Save groups only stores the recipe. Check the selected files and undo label rather than pressing Save tags to “apply” the group afterward.

docs.title: Split semicolon-separated artist credits
docs.text: Turn Juniper Vale; Mira Solberg into two stored ARTIST values. This recipe uses semicolons as an agreed separator; it leaves / and & inside names such as AC/DC or Kofi & the Tidewater Band alone.

docs.title: Inspect the source structure first
docs.text:
Open Extended tags… (Alt+T; Alt is ⌥ Option on macOS) on a copied practice file. Confirm whether ARTIST has one delimited value or several existing values. The group below processes each existing value and then removes exact duplicates across the resulting list.

In this table, each quoted item is one stored value. The brackets illustrate a list, not characters to type into a tag-panel field.

ARTIST before ARTIST after ["Juniper Vale; Mira Solberg"] ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] [" ; Juniper Vale ; ; Mira Solberg; "] ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] ["AC/DC; Kofi & the Tidewater Band"] ["AC/DC","Kofi & the Tidewater Band"] ["Juniper Vale; Mira Solberg","Juniper Vale"] ["Juniper Vale","Mira Solberg"] ["Juniper Vale; juniper vale"] ["Juniper Vale","juniper vale"]

The last row keeps differently capitalized strings. Review whether they mean the same person before choosing one spelling; an exact duplicate removal is not an artist-identity lookup.

docs.title: Build the ordered group
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits, then select one copied practice file.
  2. Open Actions → Actions…, create Practice split artist credits, and open Edit actions….
  3. Add these rows in order. Set Case-sensitive comparison to Off for the regex rows. ; is one literal semicolon.
  4. For Remove Duplicate Fields, turn Only duplicated fields with the same content On. Keep every action and the group, then Save groups.
  5. Check only this practice group and choose Apply checked groups.
Step Action Field / source Pattern / format / separator Replacement / option 1 Replace with Regular Expression ARTIST \A[ \t;]+ Leave empty 2 Replace with Regular Expression ARTIST [ \t;]+\z Leave empty 3 Replace with Regular Expression ARTIST [ \t]*;[ \t;]* ; 4 Split Field by Separator ARTIST ; Not used 5 Remove Duplicate Fields ARTIST Only duplicated fields with the same content On

The edge rows remove empty semicolon segments at the start/end of each value (\A and \z are whole-text anchors). The third row compresses internal runs of semicolons and adjacent spaces/tabs to one separator. Only then does Split Field by Separator turn text into separate values; it trims each captured piece. The final row keeps the first occurrence of each exact value, preserving its order.

Turning the final checkbox off would keep only the first artist, including when later values name different people. It is not an alternative spelling of “deduplicate.” Check the saved setting before running the group again.

docs.title: Why split after cleaning
docs.text:
A bare split can retain empty pieces when the source begins/ends with a separator or contains repeated separators. Deduplicating those pieces does not make them meaningful artist names. Cleaning delimiters before the split avoids that problem for the nonempty credits in this recipe.

A value containing only semicolons/spaces is still not a valid credit. This group does not invent a name or validate empty input. Inspect and fix those files separately. It also has no escape syntax for a semicolon that belongs inside one artist's actual name; exclude such credits from this batch.

If the source already has correct separate values, a delimiter-splitting job may be unnecessary. To join a list for a particular player, use Merge Duplicate Fields deliberately instead of replacing the list with its first %artist% value.

docs.title: Check the saved values and the player
docs.text:
After applying, inspect Extended tags…: the first practice file should show Value 1 Juniper Vale and Value 2 Mira Solberg. Actions write when run; there is no later Save-tags commit for this group. Inspect errors and use Edit → Undo … for the recorded operation in the current desktop session.

The writer must represent the list in the destination format. A player can display the same logical values differently, and some fields/formats have single-value restrictions. Read the file back and test the intended player before applying this convention throughout a library. See multi-value storage. No part of this recipe establishes player compatibility or a native save-back result on every platform.

docs.title: Read or split a track number and total
docs.text: A value such as 3/12 already carries the current track and its total. Keep that convention unless a specific report or custom-field workflow needs two values. This recipe shows a guarded extraction, then an optional split into TRACK and a custom TRACKTOTAL field.

docs.title: Choose storage before changing fields
docs.text:
TRACKTOTAL here is a custom field. It is not OpenTag's mapped MP4 total: MP4 uses TOTALTRACKS, sharing the native trkn number/total pair with TRACK. After reading an MP4, OpenTag can show TRACK=3/12 and TOTALTRACKS=12 together. Writing a standalone current number does not mean that the native total has disappeared.

For normal tag editing or auto-numbering, keeping TRACK=3/12 is usually sufficient. For a report, a format expression can read each component without changing the file. Do not create a custom field merely to make a player show a total it already understands natively.

docs.title: Prepare the practice inputs
docs.text:
Use copies with one TRACK and at most one TRACKTOTAL value per file. Exclude values containing two consecutive backslashes: Format Value treats that text as a value separator, even in a fallback that keeps existing text. The table starts with TRACKTOTAL=99 so that unmatched input visibly retains its old custom value. Only a complete pair of positive decimal numbers, with optional leading zeros, is extracted.

TRACK before TRACKTOTAL before TRACK after TRACKTOTAL after 3/12 99 3 12 05/012 99 5 12 3 99 3 99 3/no-total 99 3/no-total 99 0/12 99 0/12 99 14/12 99 14 12

The last row is numerically shaped but logically suspicious. The expression does not verify that the current track is at most the total, or that twelve files exist. Inspect those facts separately.

docs.title: Extract the total before changing TRACK
docs.text:
In Convert → Tag → Tag…, set the following destination and expression. Wait for the preview and compare it with the first table. Cancel if the calculation is only for inspection; Apply to … files writes immediately.

Field: TRACKTOTAL

Format string:

$if($stricmp($regexp(%track%,'\A0*([1-9][0-9]*)/0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$2'),%track%),%tracktotal%,$num($regexp(%track%,'\A0*([1-9][0-9]*)/0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$2'),1))

After this first conversion, the original TRACK still contains 3/12. If shortening it is also intended, review the second conversion:

Field: TRACK

Format string:

$if($stricmp($regexp(%track%,'\A0*([1-9][0-9]*)/0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$1'),%track%),%track%,$num($regexp(%track%,'\A0*([1-9][0-9]*)/0*([1-9][0-9]*)\z','$1'),1))

Run total extraction first. Shortening TRACK first removes the slash and total that the other expression needs; the total expression would then keep the old 99. The same two Format Value actions can be saved in a group, with TRACKTOTAL first and TRACK second. Save groups stores that order; applying the checked group writes immediately.

docs.title: Understand the guard
docs.text:
The regex uses \A and \z to match the whole text. 0* consumes leading zeros; [1-9][0-9]* requires a positive number. The two parenthesized groups capture current track and total, and $1 or $2 chooses one.

$regexp returns its input unchanged on a nonmatch. $stricmp compares that result with the original TRACK. A successful capture contains only digits, so it cannot equal the original slash-containing pair. Equality therefore means “keep the old field” for this particular expression. This is a guard built for this pattern, not a universal regex-match test.

$num(…,1) removes padding from the extracted component. By contrast, $num(%track%,1) alone reads the leading number and discards the total; it does not save that total anywhere. Guess Values with %track%/%tracktotal% can also split a slash, but does not validate numeric shape. A value such as 3/no-total would capture text as its “total.”

docs.title: Check the saved format
docs.text:
A core field split is not a promise of identical native storage. MP4 uses its mapped pair fields and 16-bit unsigned components; inconsistent simultaneous TRACK and TOTALTRACKS totals are rejected. Other formats may retain TRACKTOTAL only as a custom field, and ID3v1 cannot store arbitrary custom fields. See field storage and test read-back on copies before relying on a device's convention.

Unmatched inputs keep the existing custom total; they do not clear stale TRACKTOTAL values automatically. Inspect them instead of treating a successful batch as validation of every old value.

Keep file backups. Use Edit → Undo … for a recorded conversion/action in the current desktop session. Neither preview nor a custom total is a backup of metadata removed by a later operation.

docs.title: Remove a numbered prefix from titles
docs.text:
Uses Replace with Regular Expression; optional Tag → Tag preview

Works on Reviewed TITLE values in copied local files

Time About 5 minutes

Undo Recorded action changes in the current desktop session

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A filename import left 03 - Paper Boats in TITLE, although TRACK already holds its track number. Remove a recognized prefix, not every number in the title. Meaningful numbers elsewhere must survive.

In the table, · means one space, ⇥ a tab and ↵ a newline. These symbols make invisible characters readable; do not type them into a title.

TITLE before After this action 03 - Paper Boats Paper Boats 8. Low Tide Low Tide 2) North Pier North Pier ·003⇥-⇥Quiet Harbour Quiet Harbour Room 101 - Window Room 101 - Window 12 Lanterns 12 Lanterns 03-Paper Boats 03-Paper Boats 03 - Paper Boats↵04 - Low Tide Paper Boats↵04 - Low Tide 03 -· (empty text) (empty text) (empty text)

A title containing only a numbered prefix can become empty. Exclude it from the write and supply the real title first. An intentionally numbered title can also match this shape; no regex can decide its musical meaning.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits. Select one copied practice file with an understood title. Check all its Title values in Extended tags if there are several.

  2. To preview the first Title value, use Convert → Tag → Tag…, Field TITLE, and this expression:

    $regexp(%title%,'(?-m)^[ \t]*\d{1,3}[ \t]*[-.)][ \t]+',)

    Leave the third scripting argument empty after the final comma. Two apostrophes '' represent a literal apostrophe, not an empty argument. Read the result, then Cancel this preview. Applying it would format from the first value; it is not the multi-value action below. 3. Choose Actions → Actions (Quick)…, select Replace with Regular Expression, and enter TITLE in Field. Use this Regular expression:

    (?-m)^[ \t]*\d{1,3}[ \t]*[-.)][ \t]+

  3. Leave Replace matches with empty and Case-sensitive comparison off. An empty replacement removes the matched prefix; a space would leave a space behind.

  4. Choose Apply action for the practice file. The action writes immediately and processes each Title value independently. Inspect its saved values, the untouched TRACK, and any file warning.
  5. Select only other reviewed files with the intended shape. Keep hidden selections out of the batch. Run the action, then inspect each failure before considering a retry.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Pattern part Purpose (?-m) Make ^ refer to the start of the whole value, not each line ^ Require the prefix at the beginning [ \t]* Allow leading spaces/tabs, without consuming line breaks \d{1,3} Read one to three digits [ \t]* Allow spaces/tabs between number and punctuation [-.)] Require one hyphen, dot or closing parenthesis [ \t]+ Require at least one space/tab after that punctuation

The action replaces the matching prefix with nothing. It does not change TRACK, derive totals or rename the audio file. Without a match, the original text remains. An empty string remains empty; the core action can retain an empty Title value, while native storage may normalize it on write.

Each existing Title value is transformed separately. The first-value preview is useful for a practice input, but does not prove a whole multi-value field will be safe. The newline example changes only the first line's prefix. Using \s for every separator would also admit line breaks and is broader than the spacing policy taught here.

docs.title: Another delimiter or more digits
docs.text: Change the punctuation class or digit bound only after writing matching and nonmatching examples for your own files. The main pattern deliberately leaves 03-Paper Boats unchanged because there is no separating whitespace after the punctuation. Do not replace it with an unanchored \d+, which can remove meaningful numbers anywhere in a title.

docs.title: Start from filenames instead
docs.text: If the real problem is that TRACK and TITLE have not been separated at all, Filename → Tag can capture the number into its own field. Preserve a copied source before re-importing names.

docs.title: Undo a mistaken cleanup
docs.text: Use the recorded action's Edit → Undo … in the current desktop session, read its count and inspect any refusal. Completed files in a partially failed batch remain changed until recovered. Do not repeat the group merely because one file warned; later actions may already have run. Keep originals for recovery after restarting.

docs.title: Tag files from folder and file names
docs.text: Uses Filename → Tag Works on files in Artist/Album/ folders Time 2 minutes per batch Undo Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Your files have empty or wrong tags, but they are well organised on disk. The folders name the artist and the album, and the file names hold the track number and title:

Music/
└── Juniper Vale/
    └── Harbour Lights (2024)/
        ├── 01 - Low Tide.mp3
        ├── 02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3
        └── 03 - Paper Boats.mp3

You want all of that in the tags:

File ARTIST ALBUM YEAR TRACK TITLE 01 - Low Tide.mp3 Juniper Vale Harbour Lights 2024 01 Low Tide 02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 Juniper Vale Harbour Lights 2024 02 Lanterns on the Water

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
Try this on a copy of a few files first. Check the results before applying it to your library; use Edit → Undo in the same session to reverse the recorded changes. Keep the originals as a backup.

  1. Open the Music folder, or the artist's folder, and select the files. Selecting all of them (Cmd+A / Ctrl+A) is fine as long as they all follow the same layout.
  2. Choose Convert → Filename → Tag… (Alt+2; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac).

  3. Enter this pattern:

    %artist%\%album% (%year%)\%track% - %title%

  4. Click Preview and check the values for a few files.

  5. Click Apply. The tags are written to the files straight away; there is nothing left to save.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A Filename → Tag pattern is a picture of the name, with placeholders where the values are. OpenTag lines the pattern up against the end of each file's path:

pattern:  %artist%     \ %album%       (%year%)\ %track% - %title%
path:     Juniper Vale \ Harbour Lights (2024) \ 02      - Lanterns on the Water.mp3
  • \ stands for a folder level. The pattern has two, so OpenTag looks at the file name and the two folders above it. Everything higher up (Music) is ignored. Use \ on macOS and Linux too.
  • The text between placeholders must appear exactly, here -, ( and ).
  • The extension is left out automatically.
  • The whole name must fit for that file to change. Files that do not match are skipped. The Apply button shows the number of matching files and stays disabled when none match. Review every row; use the filter or sort by path to identify files that need a different pattern.

Gotcha: brackets inside album names

Placeholders take as little text as possible. For the folder Harbour Lights (Deluxe) (2024), %album% stops at the first (, so ALBUM becomes Harbour Lights and YEAR becomes Deluxe) (2024. Check the preview for such albums and run them separately with a pattern that matches their folder names, such as %artist%\%album% (Deluxe) (%year%)\%track% - %title%. That pattern leaves (Deluxe) out of the album name. To keep it, run %artist%\%album%\%track% - %title% and remove the year from the album afterwards with the regular expression \s*\(\d{4}\)$ (see Regular expressions).

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
No year in the album folder

%artist%\%album%\%track% - %title%

No track number in the file names

%artist%\%album%\%title%

Then number the tracks with Auto-numbering, after sorting the file list by file name.

Disc folders (CD1, CD2) inside the album

%artist%\%album%\CD%discnumber%\%track% - %title%

Skip a part you don't need

%dummy% matches text without storing it. For files named Juniper Vale - 02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3, where the artist is already in the folder:

%artist%\%album%\%dummy% - %track% - %title%

Two artists in the file name

The same placeholder twice gives a field two values. For Juniper Vale & Mira Solberg - Paper Boats.mp3:

%artist% & %artist% - %title%

docs.title: Sort a leading “The” without changing the artist credit
docs.text:
Uses Tag → Tag, $regexp, ARTISTSORT

Works on Copied local files with a reviewed primary Artist

Time About 5 minutes

Undo Recorded converter changes in the current desktop session

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Keep the displayed credit The Lanterns, but offer Lanterns, The as its sort name. Write ARTISTSORT; do not rewrite ARTIST merely to alter an alphabetical order. Whether a player uses that field remains player-specific.

This recipe derives one sort name from the first Artist value. It leaves the full Artist value list alone. It does not invent personal surname order or sort each member of a multi-artist collaboration separately.

The following are primary Artist input/output examples. ↵ denotes a newline; · makes a space visible. The result is the proposed ARTISTSORT, with the Artist credit unchanged.

First ARTIST value Proposed ARTISTSORT The Lanterns Lanterns, The the Lanterns Lanterns, the Juniper Vale Juniper Vale The The The Lanterns ·Lanterns, The The Lanterns↵Mira Solberg The Lanterns↵Mira Solberg (empty text) (empty text)

The extra-space and empty examples are reasons to stop and correct the source, not desirable sort names. The rule preserves text it does not recognize. It matches one literal space after a leading “The”; extra spaces belong to the captured name and survive.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Work on copied files. Save or discard pending changes and inspect the existing Artist and Artist Sort values. Keep manually curated sort names.

  2. Choose Edit → Unselect all, show the filter, and enter:

    ARTISTSORT MISSING AND ARTIST PRESENT

    Wait for auto-apply or press Enter in manual mode. A present empty Artist still passes PRESENT; inspect the preview. A present empty Artist Sort is not MISSING and is deliberately outside this selection. 3. Select only the intended visible rows, then open Convert → Tag → Tag…. Enter ARTISTSORT in Field and use:

    $regexp(%artist%,'(?-m)^(The) ([^\r\n]+)$','$2, $1')

  3. Inspect the before/after preview. Exclude malformed credits, empty results and collaborations for which the first artist is the wrong sorting policy.

  4. Apply to the practice selection. The converter writes immediately; no extra Save tags is required for its successful results. Reload and check that ARTIST is still the original credit and ARTISTSORT has the intended value. Inspect any per-file errors before a larger run.

If preferred, save the same field/expression as a Format Value action. Its apply command also writes immediately; preserve the filter/selection precondition rather than running it over existing curated sort fields.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
%artist% reads the first value. $regexp is case-insensitive by default, so both The and the match. Capture 1 remembers the original spelling of the article, and capture 2 remembers the remaining name. The quoted replacement $2, $1 places a comma and space between them. Quoting prevents the comma from becoming another scripting-function argument.

(?-m) keeps the anchors tied to the whole value. [^\r\n]+ requires a nonempty name without line breaks; a multi-line credit is left untouched. A nonmatch returns the original text, which supplies the unchanged-credit fallback for names such as Juniper Vale.

The filter excludes existing Artist Sort value lists, including present empty strings. If a file has two Artist values, the new sort name still uses only the first. Its Artist values remain separate and unchanged. For example:

ARTIST values Existing ARTISTSORT Pass main filter? Resulting ARTISTSORT ["The Lanterns","Mira Solberg"] Absent Yes ["Lanterns, The"] ["The Lanterns"] ["Lanterns"] No ["Lanterns"] ["The Lanterns"] [""] No [""] [""] Absent Yes Absent

docs.title: Only match exactly capitalized “The”
docs.text:
Add a fourth $regexp argument of 0 to respect case:

$regexp(%artist%,'(?-m)^(The) ([^\r\n]+)$','$2, $1',0)
Input Result with 0 The Lanterns Lanterns, The the Lanterns the Lanterns Juniper Vale Juniper Vale

This is the shared scripting-core flag, not Find's checkbox or a web-source parser default.

docs.title: Album artist sorting
docs.text: Use the separate ALBUMARTISTSORT field and an expression reading %albumartist% when the album-level credit needs sorting. Review its existing values and select its missing-field targets separately. Do not substitute a track artist for a compilation's album credit merely to fill a blank.

docs.title: Make OpenTag's list use a sort field
docs.text: Writing ARTISTSORT does not automatically change every column's sorting behavior. Configure an appropriate column sort expression and click its header as described in Columns. A player's own sorting preference is separate. Sort fields and compilations explains native mappings, fallbacks and format-specific behavior.

docs.title: Recover the old value
docs.text: Read the recorded Undo … step and file count in the current desktop session. Inspect pending edits afterward so a later save does not replace a restored value. Session history is bounded and is not a restart-proof backup. Keep original copies and review a player's actual behavior before a library run.

docs.title: Apply a tracklist from a text file
docs.text: Uses: Text File → Tag · Works on: selected writable audio files · Time: about 5 minutes for one album · Undo: recorded tag writes in the current desktop session; keep originals

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Your audio files have anonymous names, but a booklet or text listing has the track numbers, artist, album and titles. Import those records instead of typing the same album information into every file.

Selected file, in this order Imported track Imported title 01.flac 1 Paper Boats 02.flac 2 Lanterns on the Water

This recipe starts with two records and a controlled file order. The filename-key variation below is preferable when the records and files are in different orders. Neither method identifies the audio by listening to it.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
1. Work on copies of two ordinary whole-track audio files. Save pending edits, select only 01.flac and 02.flac, and check that they appear in that order in the file list.

  2. Choose Convert → Text File → Tag…. Set Text source to Pasted text and put this into Records to import:

    81. Juniper Vale - [Harbour Lights #1] Paper Boats
82. Juniper Vale - [Harbour Lights #2] Lanterns on the Water

  3. Put this into Import mask:

    %dummy%. %artist% - [%album% #%track%] %title%

  4. Choose Preview. Inspect the destination file, source line and captured fields for both rows. The first file should receive title Paper Boats, artist Juniper Vale, album Harbour Lights and track 1. The second should receive Lanterns on the Water and track 2.

  5. Choose Save tags to 2 files only after those associations are correct. This writes the tags immediately; it does not wait for a later Save tags.
  6. Check both files in Extended tags…, including a field you intended to retain. Fields named in the mask are replaced; fields outside it remain. Read any per-file errors before treating the whole batch as complete.

If a result is wrong, stop before importing more albums. Edit → Undo can restore recorded tag changes in this desktop session. Keep the original copies for recovery beyond that session and for comparing player behavior.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The mask reads the whole record, from left to right. It is an extraction pattern, not a scripting expression that calculates a new string.

Mask part What it reads from the first record %dummy% 81, which is discarded rather than stored as a field . A literal period and space %artist% - Artist up to the literal - separator [%album% #%track%] Album and track inside literal brackets, separated by # %title% The remaining title

The brackets here are literal record punctuation. They are not the optional sections used in an output format string. Literal spaces and separators must match the actual records. Captured whitespace is preserved, so inspect padding rather than assuming it will be trimmed.

Without a key, record 1 goes to selected file 1, record 2 to selected file 2, and so on. The number 81 does not choose the file; %dummy% discards it. A positional import requires exactly as many records as selected files.

docs.title: Read one album's saved tracklist
docs.text:
Set Text source to Text file, choose the listing, or use this in Source file:

%_folderpath%tracks.txt

The expression uses the first selected audio file. It reads one listing for the entire selection, even when that selection spans several folders. Process one album folder at a time if each has its own tracks.txt. Use UTF-8 for a new listing; check accents in the preview when decoding older text with Legacy encoding fallback (optional).

docs.title: Match by filename instead of position
docs.text:
For selected files 01.flac and 02.flac, these records deliberately put track 2 first:

02.flac;Lanterns on the Water;2
01.flac;Paper Boats;1
03.flac;North Pier;3

Use this mask:

%_filename_ext%;%title%;%track%

Now 02.flac receives the first record, and 01.flac the second. The record for unselected 03.flac is skipped. This mask does not set artist or album. If you also selected 04.flac, it would have No match, not changed and keep its tags. Review unmatched files as carefully as matched ones.

Filename keys include the extension. Two selected folders containing the same filename are ambiguous; use an absolute %_path% key instead. Match filename and path keys case-sensitively controls key comparison, not the case of the imported title. Leave it on unless the intended keys really differ only in capitalization.

docs.title: Start from a simple delimited listing
docs.text: For plain records such as 1;Juniper Vale;Paper Boats, use %track%;%artist%;%title%. Choose a separator absent from those values. A spreadsheet CSV with escaped quotes, embedded separators or multiline cells requires deliberate conversion first: this converter is not a CSV decoder. In particular, doubled CSV quotes are not automatically unescaped. Keep filenames or paths when preparing a file-keyed import.

docs.title: When preview refuses the listing
docs.text:
Problem Check before trying again Wrong number of records Remove a header before positional import; compare the record count with the selection Extra blank record Remove unintended empty lines; a final line ending is allowed, but an additional blank record is still a record Record does not match the mask Compare punctuation and spacing; use %dummy% for an unwanted prefix One file matched twice Correct duplicate keys rather than expecting later records to override earlier ones No selected files match Check extensions, absolute paths, key case and the current selection Preview became stale Run Preview again after changing input, selection or source

Do not use this record importer for multiline lyrics. Import the complete sidecar into one field with the lyrics recipe.

docs.title: Remove extra spaces without flattening every field
docs.text: Clean the edges and repeated horizontal spacing of a title while keeping its words and punctuation. This recipe targets TITLE; it does not turn every line break in comments or lyrics into a space.

docs.title: Check the practice result
docs.text:
Use copied files with these titles. In this table, · represents one ordinary space, ⇥ a tab and ↵ a line break; do not type those visible markers literally. Each input is one TITLE value.

TITLE before TITLE after ··Paper···Boats·· Paper Boats ⇥North⇥⇥Pier⇥ North Pier Quiet Harbour Quiet Harbour AC/DC··-··Live AC/DC - Live Paper⇥↵⇥Boats Paper·↵·Boats

Spaces can carry meaning in a catalogue number or an identifier. Confirm that normalizing them is wanted before adding another destination field.

docs.title: Try the expression in a preview
docs.text:
With one title value, Convert → Tag → Tag… can preview the calculation. Set Field to TITLE and use one of these expressions. · marks spaces in the result column too.

For TITLE = ··Paper···Boats··:

Format string Result $trim(%title%) Paper···Boats $trim($regexp(%title%,'[ \t]+', )) Paper Boats

The last argument of $regexp is one actual space between the comma and closing parenthesis. It is neither an empty replacement nor the characters space. $trim removes surrounding whitespace; it does not collapse the spaces between words. The inner $regexp turns each run of spaces/tabs into one space, then $trim handles the ends.

Wait for the preview and inspect it. Apply to … files writes immediately; Cancel leaves the preview unapplied. A bare %title% reads only the first stored value, so this converter variant replaces an existing multi-title list with one calculated result. The action sequence below processes each current value independently instead.

docs.title: Save a reusable cleanup group
docs.text:
1. Save or discard pending edits, then select one practice copy.
  2. Open Actions → Actions…, choose New…, and name a group Practice title spacing.
  3. In Edit actions…, add the rows below in order. For every regex row, set Case-sensitive comparison to Off.
  4. Keep each action, keep the group, then choose Save groups. Saving the group does not process the audio file.
  5. Check only this practice group and choose Apply checked groups.
Step Action Field / source Pattern / format / separator Replacement / option 1 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE \A[ \t]+ Leave empty 2 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE [ \t]+\z Leave empty 3 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE [ \t]+ One space

\A anchors the first match to the beginning of the whole field value; \z anchors the second to its end. Unlike ^ and $ in this engine, they do not also match at internal line breaks. [ \t] means an ordinary space or tab, and + requires at least one. The third action compresses the remaining runs. Doing that row first would leave one space at either edge until the later edge actions removed it.

Inspect the saved title and operation errors. Actions write when run; they do not wait for a separate Save tags. Use Edit → Undo … for the recorded operation in the current desktop session. Keep copies for recovery after quitting.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• \s{2,} is a broader whitespace expression. It can include line breaks, so using it across _TAG can damage paragraph layout. This recipe uses spaces/tabs and the specific TITLE field deliberately.
  • A single interior tab is also normalized by [ \t]+. Use a narrower rule if tabs have intentional structure in the destination field.
  • Neither variant is a universal cleanup for nonbreaking spaces or every Unicode separator. Inspect an unexpected character before choosing a rule.
  • An all-whitespace title can become empty. Decide on a real title or a deliberate removal rather than treating an empty result as successful naming.
  • Adding capitalization or punctuation removal changes this recipe's goal. Test those as separate actions before combining them.

docs.title: Keep the year from an ISO date
docs.text: Shorten 2024-05-21 to 2024 when a chosen workflow needs a year-only YEAR. Decide first whether losing the month and day is acceptable. This recipe changes metadata; it does not repair an invalid calendar date or restore missing date information.

docs.title: Compare a shortcut with a guarded rule
docs.text:
In Convert → Tag → Tag…, a single-value field can preview $left(%year%,4). It takes four characters regardless of their meaning:

YEAR before Format string Preview result 2024-05-21 $left(%year%,4) 2024 2024 $left(%year%,4) 2024 May 2024 $left(%year%,4) May unknown $left(%year%,4) unkn

The space after May in that result is real. $left is useful for a selection already known to begin with a four-digit year; it is not a date parser. Wait for the preview and Cancel if only inspecting it.

docs.title: Change only the chosen date shape
docs.text:
Use the following regex action to affect complete YYYY-MM-DD values while leaving other spellings unchanged:

  1. Save or discard pending edits and select one copied file.
  2. Open Actions → Actions (Quick)…, then Replace with Regular Expression.
  3. Set Field to YEAR.
  4. Enter Pattern \A([0-9]{4})-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}\z.
  5. Set Replace matches with to $1 and Case-sensitive comparison to Off.
  6. Choose Apply action, then inspect the saved value and operation result.
Setting Value Field YEAR Pattern \A([0-9]{4})-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}\z Replace matches with $1 Case-sensitive comparison Off YEAR before YEAR after 2024-05-21 2024 1998-12-03 1998 2024 2024 May 2024 May 2024 2024-05-21T10:30:00Z 2024-05-21T10:30:00Z 2024-99-99 2024

The last row is intentional: four digits, two digits and two digits describe shape, not calendar validity. Validate suspect dates separately; this action still extracts the first four digits from that shaped input. A timestamp with a time portion does not match this particular whole-value rule.

docs.title: Understand the capture and write timing
docs.text:
\A and \z anchor the entire value rather than each line. [0-9]{4} requires exactly four digits. Its surrounding parentheses capture the year as group 1; $1 inserts that capture in the replacement. The hyphens and remaining two-digit components must be present for a match.

Type the pattern and $1 directly into their regex-action boxes without format-string quotes. The action processes each existing value of YEAR; nonmatches keep their text. Unlike the converter's bare placeholder, it does not first reduce a multi-value field to its first item.

The action writes immediately. To save it for later, add it to a group and choose Save groups; that saves the workflow without running it. Apply the checked group only to a reviewed selection. There is no full action preview in this recipe, so test a copied file before a larger batch.

docs.title: Keep the original date when it matters
docs.text:
A title's release year, an original release date and a recording date can be different facts. Choose the right field rather than shortening every date in the library. YEAR and other date names map differently by native format; see field names and storage. An extra custom field is not a substitute for a full file backup, and ID3v1 cannot carry all custom/date information.

Inspect read-back and the intended player's display before applying the convention throughout a collection. Use Edit → Undo … for a recorded write during the current desktop session, and retain original files for recovery after quitting.

docs.title: Customize file-list columns
docs.text: Choose View → Customize columns… to decide what the file list displays, which values can be edited there, and how each column sorts. A column can show a computed value while editing a different underlying field, or can be read-only. Changing a view definition does not convert the audio format.

docs.title: Add an editable recording-code column
docs.text:
1. Select a copied practice file whose ISRC field contains the invented practice value QZABC2400003.
  2. Open View → Customize columns… and choose New.
  3. Set Name to Recording code and Value to %isrc%.
  4. Set Field (empty = read-only) to %isrc%. Leave Sort by (empty = value) empty and Numeric (sort numerically) off.
  5. Set a suitable width, such as 140, and keep its visibility checkbox on.
  6. Inspect the active-file preview, then choose OK to save/apply the layout.

The header says Recording code, its value comes from ISRC, and the editable field is still ISRC. Merely naming a column ISRC would not establish that connection. Canceling the customization dialog leaves its unconfirmed layout edits unapplied.

docs.title: Understand Name, Value, Field and Sort by
docs.text:
Control Purpose Name Literal header text. Required; it is not evaluated as a format string. Value Required display format string, using placeholders/functions. Field (empty = read-only) One writable field placeholder, or empty for a read-only column. It is not a write-back formula. Sort by (empty = value) Optional sort format. Empty uses Value as the sort key. Width Column width, constrained to 24–4,000 pixels. Alignment Left, Center or Right text alignment. Numeric (sort numerically) Compare leading numeric values before the text fallback.

For these examples, the practice file has:

Field Value 1 Value 2 ISRC QZABC2400003 (absent) ARTIST Juniper Vale Mira Solberg TITLE Paper Boats (absent) Name Value Field Sort by Displayed result Sort key Recording code %isrc% %isrc% (empty) QZABC2400003 QZABC2400003 Credits $meta_sep(artist,' + ') %artist% $lower(%artist%) Juniper Vale + Mira Solberg juniper vale Upper title $upper(%title%) (empty) %title% PAPER BOATS Paper Boats

The Credits column explicitly joins separate ARTIST values for display. Its editable target remains ARTIST, and sorting uses its first artist lowercased. The Upper title column is read-only because Field is empty; its uppercase display does not silently uppercase the stored TITLE.

A Field entry accepts a tag placeholder such as %isrc%, plus the special filename targets %_filename% and %_filename_ext%. Technical properties such as %_bitrate% cannot be written there. Scripting functions, several placeholders or literal surrounding text are not valid Field targets. To calculate and save a new metadata value, use Tag → Tag or Format Value instead.

docs.title: Sort and alignment rules
docs.text:
Click a header to sort its configured sort key, and click it again to reverse the primary direction. Shift-click adds/reverses a secondary key. The file-list guide explains ordering and how it feeds numbering and positional imports.

Numeric sorting reads a leading number; empty/nonnumeric values sort before valid numbers in ascending order, with text comparison resolving ties. Enabling Numeric changes Left alignment to Right; disabling it changes Right to Left. Alignment can then be chosen independently, and Center is not forcibly replaced by that toggle.

A display like %_length% can use a numeric technical value as Sort by when its formatted clock text is not the desired sorting representation. Use actual information placeholders from the placeholder reference; a custom tag named LENGTH is not a measured duration.

docs.title: Add, duplicate, move, hide or remove
docs.text:
• New adds a column after the current one, initially using ISRC.
  • Duplicate copies the current definition into a separately identifiable column. Give it a useful name and review its editable Field.
  • Move up / Move down change column order. Headers can also be dragged directly in the file list; dividers resize them.
  • A checkbox next to a column name shows or hides it. Keep at least one column visible.
  • Remove deletes the column definition, not the file's metadata. A removed column's sort criterion is removed too.
  • Reset to defaults replaces the draft layout with the built-in columns; review it and choose OK only when that reset is intended.

Right-clicking a header or using the View menu's column list offers quick visibility controls. Those quick changes apply and persist directly; check reported errors. The customization dialog instead collects layout edits until its OK step. Auto-size and divider double-clicks fit widths to measured listed content within limits; long lists are sampled, so some values can still need manual widening.

docs.title: Save, load and import a layout
docs.text:
Save configuration… writes the current dialog's column layout to a JSON file. It can export a valid draft before OK; canceling later does not remove that external file. Load configuration… fills the customization dialog from a supported layout. Review it, then choose OK to apply it.

The picker can also import a user-supplied Mp3tag columns.ini. Review the reported imported/skipped items and the resulting expressions; unsupported settings are not a promise of identical appearance or behavior.

A column-layout file contains the layout and sort configuration. It is separate from backing up audio tags or saving the whole application configuration through the File menu.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• A correct-looking preview does not make an invalid Field writable. Check display Value and edit target separately.
  • Hiding a column does not erase its tags, and removing it does not remove the metadata from a file.
  • A custom column can require context-dependent functions. In particular, column-name/value functions need a supplied column context and cannot be used to recursively evaluate the column itself.
  • Large expressions can make previews/sorting more expensive than a plain placeholder. Start with one field and add formatting in small steps.

docs.title: Save and restore your configuration
docs.text: Save a configuration before reorganizing your workspace, changing many options, or moving to another computer. The bundle preserves supported saved configuration. It is separate from saving tag edits and backing up music.

docs.title: Make a named configuration backup
docs.text:
1. Finish the configuration dialogs you want to preserve: choose OK or Apply in Options and Save groups for edited action groups. Unsaved dialog work is not a replacement for saved configuration files.
  2. Choose File → Save configuration…. Select a backup location and a recognizable name, such as Harbour-workspace-before-tools.json.
  3. Check the status message and the destination file. OpenTag reports how many existing supported configuration files it collected. A zero-file bundle is not a useful restore checkpoint: empty bundles are rejected on load. Finish saving the intended settings/definitions first.
  4. Keep this backup separately from the application installation and from the audio-file backup. A new application package does not carry your whole personal workspace inside it.

Saving configuration does not write pending tag-panel edits to audio. It also does not guarantee that an in-progress typed history entry or unsaved action edit has become part of the saved files. Finish those changes deliberately before treating the bundle as a checkpoint.

docs.title: What the bundle includes
docs.text:
OpenTag uses its own JSON bundle, identified internally as opentag-configuration, version 1. It collects the following files when they already exist in the current configuration folder:

Saved file What it represents settings.json Saved Options, including tool definitions, toolbar/layout preferences and other option pages actions.json Saved action groups and their definitions/order/state exports.json Saved export configurations columns.json File-list column configuration tag-panel.json Tag-panel field configuration directories.json Favorite and recent directories lists.json Supported remembered helper/history/value lists, including their saved names and favorites

The list is a whitelist, not a recursive copy of the configuration folder. An absent component is omitted. The backup filename is your label for the bundle; it does not rename action groups, tools, favorites or list entries inside it.

docs.title: Keep these separately
docs.text:
• Audio files and their backups, including artwork already embedded in them.
  • Pending tag edits and unsaved configuration-dialog changes.
  • Discogs access credentials: the access token is deliberately excluded.
  • Installed web-source files, externally referenced images/text files and other resources outside the supported saved components.
  • Library-cache data, session Undo snapshots, and provider-document access or recovery state. A configuration bundle does not transfer a phone/provider permission grant to another computer.

Definitions can contain paths to external resources without copying those resources. Likewise, a configuration can contain private folder names, tool parameters or service settings. Token exclusion does not anonymize it; inspect a copy before sharing a workspace publicly.

docs.title: Restore without losing your current workspace
docs.text:
1. Save or deliberately discard pending audio edits. A configuration load reloads the application window and discards pending tag changes.
  2. Save the current configuration under another name, such as Harbour-workspace-before-restore.json. Keep the incoming bundle too.
  3. Choose File → Load configuration… and select the intended OpenTag JSON bundle. Read the replacement warning before confirming.
  4. After a successful load, the window reloads. Inspect Options, action groups, export definitions, columns, tag-panel fields and favorite directories.
  5. Test one copied audio file before applying a restored action group or external tool to a larger selection. Restoring its definition is not a review of what that definition will do to your current files.

This is not an importer for another editor's ZIP backup. It also does not combine every saved item from two workspaces. Each included component replaces its matching saved file; files omitted from the bundle remain in place.

Target before loading Incoming bundle contains Expected saved component afterward An existing action library A different valid actions.json The incoming action library replaces that component; the old groups are not automatically merged Existing favorites No directories.json The existing directory component is kept Existing custom toolbar settings An incoming settings.json Incoming saved settings, including their toolbar definition, replace that component Existing columns An invalid included columns.json Validation rejects the bundle before component replacement begins

Validation happens for every included component before replacements begin. An unsupported bundle version, unknown filename, invalid component or empty bundle is rejected. Import also limits a bundle to 32 MiB. Do not remove validation errors by renaming an arbitrary archive to .json.

A later filesystem/write failure is different: included files are replaced sequentially, so the whole bundle is not one all-or-nothing transaction. Keep the before-restore backup, record the error, and inspect the saved state before retrying. A failed reload or error dialog is not proof that no saved component changed. Do not delete the entire configuration folder to experiment.

docs.title: Move to another computer or operating system
docs.text:
Copy the configuration backup and required external resources, then install a suitable OpenTag package on the destination. Save its current configuration before loading the incoming bundle. Recheck anything that names a location:

Item What to recheck Tool Path and parameters Executable locations and command-line conventions can differ by OS Favorite/recent/startup directories The old computer's paths may not exist on the new one Actions and exports Referenced input/output folders, cover files and text resources Web sources and credentials Install the required source files and reconfigure credentials separately Layout and columns Available screen space, display preferences and the intended sort/format expressions

Keep your named definitions and labels recognizable while correcting paths. A successful configuration load validates the supported saved formats; it does not prove that an external executable exists, that a service account is available, or that every referenced file has been copied.

For a reusable personal setup, retain a known baseline and a separate copy before each substantial experiment. Do not use session Undo as configuration version control: recorded audio-file history has a different scope.

docs.title: Locate the current configuration folder
docs.text:
On desktop, choose File → Open configuration folder. This opens the folder used by the current application, avoiding guesses based on another editor's standard/portable/Store paths. The application identifies its per-user storage as OpenTag; copying an application bundle or AppImage does not create a new portable configuration beside that executable.

Opening folders is not available through the inspected mobile command. Use the build's supported file/document dialogs where offered and keep its release/access limits in mind. Do not infer desktop configuration-transfer or save-back support from a familiar-looking menu.

Avoid editing live saved files while OpenTag is writing them. The built-in load route validates included formats before replacing components; direct live file changes bypass that validation and have different reload risks. When a configuration cannot load, include the exact error and OpenTag version in a minimal issue report, without publishing credentials or a personal library.
