docs.title: Build reusable field-value choices
docs.text: Custom field values are saved suggestions for fields such as GENRE, MOOD or COMPOSER. They help keep spellings consistent while leaving you free to type another value. Saving a suggestion does not retag existing files; choosing it for selected tracks and saving those edits is a separate step.

docs.title: Make a small MOOD list
docs.text:
1. Choose View → Field values…, or File → Options… → Field Values → Edit field values….
  2. Enter MOOD in Field and press Enter. Field identifiers are trimmed and converted to uppercase. Use the actual metadata field name, rather than a display label you gave a tag-panel control.

  3. Put one choice on each line in Custom field values:

    Reflective
Uplifting
Spacious

  4. Choose the editor's own OK and check that the values were saved.

  5. If MOOD is not in your tag panel, add an editable MOOD control through tag-panel customization. Defining a list does not add a new visible field automatically.
  6. Select one copied practice track. Open the MOOD dropdown, choose Reflective, then inspect the pending change. Use Save tags only when that is the value you intend to write.

The list persists in saved tag-panel configuration. It is not a restriction on legal metadata values, a rule that automatically repairs older spellings, or an action applied to the whole collection.

docs.title: Understand normalization and order
docs.text:
The editor trims the edges of each line, removes empty lines and exact repetitions, and keeps the first occurrence order. For example, paste this practice list, including its blank line:

  Reflective
Uplifting

Reflective
reflective

The saved choices are:

Reflective
Uplifting
reflective

Reflective and reflective remain distinct. Decide on the desired spelling rather than expecting a case-insensitive cleanup. Sort A–Z sorts the current field's list using the application's text collator; keep your entered order if you prefer a hand-arranged shortlist.

A field supports up to 5,000 choices. Entries must be nonempty single lines; invalid control characters or an oversized list can prevent saving. Technical information fields starting with _, such as _PATH, cannot receive editable custom lists. Do not rename a technical field to make it appear writable.

Switching Field captures the current field's edits in this dialog's draft. Fields with custom values lets you revisit another configured list. Clear a field's list and save if you want to remove its custom suggestions; that does not remove the field or existing values from audio files.

docs.title: Selection values, custom values and genres
docs.text:
The tag-panel dropdown can combine special keep/blank choices, values already in the selection, the custom list and standard GENRE choices. A selection value already present in the custom list is shown once. Special choices are instructions: < keep > retains each file's own value, while < blank > stages clearing the field.

Prefer values from tags in list at tag panel changes what that panel shows. With it on and at least one nonempty selection value, the dropdown uses the selection's values rather than adding the full custom/standard list. If the field is empty across the selection, custom suggestions remain available. For the practice MOOD list above:

Current selected MOOD values Prefer tag values Ordinary value choices, excluding keep/blank Reflective Off Reflective, Uplifting, Spacious Reflective On Reflective Both empty On Reflective, Uplifting, Spacious

The preference concerns the tag-panel list. File-list and Extended tags completion use custom candidates together with values from loaded files; do not assume the panel's shortlist is a global validation rule. Options → General → Auto-completion at selection boxes independently controls inline completion.

For GENRE, Show only user-defined genres omits the standard genre list. Existing values from selected files can still appear, even if they are not in your custom list. Saving the preference takes effect in OpenTag without the restart described for the original editor.

A custom genre remains text, not an extension of ID3v1's fixed indexed genre vocabulary. Use an appropriate richer format such as ID3v2 for names outside that vocabulary and inspect the actual saved file. Changing a dropdown does not extend a container's storage capabilities.

docs.title: Import and export one field's list
docs.text:
Import… reads one value per text line and merges it with the current field's dialog list. Exact repetitions are removed. It does not import audio tags, replace every field's list or assign the imported entries to tracks. Inspect the merged list, then choose the editor's OK to persist it.

The current reader handles BOM-marked UTF-8/UTF-16 and tries UTF-8 before its Windows-1252 fallback for unmarked text. An older list in another code page can display incorrectly; keep the original and convert a copy to a known Unicode encoding before importing again.

Export… writes the current field's captured list as UTF-8 with a BOM and CRLF line endings. The suggested name follows the field, such as mood.txt. Choose a separate new text-file destination; do not select an audio file or the only copy of an older list backup. This file write happens immediately. Canceling the editor afterward does not delete the exported text file. An export is a useful named checkpoint before a large list change; it is not an audio-file backup.

docs.title: Add a value while editing
docs.text:
In a tag-panel field, type the intended single-line text and press Shift+Enter. OpenTag adds that field's text to its saved custom list. An exact duplicate is not added again; empty or multiline text is rejected. If saving the list fails, read the error rather than assuming it persisted.

This shortcut stores a suggestion. It does not separately save pending audio edits. A field containing a multi-value separator has the normal tag-panel interpretation when applied to tracks; custom list management does not change multi-value syntax.

docs.title: Keep the two save boundaries clear
docs.text:
Cancel in the field-values editor abandons its unsaved list draft. Once its own OK has saved the list, canceling an outer Options dialog does not undo that saved change. An immediate list export also survives a later Cancel. Neither action commits pending track metadata.

The saved tag-panel.json component, included in a configuration backup, carries custom lists and their preferences. For sharing just one list, export that field instead of sharing your entire personal configuration. Session audio Undo is not list-version history: retain a named export or configuration checkpoint before a major edit.

docs.title: Customize the tag panel
docs.text: Choose View → Customize tag panel…, the tag panel's ⋯ → Customize tag panel…, or its Options page to choose the fields you edit most often. A control's Name is its label; Field is the actual metadata name. Showing, hiding or rearranging a control does not by itself remove metadata from an audio file.

docs.title: Add a Mood control
docs.text:
1. Open Customize tag panel… and choose New.
  2. Set Name to M&ood and Field to MOOD.
  3. Keep Default value at < keep > for this practice change.
  4. Choose Text as Type and Normal as Size of field.
  5. Leave its visibility checkbox checked and choose OK.
  6. Select one copied practice file. The panel now offers Mood; enter Calm to stage that field, then save tags when the value is intended.

The ampersand marks o as the label's Alt mnemonic. It is not part of the stored field name or value. && writes a literal ampersand. On macOS, Option combinations can remain text entry in a focused editor; use the visible control when the keyboard context does not route that mnemonic.

docs.title: Every field setting
docs.text:
Setting Purpose Name Display label; an ampersand can mark its mnemonic. Field Uppercase metadata identifier such as MOOD, ISRC or a custom name; type it without % wrappers. Default value Literal value used by the panel's default-filling rules, or the special keep/blank choices below. Type Text, Check or Multiline control. Size of field Relative width: Full, Larger, Large, Medium, Normal, Small, Smaller or Tiny. Rows Visible height of a Multiline control, from 1 to 20 rows. Disabled for other types. Visibility checkbox Whether this control appears on the panel.

A normal metadata field can appear only once in the layout. The field input normalizes names to uppercase and rejects technical information fields, with the two special layout controls described below. Do not paste %mood% into Field; that placeholder syntax belongs in a format string.

docs.title: Understand defaults before selecting a batch
docs.text:
Keep < keep > unless a default should deliberately fill selected files. When several files are selected and the tag panel is visible, its visible fields with non-keep defaults can be staged automatically. Existing pending field edits are protected from that automatic fill. The command Default values in input fields applies configured defaults to visible controls explicitly as well.

Default value Intended staged result < keep > No update < blank > Remove field Reviewed Reviewed %artist% %artist%

The final row is literal text, not a lookup of the artist. Use Tag → Tag or a Format Value action for calculated metadata. These defaults produce pending edits; save tags to write them, and inspect save-on-navigation preferences before assuming they will remain pending.

A non-keep default is not restricted to an empty existing field. It can replace selected files' loaded values when no pending edit blocks that fill. Test a default on copied files and restore < keep > when it should not continue filling later selections.

docs.title: Choose Text, Check or Multiline
docs.text:
Text offers the field's selection values, configured suggestions and applicable special choices in a drop-down. Multiline offers a textarea for notes/lyrics. Rows changes its visible height, not the allowed number of text lines or the audio file's tag format. For individually editing separate values, use Extended tags.

Check is intended for a flag such as COMPILATION. A checked change stages 1; an unchecked change stages clearing the field. The displayed checkbox can be mixed when selected files disagree. Loaded text 0, false, no and empty text count as off, ignoring case and surrounding spaces. Other nonempty values count as on; using Check for a free-text field can therefore normalize its contents when the box is changed.

The following examples refer to one loaded value from each of two selected files, before any checkbox change:

File A value File B value Checkbox state 1 1 On 0 (absent) Off 1 0 Mixed

An untouched mixed state keeps each file's values. Choosing a real on/off state intentionally standardizes that field for the selection.

docs.title: Arrange, hide or remove controls
docs.text:
Use Move up / Move down to reorder fields; Alt+Up/Down in the layout list also moves the current field. Consecutive controls share available space according to their relative sizes. Full occupies the widest slot; smaller controls can fit beside each other. Dock position and available window space affect the final arrangement.

Uncheck a field to hide it temporarily. The tag panel's own menu provides quick show/hide choices too. Remove deletes the layout entry; it does not delete that field's existing metadata. Restore defaults replaces the draft layout with the built-in one for review before OK.

The panel supports at most 100 layout fields. Invalid names, duplicate real fields, unsupported sizes/types or out-of-range row counts prevent saving. Correct the displayed error instead of assuming the saved layout has changed.

docs.title: Directory and separator controls
docs.text:
_DIRECTORY is a folder control, not an editable audio tag. Its drop-down can select files already loaded from a known folder; its browse/new-path routes can load a folder under the normal workspace/pending-change rules. It is different from renaming a folder through a converter or action.

_SEPARATOR starts a new layout row, or a new column when the panel is docked above/below the file list. Separators can be repeated. They do not write a metadata field, and ordinary default filling ignores both special controls. Other underscore-prefixed technical properties cannot be added as editable tag-panel fields.

The Display cover art checkbox shows/hides the cover section, without removing embedded images. Working with covers explains image editing and its separate confirmation paths.

docs.title: Supply consistent suggested values
docs.text:
Use Field values… or Options → Field Values to maintain a list of composer names, moods or another field's preferred spellings. A custom list offers suggestions; selecting a field's layout entry does not rewrite existing tags to match the list.

Shift+Enter in a populated tag-panel field adds its current value to that field's custom suggestions when valid. Genre has additional standard-list preferences. The field-values reference explains list import/export and how selected-file values can take priority over custom suggestions.

docs.title: Save, load and import a panel layout
docs.text:
In Customize tag panel…, Save configuration… writes the current valid layout to a JSON file. It can save a draft before OK; canceling later does not remove that external file. Load configuration… fills the dialog for review, and OK persists/applies it.

The tag panel's direct ⋯ → Load configuration… route instead loads and persists the chosen panel layout immediately. Use View → Show tag panel or physical Control+Q if the loaded layout hides the panel. Keep a known layout export before replacing it. This panel file is separate from audio metadata, custom field-value lists and the whole-application configuration backup.

Where Import Mp3tag configuration… is offered, select a user-supplied usrfields.ini or supported saved panel file. Inspect the imported fields and Not imported report, then choose OK to keep the reviewed layout. Unsupported controls/settings are not an identical-layout guarantee.

docs.title: Customize the toolbars
docs.text: The main toolbar provides selected built-in commands. The custom toolbar can also hold named external tools and action groups. Arrange buttons around the work you repeat, while keeping the menus available for commands you use less often. Rearranging a toolbar does not itself change audio tags.

docs.title: Show a toolbar or recover hidden buttons
docs.text:
Use View → Toolbars → Main toolbar and Custom toolbar to show or hide the complete bars. Those switches preserve their configured items.

The custom toolbar starts enabled but empty. It will not appear until it has a visible command, tool or action-group item. A list containing only separators and spacers does not make a useful custom toolbar appear.

If buttons disappeared, check the whole-bar switch first, then open its customization dialog and check the item visibility. Hide all inside the dialog and hiding the complete toolbar are separate settings. Use the View menu to recover them; loading a whole old configuration changes much more.

docs.title: Practice on the main toolbar
docs.text:
1. Choose View → Toolbars → Customize main toolbar….
  2. Select Save tags in the list. Use Rename… or F4 to give this button the short label Save reviewed tags. Enter keeps the name; Escape cancels the current rename. The command still performs Save tags.
  3. Select another item and use ↑ Move up or ↓ Move down. Checked items are visible in this order. Unchecking an item hides it without removing the underlying menu command.
  4. Add a Separator for a visual division, or a Spacer to push following items toward the far end of the available toolbar space.
  5. Choose OK to save the arrangement. Cancel closes the dialog without saving its draft list. Check the result on screen.

A renamed button keeps its command identity. It does not become a new macro, change the target fields, alter its shortcut or change when the operation writes. Hover or focus buttons to read their descriptions in the status area. A disabled button still follows the command's selection, source and busy-state rules.

Reset in the main-toolbar dialog restores its default item arrangement. It does not change the separate whole-bar show/hide switch. Show all and Hide all affect the dialog's item checkboxes; they are not a reset of options, files or tag values.

docs.title: Main commands available
docs.text:
The default visible command buttons are Open folder, Add files, Save tags, Reload, Filename → Tag, Tag → Filename, Actions and Numbering, with separators between task groups.

The customization list also offers the following built-in commands:

Task family Other available buttons Recover or remove Undo, Redo, Remove tag Edit and convert Extended tags, Filename → Filename, Text File → Tag, Tag → Tag, Quick action Output and inspect Playlist, Export, Find, Refresh Sources and artwork MusicBrainz, Discogs, Covers File access and workspace Show in folder, Play, Tag panel, Filter, Options

These are toolbar labels, which can be shorter than their menu labels. Redo can invoke the available Repeat behavior when there is no recorded redo step. The menu reference and action guide explain the actual operations and their write timing. Showing every button is optional; the toolbar complements the menus rather than replacing them.

docs.title: Build a custom toolbar
docs.text:
1. Create and save any external tool or action group you want to reference. Give definitions distinct, recognizable names.
  2. Choose View → Toolbars → Customize custom toolbar….
  3. In Add to the custom toolbar, choose an entry under Commands, Tools or Action groups, then choose Add.
  4. Add the other needed entries. Use visibility checkboxes, move controls, Rename…, separators and spacers as with the main toolbar.
  5. Choose OK, then enable Custom toolbar under View if it was hidden. Review selection and pending edits before running a newly added action.

Adding an item already in this custom list selects and shows its existing entry; it does not create another copy with the same identity. Remove removes the selected custom-toolbar item. Clear empties the draft custom list. Neither command deletes the original tool, action group or built-in command. Changes are kept only when the dialog is saved with OK.

docs.title: Keep labels separate from references
docs.text:
For example, suppose you saved an external tool named Inspect track and an action group named House#Credit cleanup. A custom button can have a shorter label without changing which saved definition it references:

Saved item identity Custom button label What remains unchanged tool:Inspect track Inspect The tool definition is still named Inspect track action:House#Credit cleanup Credits The action group still has its full saved name save Save reviewed tags The built-in Save tags command and write scope

The identity strings in this table explain the association; choose entries through the dialog instead of typing those strings into a metadata field. Action-group choices display their submenu path using a readable separator.

Tool and action references use the saved name. If that definition is removed or renamed, an old button can become unavailable with a reason such as This tool no longer exists. Edit the custom toolbar. Remove that stale item and add the intended current definition. Renaming the button's label alone does not retarget it. Duplicate tool names are especially confusing because a named custom button resolves the first matching tool; use distinct names rather than relying on duplicate labels to select a different program.

A named action-group button runs that group directly, even if its checkbox in the action library is off. It is different from opening the Actions dialog to apply the currently checked groups. Review the definition and copied test files before clicking it. Its work can write immediately.

docs.title: Use the customization keyboard controls
docs.text:
Focus the item list first. The same controls work in main and custom customization dialogs. Primary-modifier shortcuts use Command on macOS and Control on Windows/Linux. Alt is Option on macOS.

Key Result in the item list F4 Rename the selected item Space Toggle the selected item's visibility Primary+E Show all items Primary+D Hide all items Alt+ArrowUp Move the item up Alt+ArrowDown Move the item down Alt+PageUp Move the item to the beginning Alt+PageDown Move the item to the end

Plain Up/Down, Home and End change the selected item. Inside the rename text box, Enter keeps and Escape cancels that edit. Closing the full customization dialog with Cancel discards its unsaved list changes.

Leading, trailing and adjacent visible separators are omitted from the rendered bar; a separator near hidden items can therefore disappear. Spacers remain layout items. Keep names short: saved custom labels have surrounding whitespace removed and a 60 UTF-16-code-unit limit, so some emoji count as two units. These are button labels; the saved tool/group names are separate data.

docs.title: Keep a known layout
docs.text: A configuration backup includes saved toolbar preferences. Keep one before substantial reorganization. Main-toolbar Reset and custom-toolbar Clear are narrower tools than restoring the whole application configuration. On small screens, available space and layout change; use menus when a full toolbar would be inconvenient. This does not qualify mobile external-tool execution or desktop-only file commands.

docs.title: Open selected files in an external tool
docs.text: A tool starts a program you have installed, using paths from the current selection. It can open a player, editor or inspection application without making you browse to each track again. OpenTag does not automatically undo changes that another application makes.

docs.title: Configure one tool on a copied file
docs.text:
1. Choose one copied ordinary local audio file. Save intended pending edits first so the other application reads the intended data on disk. A tool launch does not save pending tag-panel edits for you.
  2. Open Tools → Configure tools…, or File → Options… → Tools. Choose New and give the entry a name such as Inspect track.
  3. Use Browse… for Path to select the installed program. Enter the executable path separately from its arguments. A path containing spaces belongs in this field without adding shell quotation marks around it.

  4. Leave Parameter empty if the program accepts a file path as its only argument, or enter:

    "%_path%"

  5. Start with for all selected files (otherwise only the first selected file) off. Save the options with OK or Apply.

  6. Run the saved name from the Tools menu or the file-list context menu. Check what the external application actually opened before expanding the selection or enabling per-file launching.

OpenTag begins with no configured tools and permits up to 99 definitions. Its editor changes the selected entry's fields directly; there is no separate Edit-button step. Remove, Move up and Move down manage definitions. Removing an entry does not uninstall the other program.

These instructions describe the launch contract. This guide has not executed your chosen program, checked its options, or qualified an installed version. Use that program's own argument syntax; the examples below explain how OpenTag parses text, not a promise that a particular program supports a flag.

docs.title: Understand the two parsing stages
docs.text:
OpenTag first splits the Parameter text into arguments, then substitutes the supported path placeholders inside each argument. It passes that argument list directly to the program, without invoking a command shell.

For the following examples, the selected file is:

/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac

The table shows the resulting argument list as JSON. The empty-text row means leave the Parameter box blank; "" in another row is actual typed double quotes. JSON quotes, commas and doubled backslashes describe the resulting values; paste the Parameter text, not the JSON list, into the application. Scroll a narrow table sideways to read complete argument boundaries.

Parameter text Argument list for this file (empty text) ["/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] "%_path%" ["/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] %_path% ["/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] --label "%_filename%" "%_path%" ["--label","03 - Paper Boats","/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] "" [""] "" "%_path%" ["","/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] 'two words' ["'two","words'"] "C:\Profiles\Audio Tools\preset.ini" "%_path%" ["C:\Profiles\Audio Tools\preset.ini","/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac"] "%artist%" "$upper(%_filename%)" ["%artist%","$upper(03 - Paper Boats)"] "%_path%" > report.txt ["/Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac",">","report.txt"] "%_path% Error: unmatched double quote

Double quotes group literal whitespace and are removed by the parser. A pair of double quotes can produce an empty argument. Single quotes are ordinary characters here, unlike quoting in scripting expressions or many shells. Backslashes are literal; adding \ does not create a general quote-escape language. An unmatched double quote is rejected.

Whitespace-only Parameter text also uses the default file-path argument. There is no zero-argument tool mode here: an empty box passes a path, while "" passes one empty argument. Open a program normally when no file argument is wanted.

The unquoted %_path% still becomes one argument because expansion happens after splitting. Quoting it remains a clear convention, especially when combining it with literal text. Literal paths with spaces need double quotes to group them before expansion.

The %artist% and $upper row illustrates the limited language: ordinary tag placeholders and scripting functions are not evaluated here. The recognized %_filename% inside the function-looking text expands, but the surrounding $upper(…) remains text. Inserted path text is not recursively scanned again.

Likewise, > is passed as an argument; it does not redirect output. Pipes, shell wildcard expansion and command substitution are not performed by OpenTag. The selected program decides what its arguments mean. Do not paste an entire shell command into Path or assume a converter expression is a tool parameter.

docs.title: All seven supported placeholders
docs.text:
Placeholder names are case-insensitive. For the practice file above and one listed root /Practice, these are the illustrative values on a Unix-style path system. Folder separators follow the actual platform.

Placeholder Value %_path% /Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac %_filename_ext% 03 - Paper Boats.flac %_filename% 03 - Paper Boats %_filename_rel% Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats.flac %_directory% Harbour Lights %_folderpath% /Practice/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/ %_folderpath_rel% Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/

Relative placeholders use the single listed-root context when available. With multiple roots, no usable root, or a file outside that root, they can return absolute paths. If the file is directly in the root, its relative folder path is empty. That empty substitution still occupies its parsed argument; it is not automatically omitted. Prefer %_path% when the other application requires a complete location.

docs.title: Choose one launch or one per file
docs.text:
With for all selected files off, OpenTag runs once for the first selected file in its ordered list. It does not combine every selected path into one invocation. With the option on, it prepares one invocation per selected file. Selection can include rows hidden by a filter, so inspect or reselect the intended targets before launching a batch.

Selected files Per-file option Decision Invocations prepared 2 Off Run 1 2 On Run 2 11 On Decline confirmation 0 11 On Confirm 11 100 On Confirm 100 101 On Confirm Error: more than 100 per-file targets

The UI asks before starting a per-file tool for more than ten selected files. The backend caps a per-file request at 100. That is different from the 99-definition configuration limit. Reduce a larger selection rather than assuming the confirmation removes the limit.

A batch can partly launch before a later launch fails. An error does not roll back programs already started. Check the external application's state before retrying a whole selection.

docs.title: Paths, platforms and completion
docs.text:
Use a full existing executable path, not a command name that only a shell can find through its search path. A macOS .app bundle is accepted and started through /usr/bin/open -a … --args …; how that application consumes arguments or opens windows is separate from OpenTag's parsing contract. An app bundle path on another operating system does not establish support there.

OpenTag sets the spawned process's working directory to each file's existing containing folder when available. For a macOS bundle, that process is the open helper; the GUI application's own working directory is not guaranteed here. This is separate from the listed-root context used for relative placeholders. Avoid relying on a relative program path or an assumed launch directory copied from another tool definition.

Started means launch processes were created, not that the external task finished successfully or opened a separate window for every file. OpenTag discards their standard output/error and does not report their final exit status. Check the other application's UI or output. If it edits tags, resolve any pending OpenTag edits before using Reload tags to inspect the result; a later save of old pending values could overwrite that external edit.

Tools require the desktop application and supported local-file paths. Provider documents and chapter/CUE row references are not automatically valid ordinary filesystem inputs for this command. No mobile or external-program runtime qualification is implied by a saved definition.

docs.title: Shortcuts, default tool and custom buttons
docs.text:
The first ten tool definitions use Cmd+1 through Cmd+0 on macOS or Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+0 on Windows/Linux. The tenth slot uses 0. Reordering changes slot assignments. Tool shortcuts are not dispatched while typing in an ordinary text field, and Alt-digit chords belong to other commands.

Default tool (double-click in the file list) starts at No action. Choosing a saved tool makes a row double-click run that definition using the current selection/scope rules. With No action, OpenTag falls back to Extended tags… on a row double-click; it does not make double-click do nothing. This is an explicit difference from the original editor's described No action behavior.

A custom toolbar can reference a tool by its saved name. Give entries distinct names. Renaming/removing the tool can leave an old custom button unavailable; changing the button's label does not choose a different program. Re-add the intended definition through the custom-toolbar dialog. Keep a configuration backup before changing many definitions, and recheck executable/resource paths after transferring them to another OS.

docs.title: Adapt examples from elsewhere
docs.text: The official Mp3tag community has a user-defined tools collection. Treat those command lines as ideas to inspect and adapt: program locations, quoting, supported placeholders and application options can differ. Test one copied file with the intended program before saving a batch workflow. A community example is not an OpenTag compatibility or installation guarantee.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Export creates a text file from selected audio files: a spreadsheet, track list, HTML catalogue or another report. An export configuration is the template that describes its contents. The output file is the finished report; an .mte file stores a reusable template. Export does not convert audio.

Save pending tag edits, select the files, then choose File → Export… (Ctrl+E; use Cmd+E on a Mac). Export uses the selected files in file-list order unless the template sorts them. The current desktop workflow requires local files; provider-document selections can disable the operation.

If Show selection dialog is off in Options → Export, the command runs the saved configuration immediately. Turn that option on again to edit the template or output choices in the dialog. The steps below assume the dialog is enabled.

docs.title: Make the first report
docs.text:
1. Select the Text configuration.
  2. Set Export file name to an absolute path in a practice folder, such as C:\Reports\tracks.txt on Windows or /Users/you/Reports/tracks.txt on a Mac. Browse… chooses a location without writing the report yet.
  3. Leave Append data and Create one output file per off.
  4. Choose Export. The configuration and preferences are saved, then the report is written. Existing output is replaced unless append is on.

For selected files with ARTIST = Juniper Vale and titles Paper Boats and Lanterns on the Water, Text writes one artist/title line per file. Open the output in a text editor to inspect its actual contents. The catalogue lesson builds a report in small steps; the template language explains the commands.

docs.title: Manage configurations
docs.text:
Select an item under Export configurations to edit it. Export template is a multiline editor. Changes remain when switching configurations within the dialog, but Cancel does not save those edits.

Control or shortcut Result New Create a configuration and enter its name Duplicate Copy the selected configuration with a distinct name Rename, F2, or a second separate click on its selected name Edit its name; Enter or leaving the name field keeps it, Escape cancels Double-click a configuration, Enter, or F4 Focus its template editor Remove Remove the selected configuration when the library is saved Import .mte… Read a template file into a new configuration Save configurations Save templates and preferences without exporting; keep the dialog open Export Save configurations and preferences, then write the report

Names must be nonempty and distinct without regard to case. Use Legacy import encoding (optional) when an imported .mte contains non-Unicode bytes. This controls reading the template, not encoding the report. A Unicode BOM identifies the template's encoding; valid UTF-8 is read as UTF-8. Other legacy text uses the selected/system ANSI codepage, with Windows-1252 as the fallback on macOS and Linux.

Saved configurations have .mte files in the configuration folder's export subfolder. OpenTag discovers other readable .mte files copied there. Keep a backup before editing shared configurations externally. A template made for another application still needs syntax and output checks; its extension alone does not establish compatibility.

docs.title: Choose a name and encoding
docs.text:
Export file name accepts a format string. A relative name uses the first selected audio file's folder as its base; an absolute name chooses a separate location. Fields in a name use the first row of the output group, so the name should identify the group rather than an arbitrary track.

Choosing a configuration prefills a literal $filename default. $filename(html) changes export.txt to export.html; $filename(tracks.cue) supplies that filename in the current output folder. With /lists/export.txt currently shown, $filename(sub/report.csv) supplies /lists/sub/report.csv. A rooted name supplies its own destination.

When that argument contains placeholders, functions or quoting, choosing the configuration clears the name field so the renderer can evaluate it for each output group. For $filename(%EXPORT_NAME%,utf-8) with EXPORT_NAME = report.csv, leaving the field empty produces report.csv, not out.report.csv. Type a name after choosing the configuration to override it deliberately.

Leave this field empty to use $filename(...) from the template. A nonempty dialog name overrides the template's name while leaving its encoding choice in effect. For example, $filename(csv,utf-8) chooses a .csv default but does not replace an explicitly entered report.txt name.

%_workingdir% and %_workingpath% refer to the folder the file list was last changed to, not necessarily the first audio file’s folder. They are available in report text and output-name expressions.

Use UTF-8 for new reports. Set Write BOM under Options → Export when the receiving program needs a byte-order mark. It applies to UTF-8/UTF-16, not ANSI. Don't create directories rejects destinations whose parent folder does not exist; clear that option to allow folder creation.

docs.title: Append or replace
docs.text:
Append data adds the entire rendered report to an existing output file. It does not merge headers, JSON arrays, HTML documents or CSV columns. Appending a header repeats it. The destination must already use a compatible encoding; append does not transcode earlier contents. A new BOM is suppressed when appending to a nonempty file.

Use replace while designing a report. Export writes are not tag edits and are not restored by tag-edit undo. Keep outputs separate from audio and other files you need to retain.

docs.title: Create one output file per group
docs.text:
Enable Create one output file per, then set Partition format. OpenTag evaluates this ordinary format string for every selected file. Equal text values belong to one report; different values produce different reports. Grouping is case-sensitive: Harbour Lights and HARBOUR LIGHTS differ.

For a report per album, %albumartist%|%album% works when those fields reliably identify the album. Fill missing album artists or choose a deliberate fallback. A separator avoids confusing AB + C with A + BC; values containing that separator still need care.

The output name is evaluated separately for every group. For example, %albumartist% - %album%.txt distinguishes reports in one folder. A fixed report.txt would repeatedly target the same path, so OpenTag rejects the collision. Each partition starts with fresh template variables and totals.

For a report in each audio folder, partition by %_folderpath% and name the output %_folderpath%report.txt. Alternatively, use Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Shift+E on a Mac). Per-directory export temporarily replaces the saved partition. A plain or relative name is placed under each audio folder. An absolute output folder keeps that folder and mirrors the selected folders' relative layout below it. Check destinations when files span different roots or drives.

docs.title: Open results and troubleshoot
docs.text:
Options → Messages can offer to open a finished report with its associated program. With several reports, select a written file; Show in… reveals its location. The offer is separate from whether export succeeded.

Symptom Check Export disabled Select local files, save pending edits and wait for the current operation Only one track appears Put repeated content inside $loop(...) and $loopend() Blank lines appear Literal line breaks are output; place control commands deliberately Partition collision Make the output name differ for every group, including missing-field groups Parent folder missing Create it or clear Don't create directories Incomplete report Review file errors; several output files are not one transaction Accented characters look wrong Check output encoding and the receiving program's import setting, separately from .mte import encoding

See CSV for spreadsheet import and the template gallery for ready-to-edit reports.

docs.title: Export CSV
docs.text: CSV stores a table as text: one record per track, with quoted fields separated by commas. Use it to inspect or share metadata in a spreadsheet. Exporting does not change the selected audio files, and editing the spreadsheet does not automatically write values back to them.

docs.title: Use the built-in configuration
docs.text:
1. Save pending edits and select the tracks.
  2. Choose File → Export… and select CSV (spreadsheet).
  3. Choose a destination ending in .csv, or leave Export file name empty to use the configuration's default extension.
  4. Keep Append data off for one table with one header. Choose Export.

The bundled table contains Path, Title, Artist, Album, Album artist, Track, Disc, Year, Genre and Length. It preserves file-list order, uses UTF-8 and CRLF record endings, quotes every value and doubles embedded double quotes.

For a title Paper, "folded" Boats, the title cell is written as "Paper, ""folded"" Boats". The comma remains inside that cell; doubled quotes represent one quote. A value containing a real line break can span physical lines inside a quoted cell. Counting text-file lines is therefore not always the same as counting CSV records.

docs.title: Import deliberately in the spreadsheet
docs.text:
Use the spreadsheet's text/CSV import command when double-clicking the file guesses incorrectly. Choose UTF-8, comma as the delimiter and double quote as the text qualifier. A program configured for semicolon-separated regional CSV may otherwise put the entire record in one column.

Import tracks, disc numbers, identifiers and date-like strings as Text when their spelling matters. Automatic conversion can turn 03 into 3, interpret 2/8 as a date, or round a long numeric identifier. CSV quotes keep delimiters inside fields; they do not tell a spreadsheet which data type to use. Check several records before saving another copy.

If accented names are misread, first select UTF-8 in the import dialog. Some programs use a BOM to recognize UTF-8 when opening files directly. Enable Write BOM in Options → Export if that program requires it. BOM and delimiter are independent settings.

docs.title: Build a smaller three-column table
docs.text:
Duplicate a configuration before replacing its template. This one exports Artist, Title and Track with an explicit header and CRLF records:

$filename(csv,utf-8)"Artist","Title","Track"$char(13)$char(10)$loop(1)"$replace(%artist%,","")","$replace(%title%,","")","$replace(%track%,","")"$char(13)$char(10)$loopend()

The first quoted row is literal text outside the loop, so it appears once. Each loop iteration wraps the field in double quotes. $replace changes every embedded " to ""; the surrounding CSV quotes are then added by the template. Every field uses that rule, including TRACK: metadata remains editable text even when it usually contains a number. For example, TRACK = 03"take becomes the CSV cell "03""take". Apply the same escaping when adding another field.

For one track with artist Juniper Vale, title Paper, "folded" Boats and track 03, the records are:

"Artist","Title","Track"
"Juniper Vale","Paper, ""folded"" Boats","03"

To use semicolons, change the literal separators between quoted cells in both the header and body. Keep the commas inside $replace(...): those separate function arguments and have a different purpose.

docs.title: Change ordering or split tables
docs.text:
$loop(1) keeps input order. Replace its key with $num(%track%,3) to sort numerically by track within the selected set. For several albums, use a grouping or partition strategy rather than interleaving every album's track 1.

Create one output file per can make a separate CSV per album. Give each partition a distinct filename; the template emits a header for every new document. Appending the same template repeats that header, which most spreadsheet imports treat as another data record.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
Result Remedy Everything is in one column Select the actual delimiter during import Leading zeros disappear Reimport the column as Text; changing display format after conversion may not recover the original spelling Accents look garbled Select UTF-8 or use the receiving program's required BOM Columns shift after a quoted title Double embedded quotes, and quote every arbitrary text cell Header repeats halfway through Replace the output instead of appending the full template Changes in a spreadsheet do not appear in OpenTag Export is one-way; a separate import workflow must map fields and match files deliberately

See export controls and the template language for partitioning, naming, loops and encodings.

docs.title: Template gallery
docs.text: Copy a complete template into a duplicated export configuration, select a few practice files and inspect the written output before expanding the selection. Each example chooses UTF-8 and uses explicit line breaks. Leave Export file name empty to use its default, or enter a deliberate override. See the template reference for commands and scopes.

docs.title: Numbered track list
docs.text:
$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop($num(%track%,3))$num(%track%,2). %title% — %artist%$char(10)$loopend()Files: %_total_files%; duration: %_total_time%

Select one album. Padded track keys make track 2 precede track 10; $num in the body formats the printed number separately. The summary is outside the loop and therefore covers the full report. For multi-disc albums, sort by a padded disc key followed by a padded track key.

docs.title: One line per album
docs.text:
$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(%albumartist%)$loop(%album%,1)$if2(%albumartist%,%artist%) — %album%[ (%year%)]$char(10)$loopend()$loopend()

The outer level groups album artists. The inner level emits only the first row of each album key. Optional year punctuation disappears when that row's YEAR is missing. Complete ALBUMARTIST consistently first: a missing album artist forms one empty outer group, even though the printed name falls back to ARTIST. Also distinguish separate editions before using a title as a key.

docs.title: A small HTML catalogue
docs.text:
$filename(html,utf-8)<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Track catalogue</title><h1>Track catalogue</h1><ul>$char(10)$loop(1)<li>$replace(%artist%,&,&,<,<,>,>) — $replace(%title%,&,&,<,<,>,>)</li>$char(10)$loopend()</ul><p>Files: %_total_files%</p>

For artist Kofi & the Tidewater Band and title Low <Tide>, the HTML contains Kofi & the Tidewater Band — Low <Tide> inside a list item. A browser displays the original characters as text instead of interpreting a tag. The replacements process & first so later entities do not get escaped twice.

This example places values only in text content. HTML attributes, links, JavaScript and CSS have different escaping requirements; do not move the same expression into those contexts without changing the design. No covers are embedded or extracted by this template. An image element requires an actual image file at the referenced path.

docs.title: A CSV table
docs.text: Use CSV (spreadsheet) for a complete table, or start with the smaller worked template on the CSV page. Quote fields and double embedded quotes; replacing commas alone is not a CSV encoder. The built-in CSV export already performs the necessary field quoting.

docs.title: JSON and playlists
docs.text:
The bundled JSON configuration writes an array with a per-file object. It escapes backslashes, quotes, line breaks and tabs in its text fields. Literal array brackets are quoted because [ and ] are format-string syntax. Validate the resulting JSON with the receiving program, especially after adding new fields or unusual control characters. A hand-written report that merely resembles JSON is not a substitute for a valid structured file.

The bundled Extended M3U playlist uses relative audio paths, durations and display titles. Cue sheet lists one FILE/TRACK entry per selected file in input order. A cue sheet does not combine audio files or infer musical track boundaries inside a long recording.

docs.title: Adapt the examples progressively
docs.text:
1. Verify one field on one practice file.
  2. Verify the repeated row on two files, including a title with punctuation.
  3. Add sorting, then grouping, and check the first and last row of each group.
  4. Change naming or partitioning only after the report body is correct.
  5. Test the actual receiving program and its encoding/import settings.

Keep the unmodified copy of a working template. A template that renders without an error can still choose the wrong grouping key, repeat headers, point to nonexistent images or produce a format the receiver cannot parse.

docs.title: External starting points
docs.text: The Mp3tag Community export configuration archive links to community templates for other report styles. Inspect a template and its companion files before adapting it. Import and editing workflows, supported syntax and output assumptions can differ in OpenTag. Test a small selection and inspect the actual report; inclusion in that archive does not establish that every template works unchanged here.

docs.title: Export template language
docs.text:
An export template mixes literal text, field placeholders and scripting functions. A loop repeats a section for several files. Text outside a loop is evaluated once, using the first input row where a field value is needed. A report can therefore have one heading, many track lines and one summary.

The format-string rules apply to fields, functions, optional sections and apostrophe quoting. Export adds commands and counters below. It also accepts %% for one literal percent sign and $$ for one literal dollar sign. This export-specific escaping does not make %% a valid ordinary tag-converter expression.

docs.title: Start with a repeatable row
docs.text:
For two selected files in the order Paper Boats, then Lanterns on the Water, both by Juniper Vale, this complete template writes two artist/title lines:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(1)%artist% - %title%$char(10)$loopend()

The result has a line break after each title, including the last. Read it in four pieces:

  1. $filename(txt,utf-8) chooses the default extension and encoding.
  2. $loop(1) starts a loop in the current input order.
  3. %artist% - %title%$char(10) renders one row and an LF line break.
  4. $loopend() closes the loop and prints nothing itself.

Literal template line breaks are also copied. $char(10) makes intentional line breaks visible in a one-line template. Use $char(13)$char(10) for CRLF. There is no automatic separator between iterations. Leading/trailing literal spaces remain in the report.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text: Command Arguments and result $filename([name[,encoding]]) Set the default output name/extension and optional encoding; print nothing $loop(key[,limit]) Sort the current input set by a key and render its body; limit is per equal key $loopend() Close the matching loop; take no arguments $get(name) Return a stored export value, or empty when absent $put(name,value) Store a value and return it $puts(name,value) Store a value and return empty text

docs.title: $filename: name, extension and encoding
docs.text:
Put it once, before the first non-whitespace output. Do not put it inside a loop. Leading whitespace can precede it but still belongs to the report. A second or later $filename is an error.

Template prefix Default behavior $filename(csv,utf-8) Replace the current default extension with .csv; write UTF-8 $filename(catalogue.html,utf-8) Use this name beside the current default output $filename(reports/catalogue.txt,utf-8) Use the relative subfolder below the current default's folder $filename(,utf-16) Keep the default name; write UTF-16 little-endian $filename(txt,ansi) Choose .txt; encode through the ANSI codepage

A bare argument without ., a slash, backslash or : is an extension, not a complete filename. An absolute name selects an absolute location. Arguments can use expressions evaluated in the first row of the output group. Export file name overrides this name when nonempty, leaving its encoding in effect.

Encoding names are utf-8, utf-16 and ansi, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. Omitting the encoding argument selects ANSI: the system codepage on Windows, and Windows-1252 on macOS/Linux. Bundled configurations already name a Unicode encoding. Unrepresentable characters become ?; use Unicode to preserve all names. Template-file encoding and report encoding are independent.

docs.title: $loop: sort before rendering
docs.text:
Use a field or expression as the key:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop($num(%track%,3))%track% - %title%$char(10)$loopend()

For tracks 10, 2 and 1, padded keys 010, 002 and 001 give output order 1, 2, 10. Plain %track% is a text sort and can put 10 before 2. Current desktop export uses case-insensitive text keys; equal keys keep their input order. $loop(1) gives ordinary rows one key, preserving file-list order. A bare field name such as $loop(artist) also reads that field; %artist% makes its purpose clearer.

The optional limit is a nonnegative integer evaluated in the parent context. Omit it, use an empty result, or use 0 for all rows. Without a nested loop, $loop(%artist%,1) prints the first row for each distinct artist key, rather than only the first artist globally:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(%artist%,1)%artist%$char(10)$loopend()

Two Juniper Vale tracks and one Mira Solberg track produce one line per artist. Only the first row of a key supplies ordinary fields. Consider that before adding an album or year to a unique-artist summary.

docs.title: Nested loops: one heading per group
docs.text:
When a loop contains another loop, the outer loop renders once per key and passes that key's entire member set to the inner loop. An album heading can therefore be followed by all its tracks:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(%album%)%album% — files: %_total_files%$char(10)$loop($num(%track%,3))  $num(%track%,2) %title%$char(10)$loopend()$loopend()

For Harbour Lights with Paper Boats (track 1) and Lanterns on the Water (track 2), plus Low Tide with North Pier (track 1), the result is:

Harbour Lights — files: 2
  01 Paper Boats
  02 Lanterns on the Water
Low Tide — files: 1
  01 North Pier

The outer key chooses an album and its total is the album's member count. The inner key sorts those members by track; its two leading spaces indent the track lines. After the inner loop, the outer row and counter are restored. Albums with identical names form one group even when their artists differ. Add an artist level outside the album loop when that distinction matters.

docs.title: Variables: carry a result between steps
docs.text:
Variables exist for one output document. Names are case-sensitive. Variables are not tags and do not edit audio files. Each partition starts afresh.

$filename(txt,utf-8)$puts(count,0)$loop(1)$puts(count,$add($get(count),1))%title%$char(10)$loopend()Rows written: $get(count)

After the three practice files, the final text is Rows written: 3. $puts updates silently; $put would print its value as well. $get returns the stored value's availability/truth flags together with its text, so the condition rules still apply.

Arguments are evaluated eagerly. A variable write in an "unused" $if branch can still run. The same caution applies when a branch contains an export loop. Build state changes as explicit steps in their intended order.

docs.title: Counters, totals and paths
docs.text:
Placeholder Meaning %_counter% One-based current iteration number; nested loops have their own counters %_max_counter% Iterations completed by the most recently finished loop; initially 0 %_total_files% Input rows in the current group %_total_size_raw% Sum of current-group file sizes in bytes %_total_size% Human-readable size using 1024-based units, with two decimals above bytes %_total_time_raw% Current-group duration in seconds, rounded after summing %_total_time% HH:MM:SS, with a day prefix after 24 hours %_total_time2% Duration with total hours, such as 25:01:01 %_filename_rel% Audio path relative to the actual report folder %_folderpath_rel% Audio folder relative to the report folder, with a trailing separator

Outside loops, totals cover the output partition. Inside an iteration, totals describe all rows with that loop key, including members omitted by a per-key output limit. A unique-artist loop can finish with _max_counter = 2 while _total_files = 3 after returning to the full report context.

Relative paths use the final destination, including a dialog override. For /Music/Harbour/01.mp3 reported in /Reports/catalogue.txt, the relative name is ../Music/Harbour/01.mp3. On Windows, a file on another drive or UNC share stays absolute; there is no relative path between volumes.

%_workingdir% and %_workingpath% use the app’s working folder in both report text and output-name expressions. They differ from each input audio file’s own folder placeholders.

Normal placeholders and scripting functions are available. Real file hashes %_crc%, %_md5% and %_md5audio% require reading file data and can take longer than tag-only output. Audio MD5 can be empty when the format has no such value; hashes are not invented from tags.

docs.title: Troubleshoot in stages
docs.text:
Start with one row and field, then add a loop, sorting, grouping and formatting separately. Inspect the saved report after each stage.

Problem Next check $loop without a matching $loopend Balance pairs from the inside out Unexpected optional closing bracket Quote literal [ and ], especially for JSON Wrong argument count Quote literal commas or closing parentheses inside arguments Empty replacement becomes an apostrophe Leave the argument empty; '' writes an apostrophe Titles run together Put an explicit line break inside the loop Repeated album headings Put the track loop inside the album loop Template rejected for resource limits Reduce nested work or split the selected input

The renderer limits template size, nesting, output size and evaluation work. These limits can reject an oversized report rather than hang the application. They do not make every accepted template equally quick.

docs.title: Start using OpenTag
docs.text:
OpenTag changes the information stored inside audio files: titles, artists, albums, track numbers and embedded artwork. It can also rename files from those values, import information from names, and repeat a sequence of changes. A renamed file and a changed song title are different results; choose the operation that matches the problem you want to solve.

This starting path is for a first desktop session. Use a copied album with a few ordinary audio files. Keep the originals elsewhere until you have checked the saved result in OpenTag and in the player you use.

docs.title: 1. Install a package for your computer
docs.text:
Follow Download and install. Pick the operating system and processor architecture on the release page. The source-code archive is for building OpenTag; it is not an installer. Mobile previews have different access and save-back limits, so do not use a desktop walkthrough as a promise of the same result on a phone.

After opening the application, check Help → About OpenTag when reporting a problem. Keep its version and your operating system with your notes.

docs.title: 2. Open only your practice folder
docs.text:
Choose File → Change directory… and select the copied album. This replaces the loaded list; Add directory… and Add files… add to it instead. Read Opening files before mixing several folders or turning on startup restoration.

Loading reads metadata and file properties. It does not, by itself, rewrite the files. The list is a working view, not a separate music-library copy. Check the loaded count and remove an active filter if fewer rows appear than expected. The main window explains where these counts and controls live.

docs.title: 3. Make one recognizable pending edit
docs.text:
1. Select one practice file. Check the selected count beside the filter.
  2. In the tag panel, change Album to Harbour Lights — practice.
  3. Look for its pending marker and the unsaved files count. The changed text is visible, but an ordinary tag-panel edit still needs saving.
  4. Choose File → Save tags (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S).
  5. Read the status and any file errors. Choose File → Reload tags to read the saved result again. If the album returns to the old value, investigate the error rather than repeating a larger batch.

For this exercise, check Options → Tags → Save tags when using arrow keys or a single mouse click. It is off by default. When enabled, a selection change can write pending edits, so moving to another row is no longer a reliable way to leave the file untouched.

A displayed < keep > means preserve each selected file's current value. Clearing an editable field requests removal. It does not mean “leave it alone.” Read Editing, saving and undo before editing several files together.

docs.title: 4. Choose a task and its write timing
docs.text:
Your goal Use When the result is written Give several tracks the same album Tag panel Review pending edits, then Save tags Inspect fields outside the panel Extended tags Keep changes stages edits; save afterward Fill fields from folder and file names Filename → Tag Applying the converter writes its result Give filenames consistent track/title text Tag → Filename Applying the rename changes paths Calculate a field from other fields Tag → Tag Applying the converter writes its result Repeat cleanup in a defined order Action groups Running the group writes its changes Create a report for a spreadsheet CSV export Write an external report; it is not a tag backup

The same panel can edit files from different containers, but native storage and supported writes differ. Check tag formats when a player disagrees with the editor. Extended tags also allows custom field names; another player need not display or understand those fields. For online lookup commands, start with the Tag Sources menu and review the retrieved release and track matches before applying anything.

An ordinary tag-panel text box does not calculate scripting functions. Typing $upper(%artist%) there stores that text. The format-string lesson shows where expressions are evaluated and why quoted text and optional sections matter.

docs.title: 5. Recover deliberately
docs.text:
Before saving, use Edit → Discard pending changes on the intended selection to abandon its unsaved edits. After a recorded write, inspect the operation named by Edit → Undo …. History belongs to the current session; it is not a permanent backup and does not reverse every external output. A batch can partly succeed, so check individual failures before closing.

Replacing the list or closing can discard pending work. Prompts are configurable under Options → Messages; turning one off does not save the edits. Save or discard deliberately before changing folders or loading a configuration. If another program changed a file, reload it before deciding which values to keep.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Your first tagging session walks through a complete practice album.
  • What tags are separates stored fields, filenames and player display.
  • Format strings from zero builds expressions from worked inputs and outputs.
  • Regular expressions from zero introduces matching and captures before larger cleanup recipes.

docs.title: Editing, saving and undo
docs.text: Changing a value on screen and writing it into an audio file are separate steps. Use this page to practice that distinction, save a reviewed selection, and recover from a change before continuing with a whole album.

docs.title: Make one change you can recognize
docs.text:
1. Work on a copied audio file. Select it in the file list.
  2. In the tag panel, replace its Album with Harbour Lights — practice.
  3. Look for the pending marker beside the row and the unsaved files count. The displayed album changes immediately; this is still a pending edit.
  4. Choose File → Save tags (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S).
  5. Inspect the operation result. After a successful save, that file's pending marker clears. File → Reload tags reads the saved result again.

The shortcuts with Cmd use ⌘ on macOS; use Ctrl on Windows and Linux. While learning, use menu items if a text field's focus makes a shortcut ambiguous.

A field left unchanged is kept. An explicitly cleared field requests removal. A format string typed into an ordinary tag-panel field is stored as text; use Tag → Tag to calculate it.

docs.title: Save the intended selection
docs.text:
Save tags writes pending edits for the selected files. The status bar's unsaved-file count covers the loaded list, so it can include files outside that selection. A successful save of one selection need not clear every pending marker in the window.

Before saving a batch, check the selected count, the fields changed and any active filter. A filter can hide an already selected row; hiding it does not necessarily remove it from the selection. Select the intended files again when the scope is uncertain.

A batch can partly succeed. For example, all three files below have pending album edits, but only the first two are selected for saving:

File Selected for Save Result Pending afterward 01 - Paper Boats.mp3 Yes Saved No 02 - North Pier.mp3 Yes Failed Yes 03 - Quiet Harbour.mp3 No Not attempted Yes

A failure does not turn the successful first write into a failure too. Read each file error, fix its cause, and retry the files that still need saving. Cancel stops remaining work; it does not roll back files already written. Unattempted edits remain pending. Do not close the application merely because some files in the batch were saved.

docs.title: Discard, reload or undo
docs.text:
Goal Command What to expect Abandon unsaved edits in selected files Edit → Discard pending changes Return to the loaded values without reading the files again Read selected files again after an external edit File → Reload tags Read current storage and discard those files' pending edits after confirmation Reverse a recorded write Edit → Undo … Restore the operation named in the menu, when its history step is available Reapply a reversed operation Edit → Redo … Restore its redo state, when available

Discarding pending edits is different from undoing a saved operation. Undo does not mean “clear every unsaved edit”: pending edits are retained when recorded file history is replayed. Inspect them afterward so a later save does not unintentionally write those pending values over the restored file.

History is for the current desktop session. Read its operation label and file count, including any failure notice. It is not a durable backup of the library, and changes made by another program are not automatically reversible here. A batch history operation can concern several files, beyond the current selection.

The Redo menu slot can instead say Repeat. Repeat runs the available last action or action group again on the current selection; it does not restore a historical snapshot. Use action groups to understand what that repeated operation will do.

docs.title: Know which commands write immediately
docs.text:
Tag-panel text edits, metadata cells, Keep changes in Extended tags, Cut/Paste tags and staged auto-numbering wait for Save tags. A filename cell edits a path instead of a metadata field.

Actions, applied converters, Remove tag…, and direct artwork commands write when run. They do not leave their completed results waiting for a later Save command. Managed cover edits have their own OK commit step. Follow the specific dialog's preview and confirmation instructions.

docs.title: Check automatic saving and prompts
docs.text:
Under File → Options… → Tags, Save tags when using arrow keys or a single mouse click is off by default. When enabled, a supported selection change can save pending edits from the previous selection of local files. This includes mouse/arrow navigation, Select next file, and leaving the selection through commands such as Unselect all. Extending a selection can also trigger a save of previously selected pending files. Treat selection changes as potentially writing when this preference is on.

Extended tags has a separate navigation save-mode setting for its << and >> buttons. See Tags options for its pending, ask, ignore and save choices.

Commands that would replace the list, reload or close with pending edits can ask whether to discard them. Options → Messages controls these prompts. Disabling a prompt does not save the edits automatically. Resolve the edits first when they need to survive closing the window.

docs.title: Respect storage and access limits
docs.text:
Options → Files → Preserve timestamps of modified files preserves the file's modification time during supported writes. It does not make a save invisible to backups, preserve every filesystem date, or stop metadata bytes from changing.

Tag storage is format-specific. An ordinary save can synchronize several configured tag types and remove a type selected for removal but not writing. Review Tags options before changing storage policies to solve a player compatibility issue.

Read-only local files can fail to save. Provider-backed documents have their own access and recovery state: follow Source read-only, Source access unknown or Recovery required messages. Save a copy… can preserve supported edited tag fields or an original backup when offered; pending artwork is not included in that copy request. It is not a general desktop “Save As” replacement. See the File menu.

docs.title: Download and install
docs.text: Download OpenTag from the project's GitHub releases. Open a release's Assets list and choose a package for your operating system and processor. You do not need Rust, Node.js or the source-code ZIP to run a published package. Those are part of the developer build workflow.

docs.title: Choose the right download
docs.text:
The following is the verified v0.2.12 package set. Check a newer release's own notes and assets before assuming its names, signing or requirements match. arm64 means an ARM processor; x64 means a 64-bit Intel/AMD processor. On a Mac, About This Mac distinguishes Apple silicon from Intel.

On a narrow screen, scroll this package table sideways to read its limitations.

System v0.2.12 package What to expect Windows x64 OpenTag-v0.2.12-windows-x64-setup.exe Desktop installer; no Authenticode publisher signature macOS Apple silicon OpenTag-v0.2.12-macos-arm64.dmg or .app.tar.gz Desktop application; ad-hoc signed, not notarized macOS Intel OpenTag-v0.2.12-macos-x64.dmg or .app.tar.gz Same signing limits; choose the Intel build Linux x64 or arm64 Matching .AppImage, .deb or .rpm Unsigned desktop packages, built on Ubuntu 24.04; older-distribution compatibility is not established Android arm64 OpenTag-v0.2.12-android-arm64-signed.apk Signed preview; document editing and save-back remain in progress iOS ARM64 simulator OpenTag-v0.2.12-ios-arm64-simulator-preview-debug.app.zip Unsigned simulator preview; not an iPhone/iPad installer

There is no Windows portable ZIP or Store package in this release. Copying an AppImage or a macOS application does not create a separate portable settings profile: configuration belongs to the current user. Do not apply Mp3tag's installation modes, Windows requirements or configuration paths to OpenTag.

docs.title: Check the download before running it
docs.text:
The same release includes SHA256SUMS and release-manifest.json. Download SHA256SUMS, calculate the SHA-256 of the package you downloaded, and compare all hexadecimal characters with the line for that exact filename. A mismatch means stop and download the correct asset again. Comparing with the release's checksum detects a mismatched or damaged download; it is not a replacement for trusting the download source or a publisher signature.

For example, in the folder containing the downloaded file:

macOSWindowsLinux 
shasum -a 256 'OpenTag-v0.2.12-macos-arm64.dmg'

In PowerShell:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath '.\OpenTag-v0.2.12-windows-x64-setup.exe'

Microsoft's Get-FileHash reference explains the returned hash and literal-path handling.

sha256sum 'OpenTag-v0.2.12-linux-x64.AppImage'

Change the filename to your actual architecture and package. You only need to compare the asset you downloaded; checking every line as a batch would also try to read the other packages you have not downloaded.

docs.title: Install the desktop application
docs.text:
macOSWindowsLinux
  1. Open the matching .dmg, then copy OpenTag.app to your Applications folder. With .app.tar.gz, extract the archive to obtain OpenTag.app and copy that application instead.
  2. Open the copied application. v0.2.12 has no Apple notarization, so macOS may refuse to open it under its normal policy.
  3. If you have verified and trust this download, follow Apple's app-specific opening procedure: after the opening attempt, use System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway, when offered, and confirm Open.

A managed Mac may not permit that exception. A damaged-app or malware alert is not automatically the same situation; stop and follow Apple's guidance. Do not disable Gatekeeper globally or remove security attributes as a routine installation step.

  1. Run the x64 -setup.exe and follow its installation choices.
  2. If Windows displays an unknown-publisher or reputation warning, check that the download came from the intended release. v0.2.12 has no Authenticode signature; the guide cannot provide a verified publisher name to expect. Respect organizational restrictions.
  3. Open OpenTag after installation. If the WebView2 runtime is missing, the Tauri installer uses its default bootstrapper, which can require internet access to obtain it. See Tauri's Windows installer documentation.

A runtime download failure is different from an audio-file read error. Resolve the installation problem before trying metadata operations.

For .deb or .rpm, use your distribution's package installer so declared dependencies are handled. The v0.2.12 x64 DEB package is named open-tag and declares GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1 and Ayatana app-indicator libraries. A package being available does not qualify every distribution/version.

For an AppImage, make the downloaded file executable using the file manager's permissions control, then open it. The command-line equivalent for the x64 example is:

chmod u+x 'OpenTag-v0.2.12-linux-x64.AppImage'
./OpenTag-v0.2.12-linux-x64.AppImage

See the official AppImage quickstart if the file cannot be launched. Missing runtime/FUSE support or system libraries need distribution-appropriate handling; an AppImage is not a guarantee of compatibility with every older Linux installation.

docs.title: Understand the mobile downloads
docs.text:
The Android APK is signed with the project's persistent application key. Signing allows that package identity to be checked for updates; it does not establish desktop feature parity, Google developer-verification status or permission to install under every device policy. Follow Google's Android installation guidance and the device manufacturer's instructions for a downloaded APK. Keep Play Protect enabled. Installation controls can vary by device and policy.

The iOS archive is a simulator application for a development environment. It cannot be installed on an iPhone by opening the ZIP. Neither mobile asset is evidence of App Store distribution or validated editing/save-back on your device. Use copied material and follow the build's source-access messages.

docs.title: Update without confusing settings and music
docs.text:
Help → Check for updates… checks releases and can open a release page. It does not install the update automatically. Check the new release's notes, finish pending edits, close the old application, then use its matching package. An optional startup check is configured under Updates options.

Before an update or settings experiment, choose File → Save configuration…. This writes an OpenTag JSON configuration bundle containing the supported saved options, action groups, export configurations, columns, tag-panel layout, favorite directories and remembered lists that exist in the configuration folder. It does not save pending tag edits, back up audio, or include the Discogs access token. Keep installed source files and other external resources separately when you need them.

To restore that bundle, finish or discard pending work, then choose File → Load configuration… and review the replacement warning. The application reloads its window. A configuration bundle is not Mp3tag's ZIP backup format and does not merge every setting from an arbitrary old installation.

On desktop, File → Open configuration folder locates the actual current folder; use that instead of guessing another editor's path. Do not modify live configuration files while the application is saving them. Removing the application is separate from deleting per-user configuration or music: use the operating system's app/package management and decide deliberately which backups and settings to retain.

docs.title: If the application will not start
docs.text:
Check the release/architecture, verify the checksum, and record the exact operating-system message. Do not repeatedly reinstall over an unexplained security alert. When reporting an issue, include the release filename, version, OS version and whether failure occurs before the window appears or only after opening files. Do not attach access tokens or personal music.

These steps are based on release assets, package metadata, application source and official platform instructions. They are not a claim that every native installation, OS version or mobile device has been tested.
