docs.title: Reuse loaded metadata with the Library
docs.text: The Library is a persistent cache of metadata OpenTag has read. It can avoid parsing unchanged files again when you reopen an album. It does not contain your music, scan an entire disk by itself or turn a remembered path into an accessible audio file.

docs.title: Enable it for one practice folder
docs.text:
1. Open File → Options… → Library. Enable Library starts off.
  2. Enable it. If you want to limit persistent caching, also enable Only include these directories and use Add… to choose your copied practice folder.
  3. Save the Options with OK or Apply. Merely adding a folder to the inclusion list does not load or scan it.
  4. Open that folder using Change directory… or Add directory…, with the intended subfolder setting. The first load still reads the audio files.
  5. Reopen the same unchanged files. Inspect the Library status in Options for its stored-file count, database size and last-load cache/read counts.

The status wording read from disk and stored counts entries actually stored in this cache session, not every disk read of an excluded file. With the cache disabled or unavailable, those counters can describe the preceding cache-backed load rather than a new direct scan. They are diagnostic hints, not a complete I/O audit or timing measurement.

Later loads can reuse entries when the path, modification timestamp, file size and reader/settings fingerprint match. A changed reading policy or reader revision can require a fresh read even when the physical file did not change. There is no promised speedup for every collection or storage device.

docs.title: Understand what is indexed—and what is queried
docs.text:
The Library is queried internally by the paths being loaded. There is no separate full-collection Library browser or “open every indexed track” command in the inspected UI. Open actual files, folders or playlists through the normal File commands.

Filter and Find work with the loaded file list. They do not search every cached path that is currently absent from that list. A known cache entry also does not grant provider permission, reconnect a network drive or restore a file removed from disk.

Item What it represents Is it an audio backup? Loaded file-list row Information currently shown for an opened file/row No Pending edits Unsaved field/artwork intent in the current workspace No Library entry Previously read metadata plus file/reader validity information No Embedded cover bytes Image data stored in the audio file and read when needed Part of that audio file, not the Library cache Independent copied audio file A separate file you intentionally keep Only to the extent you have verified and retained that copy

The database resides below the current configuration folder at library/library.db. It stores metadata and image descriptors; it does not move embedded image bytes or other binary payloads out of your files into the database. This differs from the binary-storage behavior described for the original editor's Library.

docs.title: Choose included folders without hiding music
docs.text:
With Only include these directories off, the cache can store files loaded from any ordinary supported location. With it on, only files within the listed folders are persistently cached. Descendant album folders belong to the selected parent scope.

Files outside that scope can still be loaded and edited; they are read from disk rather than stored for later cache reuse. A restricted but empty folder list caches nothing. The restriction is a cache policy, not a file-list filter, a ban on opening other folders, or a backup selection.

Remove in the included-directory list removes the inclusion entry, not the music folder. Existing cache rows outside a newly restricted scope can remain until maintenance removes them, but they are not eligible for scoped reuse. Recheck the intended scope before Cleanup Library: cleanup uses the directory restriction currently shown in that Options dialog.

docs.title: Know when an old value can survive
docs.text:
Consider one file already cached with TITLE = Paper Boats. These are examples of cache eligibility, rather than a complete corruption detector:

Next load Expected cache behavior Same path, size, timestamp and reader settings The stored entry can be reused The file size or modification timestamp changed Read the file again Tag-reading options or reader fingerprint changed Read under the current interpretation File → Reload tags is requested Force a new read instead of reusing the entry An external edit keeps both size and timestamp unchanged The old entry can still look valid; force a reload

OpenTag's own supported write/move/delete paths invalidate affected cache entries so a later load reads them again. That is not an automatic watch of every external program's changes. A collection manager or timestamp-preserving editor can leave the stamp unchanged.

When a value looks stale:

  1. Inspect whether OpenTag shows a pending value rather than a saved one. Resolve pending edits deliberately before discarding them.
  2. Select the affected files and choose File → Reload tags (Cmd+T / Ctrl+T). The normal pending-edit confirmation explains that reloading discards selected unsaved intent.
  3. Compare the result with the tag-reading policy and the actual saved file. Multiple stored tag blocks or a player's own cache can explain disagreement even after OpenTag's Library entry is refreshed.
  4. If deliberately rebuilding the cache is needed, use Clear Library… as described below. Clearing it does not repair file contents.

Do not infer a fresh metadata read merely from reopening a file, or infer saved metadata from what an unsaved field currently displays.

docs.title: Clean orphaned entries
docs.text:
Reconnect removable/network storage first if its cached entries should be kept. Cleanup Library checks whether cached paths remain accessible and within the chosen inclusion scope. A temporarily disconnected path can be removed from the cache as an orphan.

  1. Open the Library Options page and inspect the displayed restriction/folders.
  2. Choose Cleanup Library and watch its checked/removed counts.
  3. Use Cancel if necessary. Entries already removed remain removed; cancellation stops further checking rather than rolling maintenance back.
  4. Inspect the result and any error. Reopening a still-existing file can add its metadata again when the enabled inclusion policy allows it.

Cleanup does not delete the referenced audio files, reorganize folders, refresh every surviving tag value or discard pending edits in the workspace. It is not a substitute for Reload tags after an external timestamp-preserving edit.

docs.title: Clear and rebuild the cache
docs.text:
Clear Library… asks whether to remove every cache entry. Choose Clear to proceed or Keep to cancel. This maintenance happens immediately; canceling the outer Options dialog afterward does not restore cleared rows. The same immediate-maintenance principle applies to a completed cleanup.

Clearing retains the audio files and does not save their pending edits. The next eligible load reads metadata again and rebuilds entries as needed. An empty cache is not a durable deletion of sensitive metadata from music files, backups, exports or other applications.

Use the built-in controls rather than editing a live SQLite database or removing its write-ahead-log files. The cache is rebuildable; schema changes or an unusable database can cause it to be replaced. It should not be your only retained copy of titles, locations or album information.

docs.title: Backup, privacy and performance boundaries
docs.text:
A configuration backup includes the saved Library preferences in settings, but excludes the Library database. Restoring those preferences on another computer neither restores the cache nor copies the audio. Verify destination paths and let the cache rebuild from files that actually exist there.

Cached metadata and paths can still be private even though audio/image bytes are not stored there. Avoid sharing your configuration folder or database as an example collection without inspecting it. Clearing the Library is not a forensic erasure guarantee for storage, journals or backups.

The cache still performs filesystem checks and database I/O. Slow/removable storage, network latency or endpoint scanning can limit the benefit. Inspect the hit/read counts and actual storage behavior before attributing all loading time to tag parsing. The original documentation's Windows Defender exclusion names a different application's executable; it is not an OpenTag prerequisite or a recommendation to change your computer's security policy.

These instructions describe the current local-file cache and its controls. They do not qualify native performance, provider access, audio recovery or a particular filesystem's alias/consistency behavior.

docs.title: Playlists and cue sheets
docs.text:
A playlist is an ordered list of references to audio files. Saving one does not copy, transcode or retag the recordings. Use it to preserve a listening order or create a list for another player, then test that the references work in their intended location.

These workflows assume ordinary local desktop files and writable folders. Provider documents have different access limits. If the file list contains chapter or CUE-track rows, follow Chapters and cue sheets as rows and return to whole audio files before creating playlists.

docs.title: Load a playlist and inspect its order
docs.text:
1. Save or deliberately discard pending edits before replacing the list.
  2. Choose File → Load playlist/cue sheet… and select a .m3u, .m3u8, .pls or .cue file. Inspect the pending-edit prompt if one appears.
  3. Check the loaded rows and error messages. Missing references can be reported while other valid entries are loaded.

Opening this way replaces the loaded workspace. Playlist order becomes load order, with column sorting cleared so it does not obscure that order. An ordinary M3U/M3U8 uses path-line order; PLS uses the numeric File1, File2, … keys, even if those lines were written in another order. Repeated references to the same resolved path keep their first position. This is not a promise about every filesystem alias identifying the same recording.

Relative references resolve beside the playlist, not beside OpenTag's executable. Local file:// references are accepted; network stream URLs such as HTTP are reported as unsupported by this local-file loader. A broken reference is not repaired by a playlist label or by renaming its suffix.

For example, with both named WAV files present beside list.m3u8:

#EXTM3U
02 - Low Tide.wav
01 - Paper Boats.wav
02 - Low Tide.wav
missing.wav
https://example.invalid/live

OpenTag resolves two unique local files, in the order 02 - Low Tide.wav, then 01 - Paper Boats.wav. It reports missing.wav on line 5 and the HTTP entry on line 6. It does not fetch that URL as an audio stream. Actual audio reading can report further errors after reference resolution.

docs.title: Add files and choose the order
docs.text:
Use File → Add files… or File → Add directory… to add more audio files. A dropped/opened playlist is expanded into its referenced entries. When dropping onto the file list, hold Command on macOS or Control on Windows/Linux to add; without an add modifier, a file drop replaces the list. Use the Add commands when modifier detection or the drop target is uncertain. Adding to an existing workspace differs from the explicit replace operation: it need not clear the current sort or replace the remembered loaded-playlist context.

Review the file-list order before writing. Header sorting and manual row ordering while holding Alt (Option on macOS) affect the sequence supplied to a playlist. A playlist generator groups that sequence; it does not independently sort by track number. Changing the loaded list does not rewrite the playlist on disk.

docs.title: Choose the writing scope
docs.text:
The labels below use “all files,” but the current host supplies the visible file-list rows for that scope. A filter can therefore change it. Selected scope can include selected rows that the filter hides. Inspect both the visible and selected counts.

Command Scope used Filename handling Playlist (all files) All currently visible rows, in list order Configured filename; confirmation if enabled. Playlist (selected files) Selected rows, in list order Configured filename; confirmation if enabled. Playlist per folder (all files) All currently visible rows, grouped by containing folder Writes per folder without individual filename dialogs. Generate playlists… Selection when any rows are selected; otherwise all visible rows Filename and partition fields, live preview, then OK.

Before exporting only a filtered result, use Edit → Unselect all, then select the intended visible rows. Before generating from the entire visible list, unselect everything if the generator would otherwise choose a smaller selection. Avoid chapter/CUE rows for these whole-file playlists.

docs.title: Save a small practice playlist
docs.text:
1. Keep original music and existing playlists. Save intended tag edits first: the backend reads saved fields for filenames and extended labels.

  2. Arrange two short copied WAV clips in this order:

    Filename Seconds Artist Title 01 - Paper Boats.wav 2 Juniper Vale Paper Boats 02 - Low Tide.wav 3 Juniper Vale Low Tide

  3. Open File → Options… → Playlist. For this example, enable Write extended info and relative entries, use %artist% - %title% as the extended-info format, leave BOM off, and keep filename confirmation on.

  4. Choose File → Playlist (selected files) after selecting the two clips.
  5. In the confirmation dialog, choose a new practice.m3u8 beside the clips. This field is a literal filename: placeholders typed here are not evaluated.
  6. Choose OK and inspect the resulting text or load the new playlist. No additional Save tags step writes the playlist.

The M3U8 text is:

#EXTM3U
#EXTINF:2,Juniper Vale - Paper Boats
01 - Paper Boats.wav
#EXTINF:3,Juniper Vale - Low Tide
02 - Low Tide.wav

#EXTINF stores a rounded duration and display label. A player can use that label without rereading tags, so later tag edits can require regenerating the playlist. OpenTag writes CRLF line endings; the displayed example represents the same lines. Multi-line labels are flattened to spaces; line breaks in entry paths are rejected instead of becoming extra records. Disabling extended info writes path lines alone.

A .pls destination for the same ordered items produces:

[playlist]
File1=01 - Paper Boats.wav
Title1=Juniper Vale - Paper Boats
Length1=2
File2=02 - Low Tide.wav
Title2=Juniper Vale - Low Tide
Length2=3
NumberOfEntries=2
Version=2

docs.title: Paths, names and encoding
docs.text:
Relative entries are calculated from the output playlist's folder. The configured working-directory root bounds when relative entries are used; entries or outputs outside it can remain absolute. Different filesystem roots, such as Windows drives, may also prevent relative paths. Move a playlist with its referenced directory layout intact and test it in the receiving player.

The configured Filename of playlist is a format string. Relative output names are based on the working directory. The per-folder command resolves a relative configured name beside each group's first file; an absolute name overrides that base and still needs a distinct destination for each group. A loaded playlist can provide %_playlist_filename%, %_playlist_filename_ext% and %_playlist_folderpath%. Those are context values for that loaded playlist, not the active audio file. See Playlist options for exact controls.

  • .m3u8 is UTF-8; .pls is written as UTF-8. The optional BOM setting is separate from Export's BOM setting.
  • .m3u uses the Windows system ANSI codepage on Windows. On macOS/Linux, Windows-1252 is used only when the playlist reads back unchanged; otherwise output falls back to UTF-8. This includes unrepresentable characters and ambiguous Windows-1252 bytes such as Â©, which could otherwise decode as the different UTF-8 text ©.
  • The loader honors a Unicode BOM, reads .m3u8 as UTF-8, and otherwise tries valid UTF-8 before the ANSI fallback. A consumer can have different rules.
  • CUE loading is a separate workflow. Do not choose .cue as the extension for this M3U/PLS writer and expect a cue-sheet structure to be generated.

Without a system codepage, these entry names illustrate the .m3u fallback:

Entry name Output encoding Maré.wav Windows-1252 Â©.wav UTF-8 港.wav UTF-8

A configured ANSI codepage that cannot represent a name can cause a write error. Choose .m3u8 for Unicode instead of deleting characters merely to fit that playlist encoding. A successful write still needs a receiving-player check.

docs.title: Generate several playlists or update automatically
docs.text:
File → Generate playlists… groups files by equal Partition format results. Playlist file name is evaluated using each group's first file. The preview shows the count and at most the first 50 output paths; OK plans and writes from the current request. Preview does not reserve a path. See One playlist per album folder.

The Generate Playlists action uses selected files and runs after the action group's per-file changes, regardless of its position inside that group. Use a separate group when an earlier intermediate state is required. It has different interaction and timing from the generator dialog's preview.

Automatic playlist creation is off by default. The option can request a playlist after successful tag saves or normal renames, using the current visible-list scope and saved filename configuration without prompting for a name. Keep it off until that extra output is intentional. An automatic playlist error is separate from a successful tag save.

docs.title: Gotchas and recovery
docs.text:
• Creating a playlist writes an external file immediately. It does not make its references portable by copying the audio.
  • Choose new practice output names. Existing outputs can be replaced; do not rely on an absent confirmation or on every alias/overwrite case being blocked.
  • Don't create directories requires the output parent to exist. It does not make writing into an existing folder a preview-only operation.
  • Several outputs are rendered before writing, but a later filesystem failure does not establish that earlier outputs were rolled back.
  • Do not assume Edit → Undo deletes or restores generated playlist files. Keep originals and remove unwanted practice outputs deliberately.

docs.title: Remove tags or selected tag types
docs.text: A file can carry several metadata blocks. Removing one block is different from clearing a displayed field, and neither operation deletes the audio file. Use copied files while choosing which stored metadata to retain.

docs.title: Choose the right kind of removal
docs.text:
Goal Route When it writes Clear one field, such as COMMENT Clear it in the tag panel, or remove its row in Extended tags After Save tags Remove configured tag families from selected files File → Remove tag… When confirmed Remove explicitly chosen ID3v1, ID3v2 or APEv2 blocks Tools → Remove tag types… When Remove is chosen Remove rows from OpenTag's list Edit → Remove from list No audio/tag deletion

The Remove Fields action is another field-level route; actions write when run. Use Remove Fields when a repeatable list of field names is the task. A field absent from the tag panel can still exist in the file; inspect Extended tags.

docs.title: Remove a legacy ID3v1 block from an MP3
docs.text:
Suppose the practice file's technical information lists ID3v2.4 APEv2 ID3v1, and the goal is to retain ID3v2 and APEv2:

  1. Save or discard pending edits, then select the copied MP3.
  2. Choose Tools → Remove tag types….
  3. Check ID3v1 only. Leave ID3v2 and APEv2 unchecked.
  4. Choose Remove and inspect the operation result.
  5. Inspect the tag-type information again. It should now show ID3v2.4 APEv2; the remaining blocks keep their own values.

The dialog shows counts of selected files with each type. An absent type is disabled. Its choices are for this operation and do not depend on the Remove switches under Options.

Starting afresh from a copied MP3 with all three blocks:

Only checked type Remaining tag-type information ID3v1 ID3v2.4 APEv2 ID3v2 APEv2 ID3v1 APEv2 ID3v2.4 ID3v1

Removing a block does not copy its unique fields into another block. A title can appear to change after removal because the reader now displays a different remaining block. Compare Read/Write/Remove policies and the technical tag information when diagnosing that change.

Remove tag types… supports MP3/MPEG audio, AAC, TTA and the APE-family formats Monkey's Audio, Musepack, WavPack, TAK and OptimFROG. It is not a universal way to strip every format's native metadata. Unsupported files can report per-file errors in a mixed selection. This tool requires supported local file access and is unavailable for provider documents.

docs.title: Use the configured Remove tag command
docs.text:
File → Remove tag… (Cmd+R / Ctrl+R with the file list focused) uses the current policy:

Format family Which types are removed MP3/MPEG audio, raw AAC and TTA Types checked under Options → Tags → Mpeg → Remove APE, Musepack, WavPack, TAK and OptimFROG Types checked under Options → Tags → Ape, Mpc → Remove Other supported formats The format's supported metadata-removal path, rather than those two checkbox groups

Read the confirmation's type list. For the configured families, no Remove types selected is an error; an absent selected type needs no change. Other formats have their own container handling. Remove tag is not a guarantee that every opaque, unrecognized or non-tag container structure is erased. Use supported formats for preservation limits.

The command writes immediately when confirmed. It can remove embedded artwork held in the removed tag. A folder image shown afterward is a display fallback, not proof that the embedded artwork survived.

docs.title: Keep information that matters
docs.text:
APEv2 can contain ReplayGain values and MP3GAIN_UNDO. Removing it loses that information unless another retained copy contains it. Removing ID3v2 can lose artwork, custom fields and other data that ID3v1 cannot represent. Export or retain copies of metadata needed later before stripping a block.

Changing Read only changes what is displayed; it does not delete a tag. Changing Write and Remove affects future saves too: a type selected for removal but not writing can be removed during an ordinary save. Review both sets of switches before saving after a cleanup.

Mp3tag's reference mentions dependent Lyrics3 removal with ID3v1. OpenTag has no guide-verified promise of that coupling for every MPEG path; do not use the ID3v1 checkbox as a general Lyrics3 cleanup operation. Removing MP4 metadata can also affect per-chapter tag fields; it is separate from a dedicated chapter-structure removal command. See Advanced tag options and the format reference when keeping chapter data matters.

docs.title: Check errors and undo
docs.text:
A batch can succeed for some files and fail for others. Inspect the reported file errors before repeating it; repeating against already cleaned files is not a recovery of removed fields. Read-only files and unsupported source access can prevent the operation.

Edit → Undo … can restore a recorded removal in the current desktop session; its label identifies the operation. Redo reapplies it when available. Use that history promptly, and retain backups for changes that must be recoverable after quitting. These steps describe source-backed behavior, not a guarantee that an arbitrary damaged input can be repaired.

docs.title: Edit tags in the tag panel
docs.text:
The tag panel shows editable fields for the selected files. Use it to set shared album information while keeping each track's own title and number. Edits are pending until saved, unless an enabled selection-change save preference writes them when moving on.

The screenshot illustrates the keep-existing-values state. Layout and visible controls depend on the saved panel configuration.

docs.title: Set one album for several tracks
docs.text:
1. Select two copied tracks with different titles, Paper Boats and North Pier.
  2. Check that the panel's selected-file count is 2. Leave Title unchanged.
  3. Enter Harbour Lights in Album.
  4. Inspect the list: both rows show the album, while their titles stay distinct.
  5. Choose File → Save tags (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S), then check any errors.

Typing one value into a field applies that edit to every selected file. Leaving a mixed field alone preserves each file's own values; it does not copy the first track's title into the others.

docs.title: Read the mixed-value state
docs.text:
A shared value is displayed normally. When selected files differ, a text control is empty with the < keep > placeholder. That placeholder describes an instruction to keep existing values; it is not a missing-title diagnosis for the whole selection.

Use the field's ▾ button to choose a value. A multi-file selection offers < keep >; < blank > requests clearing the field. The list also includes distinct values from the selection, configured custom values and, for Genre, standard genres unless disabled in Field Values options.

Choice or typed text Resulting value list Choose < keep > Keep each file's loaded values Choose < blank > Field removed Type Juniper Vale \\ Mira Solberg Two values: Juniper Vale, Mira Solberg Type AC\DC One value: AC\DC Type %artist% One value: %artist%

Choose the actual dropdown entry for Keep or Blank; typing its displayed label is not the same dropdown action. Choosing Keep also abandons a pending edit to that field and restores each selected file's loaded values. It does not clear unrelated pending fields.

Two consecutive backslashes separate values in panel input. The pieces are trimmed; a single backslash is ordinary text. Avoid repeated/trailing separators: this panel parser can retain empty pieces. It differs from Format Value, whose delimited metadata output drops empty pieces. Use Extended tags to inspect and edit the individual stored values directly.

docs.title: Choose and remember suggestions
docs.text:
Suggestions help keep spelling consistent; they do not restrict a field to the list. Type a new artist, genre or composer normally when needed. Options → General → Auto-completion at selection boxes enables inline completion from the field's available values. Check the completed spelling before saving, especially when names share a prefix.

For text controls, the arrow keys open and move through the dropdown; Enter accepts its active entry and Esc closes it. In a multiline control, ordinary Up/Down move the text cursor; use Alt+Up/Down to open its value list. With a value list open, Alt+Home/End selects its first/last entry. Tab closes the popup while moving focus.

With the value list closed, Shift+Enter adds the current trimmed, nonempty single-line text to that field's custom values. This saves a suggestion, not the audio file. To edit, import or export the suggested lists, use View → Field values…; see Field Values options. A multiline value is not accepted as one custom-list entry.

docs.title: Work with checkboxes, multiline fields and defaults
docs.text:
A configured checkbox can show checked, unchecked or mixed. Changing it writes 1 or a removal request as a pending edit for the selection. An existing value such as false, no or 0 is treated as off. See panel customization before using a checkbox for a field whose existing spelling matters.

Multiline controls accept line breaks, useful for comments and lyrics. The same two-backslash value separator still applies. A line break alone does not turn one text value into several field values.

Most defaults are < keep >. A configured visible field with another default can automatically stage that default when several files are selected, as long as that field has no pending edit in the selection. Review Default value under Customize tag panel… if selecting a batch unexpectedly creates pending changes. View → Default values in input fields explicitly stages configured visible defaults, including replacements for existing pending values. Defaults are literal text, not evaluated format strings.

docs.title: Show, arrange and navigate the panel
docs.text:
View → Show tag panel / Hide tag panel toggles the whole panel. The shortcut is Ctrl+Q, including on macOS where it means Control, not ⌘. The panel's ⋯ menu or a right-click on empty panel space exposes field visibility, Display cover art, customization and configuration commands. Hiding a control or the panel does not remove its metadata.

The position menu supports left, right, top, bottom or floating layouts; resize the dock or floating panel to make the fields usable. Compact layouts can use pane tabs instead of the wide desktop arrangement. Customize fields and their order through Customize tag panel.

An underlined label identifies its configured Alt mnemonic. Alt is ⌥ Option on macOS; while typing there, use Control+Option+letter so an ordinary Option character remains text. Text fields keep their usual text-edit menu when right-clicked.

Directory is a navigation control, not a tag field or a folder-renaming command. Choosing a loaded folder selects its visible files. Typing another folder and pressing Enter, or choosing Open folder…, loads a folder and can replace the list. Resolve pending edits when asked. For renaming from metadata, use Tag → Filename.

docs.title: Inspect the cover separately
docs.text: The cover area can show embedded artwork, pending pasted artwork or a folder image fallback. A folder image is not embedded merely because it is visible. Use Working with covers to distinguish these states and choose add, remove, manage or extract operations. Their write timing is separate from typing a panel value.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Check selection count before a shared edit; an active filter does not prove that hidden rows are unselected.
  • Changing a read/write tag policy can affect saved storage beyond the one field changed. Read Tags options.
  • A field's visible label can differ from its actual identifier. Use Extended tags… when checking ALBUMARTIST versus ARTIST, or custom names.
  • Provider sources can allow editing but require Save a copy… to retain changes. Read the access message and keep copy/artwork limitations in mind.

docs.title: Undo and history
docs.text: OpenTag's desktop session history records supported changes to local audio files. It is separate from pending tag edits, text-box undo and remembered format strings. Read the operation name in the Edit menu before restoring anything: history follows the session's recorded operations, not just the files you have selected now.

docs.title: Choose the right recovery route
docs.text:
State to recover Use What to keep in mind Text just typed inside an input That input's normal undo shortcut This edits the text box; it is not file history Unsaved tag-panel or Extended tags changes Edit → Discard pending changes, or deliberate correction Discard applies to selected pending edits; it cannot recover an earlier saved file A recorded Save, rename, tag removal or action Edit → Undo … Read its label, file count and any history notice The last successful Undo Edit → Redo …, when available A new recorded change normally clears Redo A file sent to the system trash The OS trash's restore command This is outside the tag Undo journal An external program's edit, permanent deletion or older session Your independent backup/recovery process Do not assume an OpenTag step can restore it

The saved-format lists called Manage history… are reusable text histories. Clearing one does not undo file edits. A configuration backup also does not include session Undo snapshots or your audio files.

docs.title: Practice Undo and Redo on one saved title
docs.text:
Use a copied ordinary local audio file, initially saved with TITLE = Paper Boats. Keep other file-changing applications closed for this exercise.

  1. Select the practice file and change its title to Paper Boats - Practice. It is pending until Save tags writes it.
  2. Choose Save tags and check that the save succeeded. Open Edit and read Undo Save tags (1 file).
  3. Finish any active text edit and focus the file list. Choose that Undo menu item, or use Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z.
  4. Check the operation result and the restored title, Paper Boats.
  5. Read Redo Save tags (1 file) and choose it, or use Cmd+Y / Ctrl+Y. The saved title becomes Paper Boats - Practice again.

The count describes audio-file records in that history step. A step can cover several selected files, and chapter rows can refer to one underlying file. Do not infer one independent Undo step for each row or button click in a multi-file operation.

Saving a different title with the same number of characters still creates an Undo step when the save keeps the file size and modification date unchanged. Undo restores the previous tags; Redo reapplies the save, subject to normal history limits. A request that writes nothing adds no step and keeps an existing Redo step.

This also applies when a recorded action renames a file or moves its folder before saving its tags. Undo can restore the previous location and tags; Redo reapplies the recorded location and saved tags together. This concerns recorded converter/action operations, rather than the separate Move files to… command.

docs.title: Resolve pending edits separately
docs.text:
Suppose the title above was saved successfully, then you typed another title without saving. Undo can restore the recorded disk state while that newer pending title remains in the application. The pending display is not proof that Undo failed. Saving it afterward can overwrite the restored result.

Before Undo, decide what to do with pending changes:

  • Save only those you genuinely intend to keep. This can create a newer history step, so read the menu again afterward.
  • Discard unwanted pending changes deliberately for the intended selection.
  • If uncertain, record the intended values separately and inspect the current saved file before choosing either route.

Undo does not restore list membership. Files already removed from the list stay out even if a history operation restores their disk contents. Reopen those files to inspect them. Conversely, changing the selection does not restrict an existing history step to only that new selection.

Text inputs retain native typing undo. If a shortcut appears to change the field text instead of the file, finish/cancel the text edit and use the explicit Edit-menu item with the file list focused.

docs.title: What the journal records
docs.text:
Supported local Save operations, tag removal, embedded-cover changes, metadata converters, file/folder renames performed by converters/actions, and the built-in tag utilities use the journal. Action groups can combine several effects into one labeled step. Its label describes the operation; it is not a list of every field changed.

For recorded file writes, restoration puts back the captured file state. It does not recreate removed metadata by writing whatever tag formats are now checked in Options. The read policy can still affect which restored values are displayed. This differs from assuming that only the currently displayed tag block was retained. Check tag-block reading and writing when files contain several blocks with different values.

Some supported operations also record explicitly captured output images, including action Export Cover and supported source-import cover writes. Their existing image can be restored, or their newly created image removed, when that recorded step can replay. This is a specific side-file capture path, not a promise that every external output belongs to file history. Ordinary text/CSV exports, playlists, arbitrary action export output, configuration files and changes made by external tools need their own backups. Check the action's output scope before assuming an export will disappear on Undo.

File-list removal, desktop Copy/Move/Delete commands and default playback are not recorded tag-Undo operations. Undo of an older tag save is not a reversal of a later unrecorded transfer or deletion.

docs.title: Handle partial errors and changed files
docs.text:
A recorded batch can restore some files while reporting that others could not be undone. The journal checks recorded filesystem state before replay and can refuse a file changed outside OpenTag, a missing file, an occupied old rename destination or a failed snapshot/restore. Do not bypass an error by deleting the file at the destination.

Read the complete result, not just Undid …. A refused file is not necessarily available for another attempt through the same history step; Redo can retain only the successfully restored part. Preserve both versions and use your backups if the history no longer offers the required state. These guards do not establish universal detection of every external change, filesystem alias or concurrent writer. Avoid editing the same files in two applications during a recovery attempt.

A failed or canceled batch is not automatically rolled back. Completed writes can remain, while files never processed can retain pending edits. Inspect per-file errors and the current Undo label. Undo is a subsequent recovery action, not a substitute for checking partial completion.

docs.title: Session and storage limits
docs.text:
The current defaults retain at most 50 recorded operations and 2 GiB of snapshot data; older steps can be removed as limits are reached. These are retained-storage limits, not a fixed limit on the sum of the audio files' lengths. Some staged metadata writes share unchanged file storage, while other rewrites can require a whole-file snapshot. A large operation can therefore be unavailable for Undo even when a small edit was available.

On Unix-family platforms, snapshot admission also checks that at least 2 GiB would remain free on the journal volume. The inspected implementation does not apply the same free-space query on every platform. Do not fill a volume on the assumption that history will always reserve space for you.

Snapshot/storage failure normally does not stop the requested file operation. OpenTag can report cannot be undone while the operation itself succeeds, or record only part of a batch. The previous Undo label is not proof that the latest operation has a recovery copy. Read notices immediately and keep an independent backup for changes that must survive quitting.

History is scoped to the running application session. Restarting does not load the old stack; stale session snapshots are cleaned separately. Do not browse or delete the live undo cache to manage history, and do not treat it as a durable backup archive. Provider documents use separate access and recovery mechanisms and are not covered by this desktop local-file journal.

docs.title: Redo is different from Repeat
docs.text:
Redo has priority on the shared menu item and shortcut while an undone step is available. When there is no Redo step, OpenTag can offer Repeat for the available last action/group execution.

  • Redo replays a recorded result from the history stack.
  • Repeat runs the remembered action/group again against the current applicable selection. Expressions, source values and side outputs can be evaluated again; the outcome need not equal the earlier run.

Read the current label every time. Do not press Cmd+Y / Ctrl+Y expecting Redo after changing other files: it may now mean a new action run. Selection, source access and pending-edit rules still apply to Repeat.

docs.title: Clean stored metadata and container layout
docs.text: The built-in utilities remove particular stored information or change a container's layout. They are not audio repair, loudness normalization or a general promise that another player will recognize a damaged file. Choose a specific goal and test one copied ordinary local file first.

docs.title: Choose a utility
docs.text:
These commands are available under Tools and in the file-list context menu's Utils section.

Goal Command Current scope Remove explicitly chosen metadata blocks Remove tag types… Selected supported ID3v1, ID3v2 or APEv2 blocks Remove ID3v2 data OpenTag does not display Remove unsupported fields… MP3, AAC, AIFF and WAV ID3v2 tags Set FLAC padding or reorganize MP4 data Optimize… FLAC and MP4 Remove MP4 chapter structure Strip chapters MP4… Selected MP4 files with chapters

Save or discard the selected files' pending edits before starting. These commands write when applied; they do not stage a change for a later Save tags. Supported local operations can enter the session journal, but check Undo's availability and limits rather than assuming every cleanup is recoverable.

docs.title: Remove a particular tag type
docs.text:
Use Tools → Remove tag types… when the task is “remove the old ID3v1 block but retain ID3v2,” rather than “clear the displayed Title.”

  1. Inspect the file's tag-type information. On a practice MP3 it might list ID3v2.4 APEv2 ID3v1.
  2. Open Remove tag types…. Each choice shows how many selected files contain it; types absent from the selection are disabled.
  3. Check only ID3v1 for this example. Leave ID3v2 and APEv2 off.
  4. Choose Remove, inspect any errors, then check the remaining tag types. The intended result is ID3v2.4 APEv2.

These explicit choices do not use the Remove switches under Options → Tags. The separate File → Remove tag… command does use those configured policies. Read the complete tag-removal guide for supported format families, preservation limits and why the displayed title can change when a different block becomes visible.

An APEv2 block can contain ReplayGain data and MP3GAIN_UNDO. Removing the block erases that information; it does not reverse earlier gain changes. Keep the original file when future reversal or a comparison may matter. Deleting a whole ID3v2 block can also remove covers and custom fields that another retained block cannot represent.

docs.title: Inspect and remove unsupported ID3v2 frames
docs.text:
A file can contain ID3v2 frames with no editable field or cover representation in OpenTag. Remove unsupported fields… targets those frames, rather than all custom field names or every format's opaque data.

  1. Add a temporary file-list column with the format string below, or use it while inspecting a copied file:

    %_id3v2_unknown_frames%

  2. Inspect the identifiers before deleting them. For a deliberately seeded practice file, the information can read GEOB, PRIV, UFID while a normal title and cover are also present.

  3. Decide whether another application might need that data. “Unsupported by this editor” does not mean meaningless or unwanted everywhere.
  4. Choose Tools → Remove unsupported fields…, read the applicable-file count and choose Remove unsupported fields.
  5. Recheck the technical column, title and cover. Files with nothing to remove are returned without a rewrite; an empty technical value alone is not an exhaustive proof that a container contains no opaque information.

Examples of the current removal policy include private frames, general binary objects, relative-volume/event/ownership frames and some unrecognized unique identifiers. Recognized identifiers such as MusicBrainz's unique identifier are retained by their supported mapping. Do not turn this into an “erase every UFID” rule or a universal sanitization command.

The native utility targets ID3v2 in MP3, AAC, AIFF and WAV. FLAC Vorbis comments, MP4 atoms and arbitrary binary fields in other containers are outside this command. On a mixed selection, the UI filters by the applicable format list before invoking this utility.

Selected formats Remove unsupported fields targets Optimize targets MP3, FLAC, MP4 1 2 AAC, AIFF, WAV 3 0 FLAC, FLAC 0 2 MP3 1 0

These counts mean applicable targets, not a promise that every target needs rewriting or will succeed. For example, an ordinary MP3 with no unknown ID3v2 frames can be an applicable no-op.

docs.title: Optimize FLAC padding
docs.text:
FLAC reserves padding alongside metadata so that later small tag changes may fit without relocating the audio frames. Optimize… normalizes that padding to one 4,096-byte block. It can shrink excessive padding or add missing padding; it does not change the compression level or improve audio quality.

  1. Save edits and select the copied FLAC file.
  2. Choose Tools → Optimize…. Check the count and the explanation before choosing Optimize in the dialog.
  3. Check the result/errors and the retained fields/artwork. The file size can increase or decrease; a smaller file is not the sole success criterion.
  4. If a player or file manager was the original problem, refresh its view and test the actual file there. An OpenTag success message does not qualify that other program's metadata limits.

A FLAC file with a leading ID3v2 tag is rejected by this optimization path: it expects the native FLAC stream marker at the start. Keep a backup and inspect the tag types before attempting any separate cleanup. Do not remove all native FLAC metadata or rename an extension merely to bypass that error. Malformed metadata blocks can also prevent optimization.

The writer verifies the expected metadata region and unchanged encoded audio bytes before publishing the staged result. That check concerns this operation; it is not a repair guarantee for an already damaged input. Already normalized files need no rewrite.

docs.title: Optimize MP4 layout
docs.text:
For MP4, Optimize removes unused free space and places the movie/metadata structure before media data. It adjusts the layout rather than re-encoding or resampling the track. A file already in the optimized layout is returned without a rewrite.

Use the same copied-file procedure and inspect the result. A layout rewrite can require more temporary storage than a small metadata edit, and the Undo snapshot can have a larger cost. Ensure adequate free space and retain a backup; a layout change does not prove compatibility with every MP4 variant, audio/video codec or player.

docs.title: Strip MP4 chapters deliberately
docs.text:
Chapter navigation and chapter-specific fields may matter for an audiobook or long recording. Keep the original if you need those divisions later.

  1. Resolve pending edits and select the copied MP4. The command is enabled when selected MP4 information reports chapters.
  2. Choose Tools → Strip chapters MP4…. Read the number of files and chapters in the normal removal confirmation.
  3. Confirm only if losing the navigation is intended. This writes immediately; the confirmation preference can affect whether the prompt is displayed.
  4. Inspect the returned parent file and its chapter information. Listed chapter rows can be replaced by the ordinary parent row when chapters disappear.

The removal turns the targeted chapter boxes into same-sized free boxes. It does not promise a smaller file. Audio/video bytes and unrelated tag regions are kept by this path's verification; the removed chapter structure is gone. If removing the resulting free space is a separate goal, Optimize… is a separate operation with its own storage and history cost.

Selecting an MP4 chapter row applies this whole-file utility to its underlying file, not just that one chapter. Cue-sheet track rows are different: they edit the sheet and reject this utility. See Chapters before applying whole-file removal to a displayed track list. A file with no applicable MP4 chapter structure does not acquire a new chapter-removal result merely because its extension resembles an audiobook.

docs.title: Gotchas and recovery
docs.text:
Utilities can complete for some files and fail for others. Read per-file errors and check the current Undo … label and notice. With a partial failure, do not assume that Cancel or closing the dialog restored completed writes. Reduce the retry selection to files whose state you have actually inspected.

Undo restores a recorded local-file snapshot during the current session; it is not the original editor's “rewrite only the displayed tag type using current Options” recovery policy. Snapshot failures or limits can leave the operation without complete history. Quit only after keeping any state that must survive the session in an independent backup.

Provider documents and restricted sources have their own mutation/access rules; this guide does not qualify these utilities for arbitrary provider save-back, native OS dialogs or player behavior. For a problem caused by a pending value or reader policy, correct that cause before deleting stored data.

docs.title: About OpenTag and this guide
docs.text: OpenTag is an independently authored, open-source audio metadata editor. It is being developed for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, with different capabilities and release qualifications on each platform. Its compatibility and performance goals do not establish complete Mp3tag parity today.

docs.title: Identify the application you are using
docs.text:
Choose Help → About OpenTag to see the application's version and MIT license identification. Include that version, your operating system and the operation used when reporting a problem. A similar-looking screenshot or an old source checkout does not identify the package installed on your computer.

Use the project's GitHub releases for packages, source revisions, checksums and release notes. The installation chapter explains the currently inspected package set and its signing/preview limits. A successful automated build is separate from proof that every OS/device installs and behaves the same way.

docs.title: Relationship to Mp3tag
docs.text:
OpenTag is an independent project, not an official Mp3tag edition, update, support channel or endorsement. The original application remains its author's property. OpenTag's own source, examples, artwork and guide are separate work. Do not assume that a Windows-only menu, original configuration archive, third-party template or parser script transfers unchanged.

Compatibility must be assessed for the particular workflow: tag format, field mapping, expression context, replacement syntax, action order and output side effects can matter. For example, this guide distinguishes JavaScript regex in Find from the Boost-compatible core used by format strings/actions. Use the regex reference and the relevant command's worked cases instead of treating a shared function name as proof of identical behavior.

Report OpenTag problems on the OpenTag issue tracker. The Help menu identifies its actual destinations; there is no separate donation or original-editor support command in that menu. An issue report is a way to share reproducible information, not a promise of response time or recovery of personal files.

docs.title: License and credits
docs.text:
The independently authored OpenTag application and associated repository documentation carry the project's MIT license. Read that file for its permission, notice and warranty terms. Third-party components retain their own licenses; the project license does not replace their notices or license the original Mp3tag software.

The application uses Tauri for its native/web interface and Rust for the metadata engine. The regex bridge includes Boost.Regex under its accompanying Boost Software License. Source dependencies and bundled component notices are the authoritative place to inspect third-party terms. This paragraph is an orientation, not a complete dependency-license audit.

docs.title: How to use this guide
docs.text:
Choose a section for the kind of help needed:

Need Section A first successful practice session Get started and Your first tagging session A worked lesson that explains why each step matters Tutorials under Learn A procedure for an editing task Guides and the converter/action pages under Automate A specific repeated cleanup or organization problem Cookbook recipes Exact syntax, field mappings, menus or settings Reference Diagnosis and a useful issue report Troubleshooting and FAQ

The guide describes implemented OpenTag behavior using independently written explanations and invented practice data. Canonical Mp3tag topics serve as a research checklist, not a guarantee of runtime equivalence. Source reads, core/model tests, native UI tests, package checks and actual live publication are different kinds of evidence; the guide keeps their limits distinct.

Only completed chapters are published and searched. More topics remain in the writing plan. A large navigation or passing example suite does not prove that every canonical detail has been covered. Start on copies and confirm a saved result in the tools used for your own library.

docs.title: Improve a page
docs.text:
For a correction, identify the page/section, your OpenTag version, the steps tried and the actual result. A copied expression and input/output pair help more than “the script does not work.” If the issue is a missing explanation, describe the task and the point where the instructions became unclear.

The source guide lives under docs/user-guide/ in the OpenTag repository. Contributors follow its contribution and documentation-publication instructions: finish a page, validate links/examples, obtain the required current-head review and checks, then verify the published result after merge. Unfinished chapters remain drafts. Do not copy the original editor's prose, screenshots or real music metadata into a contribution; use independent explanations and suitable practice files.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Use these short answers to choose the right next step. The linked chapters contain the complete procedure and its write, format and platform limits. Start with copied files when investigating an unfamiliar result.

docs.title: Do I need to import music into an OpenTag library?
docs.text: Open a local folder or add files to the working list. The audio remains in its existing location; loading does not make a second copy. Change directory… replaces the list, while Add directory… and Add files… append. The optional Library feature is a cache of information read from files, not an audio-file backup. See Opening files and Library options.

docs.title: Why did a displayed change disappear?
docs.text: An ordinary tag-panel or metadata-cell change can still be pending. Save tags writes pending edits for the selected files, not necessarily every unsaved file in the window. A failed write leaves that file's edit pending. Replacing the list, reloading or closing can discard unsaved work; configurable prompts do not save it for you. Check the selected count, pending markers and individual errors. Editing, saving and undo walks through a save and re-read.

docs.title: Can changing the selection save a file?
docs.text: Yes, when Options → Tags → Save tags when using arrow keys or a single mouse click is enabled. It is off by default. Extended tags has a separate navigation save mode. Do not use “click another row” as a no-write test when automatic saving is enabled. Read Tags options before practicing on an original album.

docs.title: Does < keep > mean the field is empty?
docs.text: It means preserve each selected file's current value when those values differ. Leaving it unchanged keeps the differences. Replacing it assigns a common value, and explicitly clearing a field requests removal. To inspect one file, select that file alone. See The tag panel.

docs.title: Why are there two artists separated by \\?
docs.text: That notation can display multiple stored values. It does not prove that the literal separator characters are stored in the file or that a player uses the same display. Different native formats support value lists differently. Use Multi-value fields before merging or splitting artists; punctuation inside one person's name is not automatically a list separator.

docs.title: Why does my player show another title, artist or cover?
docs.text: First save, then reload the file in OpenTag to check its stored result. If OpenTag reads the intended value, check which file the player opened and which fields/tag families it uses. A player can retain an older library/cache entry, choose another tag block, use ALBUMARTIST for album grouping, or show an external image instead of embedded artwork. Do not remove every tag type to experiment. Tag formats, Sort fields and compilations, and Cover art explain the distinctions. The guide does not certify a particular player's refresh behavior.

docs.title: Why did filtering leave more files selected than I can see?
docs.text: Visibility and selection are separate. A previously selected row can remain selected when a filter hides it. Clear the filter and deliberately reselect the intended targets before a batch write. Commands also differ in scope: for example, the playlist command for all files uses visible rows, while the selected-files route can include hidden selections. See Filtering and Playlists.

docs.title: Does Remove tag delete the song?
docs.text: File → Remove tag… removes configured tag families from selected files; it is not an audio-file deletion command. Edit → Remove from list changes the working list. Delete files… and Delete files permanently… are filesystem operations with different recovery limits. Confirm the exact command before continuing. Removing tags explains policies, immediate writes and artwork consequences.

docs.title: Why did a converter or action not wait for Save?
docs.text: Applying a converter or running an action writes its result immediately. The ordinary tag-panel pending-edit workflow is not a universal transaction around every command. A preview lets you inspect a proposed result; it is not a backup or an output-path reservation. Read the command's page and Editing, saving and undo for its commit boundary.

docs.title: Will Undo recover everything after restarting?
docs.text: No. Recorded file history belongs to the current desktop session, even though it uses temporary on-disk snapshots while running. It is not a saved history library reopened at the next start. Read Undo …'s operation label and file count. History can be unavailable or incomplete, files changed elsewhere can be refused, and external reports/playlists have separate cleanup needs. Retention and free-space limits can remove older steps or prevent a large operation from being recorded. Read any history notice rather than assuming a successful write also has a complete Undo snapshot. Pending edits remain when recorded history is replayed; inspect them before saving again. Keep ordinary backups for recovery beyond the session. See Editing, saving and undo.

docs.title: Why does a format string appear literally in a field?
docs.text: An ordinary metadata text box does not calculate expressions. To calculate a field, use Tag → Tag or a suitable action. To construct a name, use a filename converter. Format strings from zero explains placeholders, optional sections, quoting and where evaluation occurs. A successful calculation can still produce an unwanted empty value, so check the preview and test input before applying it.

docs.title: Can I use the same regex everywhere?
docs.text: Start by identifying the context. Format strings, actions, filters and web-source parser commands use the Boost-compatible core. Find uses the browser's Unicode JavaScript regex implementation. Syntax, replacement processing, case defaults and line-break rules differ. A pattern working in Find is not proof it will work unchanged in an action. Follow the regex reference and the relevant command's worked examples.

docs.title: Why did only part of an action group succeed?
docs.text: An action failure can produce a per-file warning while later actions/groups continue. Earlier successful writes remain. Batch exports and playlists can still include the file with its resulting values. Read every warning and inspect the step order; repeating the whole group can apply successful transformations a second time. See Actions and action groups and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Can I paste an old editor's whole configuration into OpenTag?
docs.text: OpenTag's Save configuration… creates its own supported JSON bundle. Load configuration… replaces supported saved configuration and reloads the window; it is not an importer for another editor's entire settings backup. Individual export/source formats have their own compatibility limits. Inspect, adapt and test an imported definition on copies rather than assuming identical scripting or parser behavior. See Download and install, Export templates, and Web sources.

docs.title: Are mobile packages equivalent to the desktop application?
docs.text: No. A compact Files/Tags layout describes presentation, not filesystem access or save-back capability. Provider documents can have read-only, unknown-access or recovery states, and unsupported commands can be disabled. The published Android package and iOS simulator preview have explicit release limits. Check installation and the current release notes before using original material. A simulator archive is not an iPhone installer.

docs.title: Can editing tags improve the audio bitrate or quality?
docs.text: Changing metadata does not turn a compressed recording into a higher-quality recording. Bitrate, codec and sample rate are technical information, not ordinary editable title/artist fields. Metadata writes can change container layout and file size without converting the audio into another codec. Check Supported file formats for actual read/write capabilities; fixture checks are not a guarantee for every file.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start by identifying the failed step: opening the application, reading a file, calculating a preview, applying a write, or seeing the result in another program. A successful step before it does not prove the later one succeeded. Use copied practice files and keep the exact message before dismissing it.

docs.title: Protect work before diagnosing
docs.text:
If there are pending edits, decide whether to save or discard them before replacing the list, reloading, closing or loading a configuration. Save only the intended selection and read each file error. With selection autosave enabled, moving to another row can itself write pending changes.

After a batch, distinguish three outcomes: saved files, failed files whose changes remain pending, and files not attempted after cancellation. Cancel stops remaining work; it does not reverse completed writes. Use the current Undo … operation only after reading its label, count and any notice. Editing, saving and undo explains why pending edits can survive an Undo and overwrite its restored result if saved without inspection.

docs.title: The application does not open
docs.text:
1. Confirm the exact release filename, operating system and architecture.
  2. Compare the downloaded package's SHA-256 with that release's checksum.
  3. Record the OS message and whether the application window ever appeared.
  4. Follow the package-specific installation guidance. A security-policy block, missing runtime, corrupted download and failed audio read are different problems.

Do not globally disable security controls or repeatedly replace an unexplained package. No guide instruction can grant installation permission on a managed computer or establish support for an untested OS version.

docs.title: Files are missing from the list
docs.text:
Check these in order so a view problem does not become an unnecessary write:

  1. Check the loaded count. Did Change directory… replace an earlier list, or did Add directory… append to it?
  2. Clear the filter. A loaded file can be hidden by a valid query; an invalid query has its own error state.
  3. Check Options → Directories → Read subfolders. Reopen the folder after changing it.
  4. Check Options → Files → Restrict incoming files to. This limits files discovered in folders, not every explicitly added file.
  5. Read the file-error area. A supported extension does not make a damaged, inaccessible or unsupported variant readable.

A playlist references other paths and can contain missing or rejected remote entries. A CUE sheet can produce track rows rather than one ordinary audio row. Consult Opening files, Playlists, and Chapters. Do not treat an empty result as proof the original files were deleted.

docs.title: A tag write failed or the old value came back
docs.text:
1. Select one copied file and make a recognizable change to an ordinary field, such as its album.
  2. Choose File → Save tags, then read that file's result. A success count for other files is not its success.
  3. If the save failed, retain the pending edit while checking the reported access/format problem. Confirm the file is writable in its actual source. Another program using the file or a restricted location may require action outside OpenTag; do not change broad permissions as a first experiment.
  4. After a successful save, use File → Reload tags and compare the value. Reload can discard pending edits, so resolve them before accepting it.
  5. If the saved value is still unexpected, inspect the native storage and read/write policy with Tag formats and Tags options.

A provider document can require source-access refresh or recovery rather than an ordinary local save. Follow its actual Source read-only, Source access unknown or Recovery required state. Save a copy…, when available, has its own fields/cover limits; it is not a universal desktop Save As or proof that the original provider document was updated.

docs.title: The player still shows old or different information
docs.text:
First establish the saved result with a reload in OpenTag. Then check that the player opened the same path, including any rename. If it did, inspect its metadata/library refresh behavior and the fields/tag families it chooses. Do not assume a different displayed album artist or image proves a failed write. The player may use a grouping field, another tag block, or an external folder image. Test one copied file after an intentional player refresh.

See Sort fields and compilations, Tag formats, and Cover art. Do not remove every tag family or embedded image to diagnose a display cache. This procedure cannot certify an individual player's behavior.

docs.title: A calculation or regex preview is wrong
docs.text:
Reduce the example before applying anything:

  1. Copy the exact input field value, preserving significant spaces, line breaks and value-list boundaries.
  2. Record the exact converter/action, field target and formula. A plain text field, filename converter and filter do not share one evaluation context.
  3. Test one small expression in the intended preview. Check spelling and the available placeholders before adding more functions.
  4. Check commas, apostrophes, literal parentheses, empty arguments and quoting with Format strings.
  5. For regex, record pattern, replacement and case setting separately. Find uses JavaScript Unicode regex; the shared core uses Boost-compatible syntax. Filter and web-source defaults also need their own context.
  6. Compare both a matching and a nonmatching practice value. “No change” can mean no match, rather than a reported parser error.

Do not copy a successful Find pattern into a write action without checking that action's dialect and preview. Follow Regular expressions and Format strings from zero for worked examples. A correct expression still needs appropriate metadata and source context; unavailable context is not repaired by adding arbitrary quotes.

docs.title: A rename or generated output fails
docs.text:
Inspect the complete proposed path, not only its last filename. Check missing artist/album fields, unexpected leading separators, current working-directory context, extension handling and the destination that already exists. A second run can build on the first run's changed path. Use the folder-layout recipe to practice relative roots and optional components before changing a library.

Do not treat preview as a reservation or assume every filesystem case/alias collision is protected identically. If an operation partly succeeded, inspect the reported final paths before retrying. Reports, playlists and saved images are external files with command-specific overwrite/history behavior. Keep backups of outputs worth preserving; session Undo is not a general output rollback service. See Export and Playlists.

docs.title: An action group produces warnings or repeats a bad result
docs.text:
Open the group definition and read the order of checked groups and actions. A failed action can warn for one file while later actions continue. Export and playlist actions are deferred group outputs and see the group's final values. Turning off a warning dialog under Options → Messages does not turn that warning into a successful transformation.

Inspect a practice file after each necessary stage, or duplicate the group and reduce it to the failing part. Do not blindly rerun a group whose earlier steps already changed fields or paths. Keep the original definition when reporting a problem. Actions and action groups explains continuation, output timing and recorded versus external side effects.

docs.title: A tag source or update check fails
docs.text:
Identify the stage before changing settings: fetching a response, parsing it, matching tracks, downloading artwork, or applying reviewed metadata. A network response alone does not prove the parser or tag write succeeded. Record the source/provider name, request stage and exact message. Do not expose access tokens, authorization headers or personal account data in a report.

For a custom web source, use its installation guide and parser reference. A script for another engine may need adaptation. Isolate parsing with a non-sensitive saved/minimal response rather than repeatedly calling a live service while editing a pattern. Respect the service's own access requirements.

A failed Check for updates… only establishes that the release list could not be read for that check. It does not prove the installed version is current or that every tag-source service is unavailable. See Updates options.

docs.title: Report a reproducible problem
docs.text:
Help → Report an issue opens the project's GitHub issue page on desktop. On the current mobile Help route, a message provides the URL instead of using the desktop opener. A useful report contains:

  • OpenTag version from Help → About OpenTag, OS version, architecture and package filename when installation is involved.
  • The exact menu/dialog/action, selected and visible file counts, filter state, and whether unsaved edits were present.
  • File/container type and whether the row is ordinary audio, a chapter/CUE row or a provider-backed document.
  • Numbered steps, expected result, actual result and the exact displayed error.
  • For formulas, copyable input, expression, replacement and case options. For layout issues, a screenshot showing the relevant controls and window size.
  • A generated or minimal copied fixture only when needed and safe to share.

The current Help menu has no Open log folder command or promised automatic support archive. Start with the visible operation/file errors and dialog messages. If diagnostic output is requested, review it before sharing: paths, script contents, configuration and service responses can contain private data. Dismiss clears visible errors; it neither fixes the cause nor retries the operation. Preserve the message first.

Configuration backups contain supported saved configuration, not a forensic record of every operation or a backup of pending edits/audio. Do not upload a whole configuration or library merely because one field failed. The Help menu and installation page describe the actual support and configuration commands.
