docs.title: Clean up a messy library
docs.text:
Practice a repeatable cleanup on one copied album before deciding what belongs in a larger collection. In about 20 minutes you will survey the files, save a focused action group, check its output, stage track numbers, and rename from the reviewed tags. Each stage has its own write boundary.

  • Three copied, writable whole-track files, ordered as 01_copy.mp3, 02_copy.mp3 and 03_copy.mp3; keep the originals elsewhere.
  • Each has ARTIST = Juniper Vale, ALBUM = Harbour Lights, one TITLE value from the table below, and no ALBUMARTIST.
  • Add PRACTICE_NOTE = Delete after this lesson to these practice copies in Extended tags, save, and keep all other useful fields.

In the table, · represents an ordinary space. Type real spaces in the practice titles, not the dot characters.

Practice file TITLE before TITLE after cleanup 01_copy.mp3 ··paper···BOATS·· Paper Boats 02_copy.mp3 ·lanterns··ON·the·water· Lanterns On The Water 03_copy.mp3 north··PIER North Pier

This is a particular editorial policy for invented practice text. It does not mean every title, abbreviation, credit or custom field in your real collection needs the same treatment.

docs.title: 1. Survey one album before changing it
docs.text:
Open the copied folder and inspect Filename, Title, Artist, Album and Track in the file list. Use View → Customize columns… if you need to inspect or adjust the displayed columns; custom columns explains adding fields such as album artist. A display column does not create or repair a stored field.

Select one file and inspect Extended tags…. Confirm the starting values, including the practice-only note. Close without further edits. Resolve file-read errors and save pending edits before running actions.

docs.title: 2. Ask one useful filter question
docs.text:
Show the Filter with View → Show filter and enter:

ALBUMARTIST MISSING

Wait for automatic application, or press Enter in manual mode. All three practice files should remain visible. MISSING asks whether that field is absent; an existing empty value is a different condition. The filter changes the view and writes no tags.

Clear the filter before the next stage. Choose Edit → Unselect all, then select only the three practice copies. Filtering is not a promise that previously selected hidden rows are unselected.

docs.title: 3. Build a narrow reusable action group
docs.text:
Open Actions → Actions…, choose New…, name it Practice album cleanup, then choose Edit actions…. Add these six actions in the displayed order. Choose Keep action after each one.

Scroll this table sideways on a narrow screen to keep each pattern intact.

Step Action Field Pattern / format / choice Replacement / additional setting 1 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE \A[ \t]+ Leave empty; case-sensitive comparison Off 2 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE [ \t]+\z Leave empty; case-sensitive comparison Off 3 Replace with Regular Expression TITLE [ \t]+ One actual space; case-sensitive comparison Off 4 Case Conversion TITLE Mixed Case Words begin after (-_ 5 Format Value ALBUMARTIST %artist% No replacement box 6 Remove Fields PRACTICE_NOTE No format string Remove this field only

The first two regexes remove spaces/tabs at the very start and end of each title value. \A and \z mean the whole value's edges. The third compresses remaining runs of spaces/tabs into one real space. Do not type quotation marks around that replacement or leave it empty: an empty replacement would join the words.

Mixed Case capitalizes word beginnings and lowercases other letters. It produces the practice results above, including On The; it does not know your preferred short-word style, acronyms or intentional artist spelling. The capitalization recipe teaches a separate exceptions policy.

%artist% reads the first artist value and sets one album-artist value. That is suitable for this single-artist exercise. For compilations, set the intended shared album artist deliberately; for several artist values, choose a list-aware policy. Do not assume one expression establishes the correct album credit in every collection.

The last row removes the named practice field. It does not remove every unknown field. Before deleting real identifiers, lyrics or comments, inspect what they contain and which other programs need them.

docs.title: 4. Save the group, then run it deliberately
docs.text:
Check the action order, choose Keep group, then Save groups. The group is now reusable, but saving its definition has not processed the audio.

Check only Practice album cleanup and choose Apply checked groups. These actions write immediately. Selecting a group row chooses what to edit; its checkbox chooses what runs. Read the result and every per-file error. An error does not promise that earlier actions were rolled back, and ordinary action warnings can allow later actions to continue.

docs.title: 5. Verify a result and the fields you kept
docs.text:
Inspect each file's title against the starting table. Each ALBUMARTIST should now be Juniper Vale, and PRACTICE_NOTE should be absent. Verify that ARTIST, ALBUM and useful unrelated metadata remain as intended.

Run ALBUMARTIST MISSING again: these successfully cleaned copies should no longer match. Clear the filter and deliberately reselect the practice files before continuing. A clean result for this one query does not prove that every field in the album is correct.

docs.title: 6. Number only a known sequence
docs.text:
Sort by Filename so 01_copy.mp3, 02_copy.mp3, 03_copy.mp3 are in that order. Confirm that this is the intended listening order; numbering cannot discover it from the music.

Open Convert → Auto-numbering…. Set Begin at track to 1 and the track Minimum digits to 2. Leave total count, disc numbers and all counter-change/reset options off for this one-album run.

Choose Preview. Expect 01, 02, 03. Choose Stage numbers, inspect the pending values, then File → Save tags to write them. Staging alone has not saved the numbers. Some tag formats store numeric values without leading zeros; the filename expression below adds its own padding.

docs.title: 7. Rename only after tags are correct
docs.text:
Save remaining pending edits, select the same three copies and choose Convert → Tag → Filename…. Use:

$num(%track%,2) - %title%

Preview the destinations against the staged/saved track values:

Practice file Numbering result Rename destination 01_copy.mp3 01 01 - Paper Boats.mp3 02_copy.mp3 02 02 - Lanterns On The Water.mp3 03_copy.mp3 03 03 - North Pier.mp3

Check the actual destination folders and existing files too. If a rename is refused or the preview is wrong, inspect the cause; do not delete an existing destination to force this lesson through.

Apply the reviewed rename. This changes the filenames immediately and keeps their audio extensions; it is not another pending text edit.

docs.title: 8. Stop at a verified album, then reuse selectively
docs.text:
Compare the result with the kept originals. Check titles, credits, track order, filenames and any player behavior you care about. Use Edit → Undo by its operation label to reverse recorded changes in the current desktop session; the cleanup, saved numbering and rename are distinct stages. Keep originals for recovery after quitting.

For another album, survey first. Reuse the saved group only when its title, album-credit and field-removal rules suit that album. A title already clean may be unchanged by the spacing rules, but a newly added exception or a different credit structure still needs a fresh trial. Avoid applying the group blindly to a whole mixed collection.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Columns and filters help ask precise questions before editing.
  • A saved action group is an ordered policy, not an automatic judgement of quality.
  • Actions write immediately; auto-numbering stages edits; saving writes those edits.
  • Field removal and album credits need explicit, collection-specific decisions.
  • Review tags before deriving filenames, and inspect each stage's errors and undo label.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Build your first action group: explore ordering and repeat behavior in smaller steps.
  • Find missing fields: distinguish absent fields, empty values and useful queries.
  • Number tracks per folder: handle more than one album after reviewing boundaries.
  • Remove reviewed junk fields: design a deliberate retention policy.

docs.title: Export a CD catalogue
docs.text:
Build a readable album-and-track catalogue, then save a spreadsheet copy. This lesson takes about 15 minutes and uses only practice files. You will see how one template becomes a report before adding groups or multiple outputs.

  • OpenTag desktop app installed, with copied audio files loaded.
  • Pending edits saved or discarded, and the three practice files selected.
  • A separate practice folder available for reports.

Use these tags and select the files in the order shown:

Album artist / Artist Album Track Title Juniper Vale Harbour Lights 2 Lanterns on the Water Juniper Vale Harbour Lights 1 Paper Boats Mira Solberg Low Tide 1 North Pier

docs.title: 1. Make a copy of the text configuration
docs.text:
Choose File → Export… (Ctrl+E, or Cmd+E on a Mac). Select Text, choose Duplicate, then Rename the copy to Practice catalogue. Keep Append data and Create one output file per off.

Set Export file name to practice-catalogue.txt in your separate report folder using Browse…. That location is the output; the configuration is the reusable set of instructions.

docs.title: 2. Repeat one simple line
docs.text:
Replace Export template with:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(1)%artist% - %title%$char(10)$loopend()

Choose Export, then open the report in a text editor. It should contain:

Juniper Vale - Lanterns on the Water
Juniper Vale - Paper Boats
Mira Solberg - North Pier

$loop(1) preserves the selected file-list order. The line break belongs inside the loop so every track gets one. The original audio files are not changed by this report.

docs.title: 3. Group albums and sort their tracks
docs.text:
Reopen Export, select Practice catalogue, and replace the template with:

$filename(txt,utf-8)$loop(%album%)%album% — files: %_total_files%$char(10)$loop($num(%track%,3))  $num(%track%,2) %title%$char(10)$loopend()$loopend()

Export to the same practice report, keeping append off. The output becomes:

Harbour Lights — files: 2
  01 Paper Boats
  02 Lanterns on the Water
Low Tide — files: 1
  01 North Pier

The outer loop chooses an album and writes its heading once. The inner loop receives only that album's rows and sorts by padded track number. The two spaces before $num indent the lines. %_total_files% in an album heading counts that album, rather than the whole selection.

Albums with the same title would combine here. This practice set has distinct titles; for a mixed library, add an album-artist grouping level or choose a partition key that identifies each album edition.

docs.title: 4. Write a separate file for each practice album
docs.text:
Reopen Export and enable Create one output file per. Set Partition format to %album%, then set Export file name to %album%.txt in the same report folder. Keep the grouped template and append off.

Export and inspect Harbour Lights.txt and Low Tide.txt. Each report should contain only its album's heading and tracks. Partitioning divides the input into documents before the template renders. The album loop then sees one album within each document.

The name must vary between groups. If both used practice-catalogue.txt, OpenTag would reject the output collision rather than overwrite one album with the other. Empty or inconsistent album values need attention too.

docs.title: 5. Save a spreadsheet copy
docs.text:
Reopen Export, turn Create one output file per off, select CSV (spreadsheet) and choose practice-catalogue.csv in the report folder. Export, then use the spreadsheet's text/CSV import command. Select UTF-8, comma-separated fields and double quotes. Import track-like and identifier columns as Text if their exact spelling must survive.

Check that there are three data records plus a header. This is a separate configuration and output format. Editing the spreadsheet does not write tags back to the audio files.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A configuration stores the template; an output file stores its result.
  • A loop repeats a row, and an inner loop can repeat tracks under one heading.
  • A sort key controls ordering independently of printed track formatting.
  • A partition creates separate reports and needs a distinct name for each.
  • CSV import settings determine how a spreadsheet interprets text values.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Export controls, naming and append
  • Template language, variables and totals
  • CSV quoting and spreadsheet import
  • HTML and other report templates

docs.title: Build your first action group
docs.text:
Save a three-step title cleanup and run it again from the menu. In about 15 minutes you will record the original title in a comment, replace underscores with spaces, and normalize capitalization.

  • Two copied audio files, with original copies kept elsewhere.
  • First file: TITLE = paper_boats (LIVE), with COMMENT absent.
  • Second file: TITLE = north_pier (LIVE), with COMMENT absent.
  • Pending edits saved or discarded; only the first practice file selected.

The comment is a teaching aid, not a substitute for a file backup. The first action replaces any existing comment, which is why these practice files start without one.

docs.title: 1. Create a named group
docs.text:
Choose Actions → Actions… (Alt+6; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac). Under Groups, choose New… and name it Practice title cleanup. Select that group and choose Edit actions….

The group is a saved ordered list of actions. Creating or editing the list does not itself change the music file. Applying the group will.

docs.title: 2. Record the title before changing it
docs.text:
Choose New…, select Format Value in Action type, and enter:

Setting Value Field COMMENT Format string %title%

Choose Keep action. The first action should appear in the list.

When this action runs, %title% reads that file's current title and writes it to COMMENT. It creates the comment if missing. Nothing in this expression edits TITLE.

docs.title: 3. Replace underscores
docs.text:
Add a second action of type Replace:

Setting Value Field TITLE Original string _ Replace with One actual space Only as whole word Off Case-sensitive comparison Off

Choose Keep action. This replacement changes every underscore in the title. Its search and replacement boxes are literal text: do not type quotes around the space.

docs.title: 4. Normalize capitalization
docs.text:
Add a third action of type Case Conversion:

Setting Value Field TITLE Case Mixed Case Words begin after (-_

Choose Keep action. Mixed Case capitalizes the beginning of words and lowercases their remaining letters. Here paper boats (LIVE) becomes Paper Boats (Live). It does not know which abbreviations or artist spellings should remain uppercase.

docs.title: 5. Check the order before running
docs.text:
Use ↑ Move up and ↓ Move down until the list reads:

Order Action Field Result after this step 1 Format Value COMMENT paper_boats (LIVE) 2 Replace TITLE paper boats (LIVE) 3 Case Conversion TITLE Paper Boats (Live)

Each action reads the results of the actions above it. Moving the comment copy to the bottom would record the cleaned title instead of the original. The group name does not determine execution order; the displayed list does.

Choose Keep group, then Save groups. Saving keeps the reusable settings; it has not run them on the file.

docs.title: 6. Run only this group
docs.text:
In the group list, check only Practice title cleanup. A selected row identifies what to edit; the checkbox identifies what will run. Choose Apply checked groups.

The actions save immediately. Inspect the selected file:

Field Before After TITLE paper_boats (LIVE) Paper Boats (Live) COMMENT Missing paper_boats (LIVE)

There is no extra Save tags step after applying an action group. Check the operation result; an error in a later step is not a guarantee that earlier file changes were rolled back.

docs.title: 7. Reuse the group
docs.text:
After the dialog closes, select only the second practice file. Open the Actions menu and choose Practice title cleanup. The saved group runs again without reopening its editor.

The second title becomes North Pier (Live), and its comment becomes north_pier (LIVE). The expression used the second file's title, not a fixed title copied from the first file.

Actions (Quick)… (Alt+Shift+6) is the one-action route. It is useful for a single replacement; this three-step sequence belongs in a group. Quick actions also save when applied, and their previous settings are remembered.

docs.title: 8. Understand repeat and undo
docs.text:
Edit → Undo reverses recorded changes in the current desktop session. Use it immediately after the second practice run and inspect that file's title and comment again. Another undo can reverse the first run; work backward through the operation labels instead of assuming one undo always restores the entire lesson.

The Edit menu can offer Redo or Repeat, depending on the history. When it offers Repeat for the last action selection, it can run that selection again. When it offers Redo, Cmd+Y / Ctrl+Y redoes the undone operation. Read the menu label before using the shortcut.

The saved group remains available after undo. Undoing a file change does not remove the reusable group definition.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A group stores actions; applying it saves file changes.
  • The list order determines what each action reads.
  • A checkbox controls execution; selecting a row controls editing.
  • Format Value calculates a field, Replace changes literal text, and Case Conversion follows a capitalization rule.
  • A named menu entry reuses the group on the current selection.
  • Session undo and a permanent file backup serve different recovery needs.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Move guest artists to titles
  • Format strings
  • Multi-value fields

For a larger collection of groups, Cleanup#Titles creates a Cleanup submenu containing Titles. Prefix a mnemonic character with &, such as &Cleanup#&Titles, to use Actions (Alt+A), then C, then T. Use && when a group's displayed name needs a literal ampersand.

docs.title: Your first tagging session
docs.text:
In about fifteen minutes you'll open an album, fix tags on one file and then on all of them at once, look inside a file's complete tag, and rename every file from its tags. You'll also undo a change, so you can recover a change during the session. Keep your original files as a backup.

You need:

  • OpenTag installed (download a desktop package)
  • A folder with a few music files, ideally one album

Practise on a copy

OpenTag changes your files when you save. Copy an album folder to your desktop and use the copy for this tutorial. The screenshots use an invented album, Harbour Lights by Juniper Vale. Your own music will look different, and the steps are the same.

docs.title: 1. Open the album
docs.text:
Choose File → Change directory… (Cmd+D / Ctrl+D) and pick the album folder. You can also drag the folder from Finder, Explorer or your file manager onto the OpenTag window, or click Open folder in the toolbar.

The main window with the album open and the first file selected.

The window has two main parts:

  • The file list on the right has one row per file. Its columns show the file name and the most important tags. Click a column header to sort by it.
  • The tag panel on the left shows the tags of the file you selected. This is where you edit.

The bar at the bottom of the file list describes the selection: how many files, their playing time and size, and the audio format of the selected file.

Don't see subfolders?

By default OpenTag also lists the files in subfolders, so a box set with CD1 and CD2 folders appears as one list. You can change this under File → Options… → Directories → Read subfolders.

docs.title: 2. Look at one file's tags
docs.text:
Click the first file in the list. The tag panel fills with its fields: Title, Artist, Album, Year, Track, Genre and more. If the file has cover art, it appears at the bottom of the panel with its type, size and format.

Each field has a ▾ button on the right. It opens a list of values you can pick from. For Genre, that includes the standard genre names.

docs.title: 3. Edit a field and save
docs.text:
Let's add a comment to this file.

  1. Click in the Comment field and type First tagging session.
  2. Look at the file list: the changed value is shown in the accent colour, and the status bar at the bottom of the window says 1 unsaved file. Your edit is pending: OpenTag remembers it, but the file on disk is unchanged.
  3. Press Cmd+S / Ctrl+S, or click Save tags under the tag panel.

The status bar now reports Saved tags: 1 file. The comment is written into the file, and any music player will see it.

Why edits wait for you to save

Pending edits let you change many fields, check them in the file list, and then write everything in one go. Until you save, you can throw edits away with Edit → Discard pending changes (Cmd+B / Ctrl+B). Save writes the pending edits of the selected files. If you edited several files, select them all before you save. When you try to close OpenTag or open another folder with edits still pending, it asks what to do.

docs.title: 4. Edit all files at once
docs.text:
Apply a shared value to every selected file. Suppose the whole album should have the genre Folk instead of Indie Folk.

  1. Click any file in the list, then press Cmd+A / Ctrl+A to select all files.
  2. Look at the tag panel. Fields that are the same in every selected file show that value: Artist, Album, Year, Genre. Fields that differ, like Title and Track, show < keep >.

With several files selected, fields that differ show < keep >. Leaving them alone keeps each file's own value.
  1. Select the text in the Genre field, type Folk and press Cmd+S / Ctrl+S.

All eight files now have the genre Folk, and every title and track number is untouched. < keep > is the most important idea in the tag panel: a field you don't touch is never changed.

How do I empty a field in every selected file?

Typing nothing leaves the field at < keep >. To clear it, open the field's ▾ list and choose < blank >, then save.

docs.title: 5. See everything in a file's tag
docs.text:
The tag panel shows the common fields only. A file can hold many more: composer, lyrics, sort names, identifiers from online databases and fields that other programs invented.

Select one file and press Alt+T (Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac), or click Extended… under the tag panel.

Extended tags lists every field of the file. The title bar shows the tag type, here ID3v2.3.

Here you can edit any field, give a field several values with ＋ Add value, and add fields of your own with ＋ Add field. Close the dialog with Cancel for now.

docs.title: 6. Rename the files from their tags
docs.text:
Look at the file names in the list: 01_low_tide.mp3, track04.mp3, 05 - juniper vale - salt & cedar.mp3. Every file is named differently. The tags are tidy, though, so let OpenTag build the names from them.

  1. Select all files (Cmd+A / Ctrl+A).

  2. Open the Convert menu and choose Tag → Filename… (Alt+1).

  3. In Format string, type:

    $num(%track%,2) - %artist% - %title%

    %track%, %artist% and %title% are placeholders: OpenTag replaces each with that field's value. $num(…,2) writes the track number with two digits, so 4/8 becomes 04.

  4. Click Preview. Each file shows its current name and, below it, its new one.

    Preview shows every new name before anything changes. The extension is kept.

  5. Check the list, then click Apply to 8 files.

The files are renamed immediately. Renaming changes no tags, so there's nothing to save.

docs.title: 7. Undo, and change your mind
docs.text:
Suppose you'd rather have names without the artist. Choose Edit → Undo (Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z). The menu item names the step it undoes, and the files get their old names back. Press Cmd+Y / Ctrl+Y to redo it.

Undo can restore saved tags and renames recorded in this session. Check the menu label before undoing, and keep the practice copy until you have verified your results. You can also undo the genre change from step 4.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• The file list shows your files; the tag panel edits the selected ones.
  • Edits are pending until you save them with Cmd+S / Ctrl+S.
  • With several files selected, < keep > protects the values that differ, and < blank > clears a field.
  • Extended tags (Alt+T) shows every field in a file.
  • Tag → Filename builds file names from tags with a format string. Always preview first.
  • Undo (Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z) reverses saves and renames.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Zero-padded track numbers: adapt the naming pattern you just used.
  • Tags from folder and file names: fill tags from names when working in the opposite direction.
  • Format strings: look up optional parts, quoting and conditions for more complex names.

docs.title: Format strings from zero
docs.text:
Build a title from existing tags, add a function, then choose a fallback when a field is missing. This lesson takes about 15 minutes. You will use the live preview before saving a practice change.

  • OpenTag installed and a few copied audio files available.
  • Pending edits saved or discarded.
  • One selected practice file with ARTIST = Juniper Vale, TITLE = Paper Boats, ALBUM = Harbour Lights, TRACK = 3/8 and YEAR = 2024.
  • ALBUMARTIST and DISCNUMBER absent on that practice file.

Use Extended tags… (Alt+T; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac) to inspect the fields first. Keep the original file untouched elsewhere.

docs.title: 1. Read a field into the preview
docs.text:
Choose Convert → Tag → Tag… (Alt+5). Set Field to COMMENT and Format string to:

%title%

Wait for the preview. It should show COMMENT: Paper Boats. Nothing has been saved while you are only editing the expression.

The percent signs mark a placeholder. %title% reads TITLE from the current file. It does not mean the word "title", and it does not select the destination; Field does that separately.

docs.title: 2. Add ordinary text
docs.text:
Replace the expression with:

%artist% - %title%

The preview becomes Juniper Vale - Paper Boats. OpenTag fills both placeholders for each selected file and copies the spaces and hyphen between them literally.

Expression Result for the practice file %title% Paper Boats %artist% - %title% Juniper Vale - Paper Boats From %album% From Harbour Lights Missing: %discnumber% Missing:

A missing field contributes empty text. It does not remove nearby fixed text automatically. The last row still contains a trailing space.

docs.title: 3. Transform a value with a function
docs.text:
Try:

$upper(%title%)

The preview becomes PAPER BOATS. Read it from the inside out:

  1. %title% produces Paper Boats.
  2. $upper(…) receives that text as its argument.
  3. It returns PAPER BOATS to the rest of the format string.

The original TITLE is still Paper Boats. The function calculates a result for COMMENT; it does not edit its source field on its own.

Functions can take several arguments, separated by commas:

$num(%track%,2) - %title%

Here %track% supplies 3/8, and 2 requests a minimum width of two digits. The result is 03 - Paper Boats. The total /8 is discarded by this numeric conversion.

docs.title: 4. Nest two small steps
docs.text:
Try:

$upper($left(%title%,5))

$left(%title%,5) returns the first five characters, Paper. $upper then turns that into PAPER. The closing parentheses end the inner and outer functions in that order.

When an expression fails, build it in these small stages. First preview the placeholder, then the inner function, then the outer function. A long expression is easier to understand once each piece has a known result.

Try it: a shorter album label

Build HARBOUR from the first seven characters of ALBUM.

Answer

$upper($left(%album%,7)) produces HARBOUR.

docs.title: 5. Omit an optional piece
docs.text:
Try:

%album%[ (%year%)]

The preview shows Harbour Lights (2024). Square brackets mark an optional section. The year is present, so OpenTag includes that section, including its space and round brackets.

Now try a missing field:

%album%[ (disc %discnumber%)]

The result is Harbour Lights; the whole optional section disappears. Putting the leading space inside the square brackets keeps the output from ending in an unwanted space.

An optional section depends on field availability, not on whether its literal text looks nonempty. [bonus] alone disappears. Use ordinary bonus when the text should always be present.

docs.title: 6. Choose a fallback
docs.text:
For a missing album artist, try:

$if2(%albumartist%,%artist%)

The result is Juniper Vale. $if2 takes the first argument when its availability/truth flag is true; otherwise it uses the second. A field placeholder is true when it has a nonempty first value, which makes this a useful field fallback.

Conditions use those flags, not the visible digits 1 and 0. Compare:

Expression Result Reason $if(%year%,dated,undated) dated The year field is present $if(1,dated,undated) undated Literal text carries no true flag $if($eql(%year%,2024),current,other) current The comparison supplies a true flag

Use a comparison when the condition asks a question about a value. For example, $grtr($len(%title%),10) asks whether the title is longer than ten characters. Do not assume a function returning the text 0 has the same flag as a false comparison.

docs.title: 7. Quote characters that belong to the text
docs.text:
Inside a function call, commas separate arguments and ) closes the call. Quote them when they belong to the text instead:

$replace(%title%,'Paper','Paper, folded')

The result is Paper, folded Boats. The comma inside quotes is part of the replacement, not an extra function argument.

Expression Result '%title%' %title% It''s %title% It's Paper Boats $replace(%title%,Paper,) Boats $replace(%title%,Paper,'') ' Boats

'' writes one apostrophe. To supply an empty replacement argument, leave that argument empty, as in the third row. The space before Boats remains because the search text did not include it.

docs.title: 8. Save one reviewed result
docs.text:
Return to:

%artist% - %title%

Check that Field is still COMMENT, wait for the preview, then choose Apply to … files. This writes the comment immediately. Inspect it in Extended tags…. Use Edit → Undo in the current desktop session to reverse the recorded change when you finish practicing.

An empty result can remove a destination field. A filename destination has different rules: an empty name is rejected and separators may create folders. Learn the text operations first, then use the filename rules when that is the actual goal.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Placeholders read values; the destination chooses where a result goes.
  • Functions transform arguments and can be nested from the inside out.
  • Optional sections keep punctuation with the field that controls it.
  • Comparisons and field availability supply condition flags.
  • Quoting protects special characters; an empty argument differs from ''.
  • A preview is a calculation; applying this converter writes the change.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Format strings reference
  • Regular expressions from zero
  • Regular expressions reference

docs.title: Give every album a cover
docs.text:
Embed each album folder's own image without giving the whole selection one album's picture. In about 15 minutes you will distinguish folder previews from embedded artwork, filter a copied selection, import its images and verify the saved result. You will also learn when resizing and online artwork lookup belong in separate steps.

  • Two copied album folders, each with a different, known folder.jpg.
  • A few copied local audio files whose writable tag formats support embedded artwork, such as MP3 with ID3v2 enabled.
  • The original audio and full-resolution images kept elsewhere.
  • Pending edits saved or discarded before using cover actions.

The images can be your own practice drawings. Check that each opens as a real JPEG; renaming an unrelated file to .jpg does not convert it. This lesson uses those local images and needs no live provider search.

docs.title: 1. Prepare a folder for each album
docs.text:
Use this arrangement, with a distinct picture in each album folder:

Practice/Harbour Lights/folder.jpg
Practice/Harbour Lights/01.mp3
Practice/Harbour Lights/02.mp3
Practice/Low Tide/folder.jpg
Practice/Low Tide/01.mp3

Open Practice with File → Change directory… and include its subfolders when loading. Wait for the file reads to complete. Resolve read errors instead of treating an unreadable file as proof that it has no cover. The opening-files guide explains the subfolder option and how to load another folder deliberately.

docs.title: 2. Identify what is actually embedded
docs.text:
Select one track and inspect the tag panel's cover window. A label Folder image / Not embedded in the file means OpenTag is showing an external image. The audio does not gain a picture merely because that preview is visible. Selecting files from different folders can also make the display differ from selecting one file.

A shared embedded image, Covers vary, No artwork and an artwork loading/error message mean different things. When uncertain, select one file at a time or inspect Edit → Manage covers…. Do not treat a failed image display as a confirmed embedded-cover count of zero.

docs.title: 3. Find only tracks without embedded pictures
docs.text:
Show the Filter with View → Show filter and enter:

"%_covers%" EQUAL 0

Wait for automatic application, or press Enter in manual mode. The query counts embedded entries, including pictures that are not Front Cover. It does not count folder.jpg beside a track.

Track snapshot Embedded pictures Folder image exists Matches filter A 0 Yes Yes B 1 Yes No C 0 No Yes

The filter finds missing embedded art; it does not prove that a suitable source image exists. Check the copied folders before continuing. A track with only a back cover already has one embedded entry and will not match.

Choose Edit → Unselect all, then select only the intended visible practice tracks. A filter hides rows; it does not guarantee that an old hidden selection has been cleared. Read the selected-file count.

docs.title: 4. Import the image from each file's own folder
docs.text:
Choose Actions → Actions (Quick)…, then Import Cover from File. Set the controls as follows:

Setting Value Image filename format %_folderpath%folder.jpg Import cover as Front Cover Delete existing covers Off

%_folderpath% is evaluated separately for every audio file and already ends with its native folder separator. The Harbour Lights tracks read Harbour Lights' image; Low Tide reads Low Tide's image. An absolute path chosen with Browse… would instead point every selected track to that one image, which is not this lesson's goal.

Choose Apply action, then read the result and all file errors. Importing writes immediately; a later Save tags is not required for the completed cover action. A missing or invalid image reports a warning; it does not download a replacement. Other selected files or later actions can still be processed, so inspect partial results before retrying.

docs.title: 5. Verify the written files, not only the old preview
docs.text:
Clear the filter to see the whole copied set. Select each practice file separately and inspect its saved embedded pictures. Check the correct album image, its type/description and the number of entries. If successful, the newly covered files no longer match the zero-cover filter.

With deletion off, import adds artwork while retaining the existing pictures. Rerunning on an already covered track can add another copy. Starting with the missing-cover selection avoids intentionally adding the same image to every already illustrated track. It is not a global duplicate-picture detector.

Leave Delete existing covers off in this lesson. Turning it on removes all previous embedded pictures, including back covers and booklets. To replace one chosen picture while retaining others, use Manage covers and its explicit plan, then OK. A batch of file writes is not one atomic transaction; inspect any failures and keep the original copies.

docs.title: 6. Shrink a test image only when needed
docs.text:
Keep the original full-resolution image. Select one successfully covered practice file, clear any filter, and inspect every embedded picture it has. Choose Actions → Actions (Quick)… → Adjust Cover and use:

Setting Value Image format Original Quality High (90 for JPEG) Resize cover On Size in pixels 600 Size policy Maximum size Scaling Scale proportionally

Choose Apply action only if changing all embedded pictures in that file is intended. This action does not restrict itself to Front Cover. For a single selected image instead, use Manage covers… → Adjust… and confirm the planned list with OK.

Original dimensions Expected dimensions with these settings 1200 × 800 600 × 400 400 × 300 400 × 300

Maximum size keeps the longer side at or below 600 while retaining the proportions. Already small images are not enlarged. The separate folder image is untouched. Original format does not force JPEG or a square image; follow a player's actual requirements rather than assuming one size or encoding suits every device. Quality alone also does not force recompression of an already unchanged JPEG.

Inspect the saved dimensions and errors, then test the player if that is the intended destination. Successful storage does not prove its display supports this picture format, role or size.

docs.title: 7. Obtain missing source images as a separate decision
docs.text:
For a real album lacking folder.jpg, decide which release image is correct before importing it. Existing desktop commands Tag Sources → Covers: MusicBrainz… and Covers: Discogs… provide a covers-only lookup. Search one album, review its edition and displayed artwork, and inspect the Write cover art, Replace existing artwork and Save image to file choices. Save cover to … files writes the selected artwork immediately without changing the tag fields in this covers-only route.

Save cover as… saves the displayed online image to an external destination and is distinct from embedding it. An external image saved this way remains when the lookup dialog is closed. Network availability, provider credentials, release coverage and image choices can limit a lookup; a successful local import does not verify those remote services. See the Tag Sources menu and Tag Sources options before a live lookup.

docs.title: 8. Recover before moving on
docs.text: Use Edit → Undo and read the operation label for recorded cover writes in the current desktop session. The import and adjustment are separate operations. Undo for tags is not a general deletion or restoration tool for external images. Keep the original audio and source pictures until you have checked the final result and any target player.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A folder preview and an embedded image are different storage choices.
  • The cover-count filter asks about embedded entries, not sidecar existence.
  • Per-file folder placeholders choose each album's image; a fixed absolute path does not.
  • Import, adjustment, Manage covers plans and external-image saving have different write boundaries.
  • Repeating an import can add pictures; resize scope and online release selection deserve separate review.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Embed each folder's image: exact names, wildcard order and repeated-import counts.
  • Working with covers: partial membership, order, roles and planned batch edits.
  • Shrink oversized covers: maximum/minimum, proportional and square policies.
  • Find files without embedded covers: precise counts and mixed selections.

docs.title: Regular expressions from zero
docs.text:
Clean 03 - Paper_Boats (Live 2024) into Paper Boats, while learning why each piece matches. This lesson takes about 20 minutes. Use a practice copy and the live Tag → Tag preview; save only after the whole result makes sense.

  • A copied audio file with TITLE = 03 - Paper_Boats (Live 2024).
  • Pending edits saved or discarded.
  • Familiarity with placeholders and function arguments from Format strings from zero.

docs.title: 1. Give the pattern one small job
docs.text:
Open Convert → Tag → Tag… (Alt+5; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac), set Field to COMMENT, and enter:

$regexp(%title%,'_',' ')

The preview should show 03 - Paper Boats (Live 2024).

Read the three arguments separately:

Argument Job %title% Supply the text to inspect '_' Match the underscore character ' ' Replace every match with one space

A regular expression is a pattern describing the text to match. $regexp searches the input and replaces matches. An underscore has no special pattern meaning, so this first example behaves like literal replacement. Keep Field as COMMENT for now so the source title stays available while you experiment.

docs.title: 2. Recognize a changing number
docs.text:
Replace the expression with:

$regexp(%title%,'^\d+',)

The result is - Paper_Boats (Live 2024), including the leading space. The final argument is empty because the goal is deletion. Do not substitute '': that means one literal apostrophe in a format string.

Pattern part Meaning What it matches here ^ Start of the input Position before 0 \d A digit 0 or 3 + One or more of the preceding item Both digits, 03

The + lets the same pattern handle 3, 03 or 103. The ^ protects numbers elsewhere, including the year at the end.

docs.title: 3. Include the separator in the match
docs.text:
Deleting the number left its separator behind. Replace the pattern with:

$regexp(%title%,'^\d+\s*-\s*',)

The result is Paper_Boats (Live 2024).

\s* means zero or more whitespace characters. The first one consumes spaces between the number and hyphen; the second consumes spaces after the hyphen. - is literal here. Requiring the hyphen helps distinguish a track prefix from a title beginning with a meaningful number.

Input Pattern Replacement Result 03 - Paper_Boats (Live 2024) ^\d+\s*-\s* Leave empty Paper_Boats (Live 2024) 3-Paper Boats ^\d+\s*-\s* Leave empty Paper Boats 2024 Nights ^\d+\s*-\s* Leave empty 2024 Nights

In the last row, the required hyphen is absent. No match leaves the input unchanged; it is not a regex error.

Try it: require at least one space

Which quantifier would require whitespace instead of allowing none?

Answer

\s+ requires one or more whitespace characters. \s* permits zero.

docs.title: 4. Capture text to reuse it
docs.text:
Instead of deleting a prefix, capture the pieces:

$regexp(%title%,'^(\d+)\s*-\s*(.*)$','$2')

The result is again Paper_Boats (Live 2024). The round brackets create numbered capture groups:

Group Captured text $1 03 $2 Paper_Boats (Live 2024)

.* captures zero or more of any ordinary character. The final $ marks the end, so the pattern describes the whole title. $2 in the replacement copies the second captured group. The quotes around it protect the dollar sign from the outer format-string parser.

For comparison, replacing with '$2 — track $1' produces Paper_Boats (Live 2024) — track 03. Capture references rearrange matched text; they do not read tag fields.

docs.title: 5. Match literal brackets and a year
docs.text:
The version suffix is another independent job:

$regexp(%title%,'\s+\(Live \d{4}\)$',)

The result is 03 - Paper_Boats.

Pattern part Why it is present \s+ Remove the space before the suffix too \( and \) Match actual round brackets rather than create a group Live Match that word and its following space \d{4} Match exactly four digits $ Require the suffix at the end

OpenTag ignores case by default in $regexp, so live also matches. Add a fourth argument 0 when the case must be significant: $regexp(%title%,'\s+\(Live \d{4}\)$',,0).

This pattern removes a very specific suffix. It will not remove (Live) without a year or (Studio 2024). Add new rules only after deciding those values should also change.

docs.title: 6. Combine the three verified steps
docs.text:
Use the prefix and suffix cleanup as nested functions, then change underscores into spaces:

$replace($regexp($regexp(%title%,'^\d+\s*-\s*',),'\s+\(Live \d{4}\)$',),_,' ')

Read from the inside outward:

Step Intermediate text Read %title% 03 - Paper_Boats (Live 2024) Remove track prefix Paper_Boats (Live 2024) Remove the version suffix Paper_Boats Replace underscores Paper Boats

The preview should now show Paper Boats. Keeping the jobs separate made the combined expression explainable; it also makes it easier to find which step needs changing when a new naming convention appears.

docs.title: 7. Look around without consuming text
docs.text:
For one more pattern technique, try this standalone expression:

$regexp(%title%,'\d{4}(?=\)$)',YEAR)

It produces 03 - Paper_Boats (Live YEAR). (?=\)$) is a lookahead: the digits must be followed by a closing bracket at the end, but that bracket is checked rather than included in the match. It therefore survives the replacement without being copied back.

Lookarounds are useful when the surrounding context decides whether a match is valid but should remain unchanged. Use an ordinary capture group when that communicates the task more clearly.

docs.title: 8. Apply the reviewed cleanup
docs.text:
Return to the combined expression in step 6. Change Field from COMMENT to TITLE, wait for the preview and check the exact output. Choose Apply to … files to save Paper Boats into the title. Inspect the result and use Edit → Undo to reverse the recorded practice change in the current desktop session.

Before applying the expression to a collection, test copies that include missing prefixes, unusual punctuation and suffixes you want to retain. Successful matching on this lesson's one input is not proof that every title in a library follows the same convention.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Match fixed characters first, then describe the parts that vary.
  • Use anchors to protect unrelated numbers elsewhere in the title.
  • Include unwanted separators in a deletion pattern.
  • Capture groups save text for $1, $2 and later references.
  • Escape literal regex punctuation and quote patterns inside $regexp.
  • Lookarounds check context while leaving that context outside the match.
  • Verify each transformation before nesting or saving it.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Regular expressions reference
  • Format strings reference
  • Move guest artists to titles

docs.title: Rename files and folders
docs.text:
Build a two-disc folder layout from tags, review the complete destinations, then rename a small practice selection. This lesson takes about 15 minutes. The audio extension is retained and the tag values remain unchanged.

  • Two copied audio files in one writable practice folder.
  • Pending edits saved or discarded.
  • Both files: ARTIST = Juniper Vale, ALBUM = Harbour Lights.
  • First file: TITLE = Paper Boats, TRACK = 1, DISCNUMBER = 1.
  • Second file: TITLE = North Pier, TRACK = 1, DISCNUMBER = 2.
  • Original copies kept outside the folder being reorganized.

Select both files after checking their tags in Extended tags… (Alt+T; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac). Their current filenames can be different from their titles; this converter will read the tags.

docs.title: 1. Preview a filename before adding folders
docs.text:
Choose Convert → Tag → Filename… (Alt+1), and enter:

$num(%track%,2) - %title%

Choose Preview. For MP3 copies, expect 01 - Paper Boats.mp3 and 01 - North Pier.mp3. For another audio extension, that extension remains instead. Do not apply yet; first build the intended folder layout.

$num reads the track number and pads it to at least two digits. %title% supplies each title. The fixed - keeps its two spaces.

docs.title: 2. Add an album folder
docs.text:
Change the expression to:

%album%\$num(%track%,2) - %title%

Run Preview again. The album part before the backslash becomes a folder:

Harbour Lights/01 - Paper Boats.mp3
Harbour Lights/01 - North Pier.mp3

Backslashes in the format string separate folders on macOS, Windows and Linux. The preview can display platform-native path separators. This relative destination is under each source file's current containing folder.

docs.title: 3. Keep disc numbers in the path
docs.text:
Both tracks start at 1 because they belong to different discs. Add a disc folder so the layout retains that information:

%album%\CD$num(%discnumber%,1)\$num(%track%,2) - %title%

Run Preview. For the two MP3 practice files, the final relative paths are:

Harbour Lights/CD1/01 - Paper Boats.mp3
Harbour Lights/CD2/01 - North Pier.mp3

Read the expression in order:

Piece Role %album% Name the album folder \ Start the next path component CD$num(%discnumber%,1) Build CD1 or CD2 from the disc tag \ Begin the filename inside that disc folder $num(%track%,2) - %title% Build the filename stem

Do not use this fixed CD… piece on files with missing disc tags: the numeric function would produce CD0. Choose a selection with known disc tags, or deliberately design an optional folder rule afterward.

docs.title: 4. Check the safety rules
docs.text:
Before applying, verify each destination:

  • The root is correct. A relative path stays under the source folder. If the selection spans several source folders, they do not automatically converge on one archive root. An absolute expression is needed for that.
  • Every destination is distinct. Track 01 titled Intro can occur on more than one disc. Keep enough album/disc/title information to avoid two inputs producing the same destination.
  • Tag values are usable. Missing album or title fields can produce incomplete names. A valid expression is not proof that every source tag was filled correctly.
  • Existing files are accounted for. A preview does not reserve a destination forever; a new collision or changed source can block applying.

Literal separators in the expression create folders. A slash or backslash coming from a tag value is treated as part of a name and uses the configured replacement, initially _. For example, an artist value Kofi/Mira becomes the component Kofi_Mira under the default setting; it does not create two artist folders. Other forbidden characters from values become underscores.

docs.title: 5. Apply the reviewed plan
docs.text:
When the final preview is correct, choose Apply to … files. The files are renamed or moved immediately. There is no second Save tags step. Inspect the two disc folders in the file manager and check the operation result for errors.

If a file moved outside the folders currently shown in the file list, Keep moved files determines whether it remains listed. Inspect the destination before assuming a missing row means the file was deleted. Creating the new layout does not promise to remove old empty folders or move unrelated sidecar images and text files with the audio.

docs.title: 6. Practice recovery
docs.text:
Use Edit → Undo (Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z) in the same desktop session to reverse the recorded rename. Inspect the original paths afterward. Undo can also encounter occupied destinations; keep the untouched copies for recovery beyond that session.

Changing an expression or selection invalidates the preview. Source changes or an expired plan can also require a new preview. Repeating a relative folder format after moving the files may nest the layout again, because the source files now have different containing folders.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Tag → Filename reads tags and changes paths when applied.
  • Literal separators create folders; separators inside values are replaced.
  • Disc folders retain information that track numbers alone cannot express.
  • Relative paths depend on the current source folder.
  • A reviewed plan still needs successful file operations and inspection.
  • Session undo helps reverse a recorded rename; copies provide longer-term recovery.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• File and folder rules
  • Zero-padded track numbers
  • Tags from folder and file names

docs.title: Get tags from filenames
docs.text:
Turn reliable names into saved track, title, artist and album fields. In about 15 minutes you will read two filenames, add their parent-folder information, and learn to recognize a pattern that matches but captures the wrong meaning. The names themselves will stay unchanged.

  • Two copied, writable whole-track audio files; keep the originals elsewhere.
  • A practice layout like the one below, with no unsaved OpenTag edits.
  • Familiarity with selecting files and opening Extended tags….
Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights (2024)/01 - Paper Boats.mp3
Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights (2024)/02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3

Use copies already named that way, or name your practice copies in your file manager before opening them. Do not change an audio extension to pretend a different format. This lesson writes tags from your names; it does not verify their musical accuracy.

docs.title: 1. Inspect names and tags separately
docs.text:
Open the copied album through File → Change directory…. Select the first file and open Extended tags…. Compare its TITLE and TRACK with 01 - Paper Boats.mp3 in the file list. A good filename and an empty title can coexist because they are stored in different places.

Close Extended tags without changing anything. Select both practice files. Save or discard any pending edits before using a converter. Its Apply step writes immediately, unlike ordinary tag-panel edits that wait for Save.

docs.title: 2. Draw a pattern of the filename
docs.text:
Choose Convert → Filename → Tag… and put this in Filename pattern:

%track% - %title%

Read it as “capture a track, then find a space, hyphen and space, then capture the title.” Here %track% names a destination field. It does not read an existing track value. The extension is omitted automatically.

Choose Preview. You should see these captures:

Filename TRACK TITLE 01 - Paper Boats.mp3 01 Paper Boats 02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 02 Lanterns on the Water

Inspect both rows. A preview is the place to discover a wrong separator or an unexpected title, before applying it to audio files.

docs.title: 3. Apply and verify the first conversion
docs.text:
Choose Apply to 2 files. The captured fields are saved now. Open each file's Extended tags and check TRACK and TITLE; other fields, such as an existing comment, are retained. The audio filenames remain unchanged.

There is no extra Save tags step for these completed converter writes. Read operation errors before assuming both files succeeded. Session Edit → Undo can reverse recorded changes; keep the original files for recovery beyond that session.

docs.title: 4. Read the artist and album folders too
docs.text:
Select the same two files, reopen Filename → Tag…, and use:

%artist%\%album% (%year%)\%track% - %title%

Use literal backslashes in the pattern on macOS and Linux too. They divide the folder levels. This relative pattern takes the last two folders plus the filename, so the earlier Music folder is irrelevant.

Preview again. Both files should gain ARTIST = Juniper Vale, ALBUM = Harbour Lights and YEAR = 2024, while keeping their respective titles and tracks. The literal ( and ) separate the year from the album. Apply only when those captures match your actual layout, then inspect the saved fields. Those captured fields replace any previous values there.

docs.title: 5. Learn what a successful match cannot tell you
docs.text:
Captures take the shortest text that allows the rest of the pattern to match. That is a matching rule, not an understanding of album names. With the folder pattern above:

Album folder Captured ALBUM Captured YEAR Harbour Lights (2024) Harbour Lights 2024 Harbour Lights (Deluxe) (2024) Harbour Lights Deluxe) (2024

The second row matches syntactically, but its year is wrong. Cancel that preview and handle that naming convention separately. One explicit pattern for it is:

%artist%\%album% (Deluxe) (%year%)\%track% - %title%

This deliberately omits the literal (Deluxe) from ALBUM. If you want it in the stored album name, choose a different explicit extraction and cleanup policy instead. A separator repeated inside an artist or title deserves the same careful preview.

For a filename 03 - North Pier - archive.mp3, unwanted suffix text can be consumed with %dummy%:

%track% - %title% - %dummy%

That produces track 03 and title North Pier, without a DUMMY field. It does not know whether archive is disposable; that is your decision. Adjacent captures such as %artist%%title% are refused because there is no separator defining where one value ends.

docs.title: 6. Distinguish a mismatch from a bad capture
docs.text:
A file named 01. Paper Boats.mp3 does not fit %track% - %title%. Preview marks it No match, not changed. Check these rows rather than assuming every selected file was retagged. Change the pattern to fit a separate selection; do not remove meaningful punctuation from every file to force one pattern to work.

A matched row can still be semantically wrong, as the Deluxe example shows. Check captured text and actual destination fields, not only the number on the Apply button. Patterns are neither regular expressions nor a place to put $upper(...); clean captured values as a separate step.

docs.title: 7. Undo deliberately
docs.text: Open Edit and read the Undo operation label. Undo the latest folder extraction and inspect the artist/album fields; another undo can reverse the earlier track/title conversion. Work backward through actual recorded operations rather than assuming one undo reverses every step of a lesson. Your copied filenames have stayed the same throughout.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Filenames and tags are independent; a converter can connect them deliberately.
  • A capture pattern names destinations and matches literal separators.
  • Relative folder patterns read trailing path levels; %dummy% discards a part.
  • A nonmatch stays unchanged, while a successful match still needs a meaning check.
  • Applying a converter saves immediately, and undo follows recorded operations.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Tags from folder and file names: disc folders, repeated artist captures and other layouts.
  • Filename → Tag reference: exact extension and matching rules.
  • Guess Values: use %title% as a source format string and %artist% / %title% as the guessing pattern when Juniper Vale / Paper Boats is already in a tag, rather than in a filename. The source is read before those destination fields are replaced; applying that action also writes immediately.
  • Clean up a messy library: tidy known metadata after checking the extraction.

docs.title: OpenTag on Linux
docs.text: Choose a package for your distribution and processor, use the desktop file manager deliberately, and distinguish application-runtime dependencies from optional notification-area support. Keep one copied album for the first run.

docs.title: Choose an actual published package
docs.text:
The published v0.2.13 release offers these Linux assets:

Scroll the download table sideways on a narrow screen to read complete filenames.

Processor Package choices x64 / x86-64 OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.AppImage, OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.deb, OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.rpm arm64 / AArch64 OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-arm64.AppImage, OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-arm64.deb, OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-arm64.rpm

Choose DEB or RPM when that package format suits your distribution, and let its package manager resolve the declared dependencies. Choose the matching AppImage when you want that distribution format. A source archive is not one of these runnable desktop packages.

The packages are unsigned. The release build uses Ubuntu 24.04 for each Linux architecture; that build environment does not qualify every older distribution, container, desktop session or CPU. Read a newer release's own notes before assuming its requirements and filenames are unchanged.

docs.title: Verify and open the package
docs.text:
Compare the downloaded file's hash with SHA256SUMS from the same release. For the x64 AppImage, run this in the folder containing it:

sha256sum 'OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.AppImage'

Change the filename for a DEB/RPM or arm64 download. Compare every hex digit with the exact asset's entry. This checks integrity against that release, not a publisher signature or every dependency on your system.

For a DEB/RPM, open the package in your distribution's installer and review its proposed changes. The actual v0.2.13 x64 DEB package is named open-tag, version 0.2.13, architecture amd64. It declares these runtime packages:

libayatana-appindicator3-1
libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0
libgtk-3-0

Those are that DEB's declarations, not package names to paste unchanged into every distribution. A missing WebKitGTK/GTK dependency is an application startup problem, separate from an unsupported audio file after the window opens. The package's dependency list alone does not establish older-system binary compatibility.

For an AppImage, use your file manager's executable-permission control, then open it. The corresponding terminal steps for the x64 example are:

chmod u+x 'OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.AppImage'
./OpenTag-v0.2.13-linux-x64.AppImage

The official AppImage quickstart explains the file-manager and terminal routes. If launch reports missing runtime/FUSE support or system libraries, use distribution-appropriate help for that exact message. The AppImage being executable is not proof that all of its runtime needs are met. You do not need Rust/Node just to run a published package.

docs.title: Use the file manager and command line
docs.text:
The inspected x64 DEB installs an OpenTag application entry whose command is opentag. Its entry does not declare file MIME associations or a %F file-argument placeholder. Do not assume a double-clicked audio file is registered to open in OpenTag. Use File → Add files…, Change directory…, or drop copied files/folders into its window.

A plain window drop replaces the list; holding Ctrl adds to it. File → Open in file manager reveals files/the current folder through desktop integration. Play uses the system's associated application. Availability and behavior depend on the desktop session and file manager; a file path can load successfully even when a reveal/default-player action is unavailable.

For the DEB's installed executable, this terminal example opens an existing copied folder. Replace the example location with your own:

opentag '/fp:/home/you/Music/Practice Album'

For an AppImage, use its actual filename/path as the executable instead. The quoted argument preserves spaces and requests a folder load, not unattended tagging. Recognized requests from another desktop launch are forwarded to the existing instance. See the command-line reference for /add, absolute paths, pending-edit decisions and load order.

docs.title: Shortcuts, focus and the status area
docs.text:
Shared Primary shortcuts use Ctrl on Linux. Application shortcuts only work if the desktop/window manager delivers them to OpenTag. If a chord is intercepted, choose its visible menu command before changing the task. Text fields and AltGraph keep their text-entry behavior.

Chord Focus OpenTag result Ctrl+D File list Change directory Alt+T Text field Extended tags AltGraph+T Text field Text entry Ctrl+Tab File list Next pane Delete File list Remove rows from list Ctrl+Delete File list Move files to Recycle Bin or trash

A plain Delete removes rows and keeps disk files. Trash and permanent filesystem deletion are separate operations; read the command label. Ctrl+S writes selected pending tag edits, while actions/renames have their own Apply/write boundaries.

Both Options → General → Notification area choices begin off. Always show icon in notification area keeps an icon available; Minimize to notification area can hide the minimized window/taskbar entry. The tray menu's Show OpenTag, or clicking the icon, restores it.

The implementation needs an AppIndicator library and a compatible desktop status area. It probes Ayatana/AppIndicator availability before creating the icon and reports an error if unavailable. Installing a library is not proof that your desktop displays indicators; inspect the actual result. The window is hidden for this option only after icon setup succeeds. Use the window and normal menus if notification-area support is unavailable.

docs.title: Mounted paths, labels and writes
docs.text:
Open audio through its current mounted path. A familiar device label does not prove that it is mounted at yesterday's path, writable or still online. Keep the source available until a write finishes and inspect any file error. For a failed write, try one copied file in a known writable local folder before assuming the metadata format is at fault.

%_volume% is optional information about the path's volume label, not a mount command or a stored audio tag. Linux lookup consults the mount table and known device labels; missing/unavailable labels can give empty text. If you add a display-only column, this format gives a visible fallback:

$if2(%_volume%,Unlabeled)

A reported Music Drive label displays Music Drive; an empty/missing label displays Unlabeled. This display choice does not mount the drive, assign a label, grant access or repair an audio file. The label cache can lag a mount/label change; inspect the actual path and reload when diagnosing it.

Literal backslashes in filename formats still separate folders on Linux. Tag-derived slashes have a separate replacement policy. Case and naming rules depend on the actual filesystem, including a mounted external volume; portable filename guidance is a component policy, not a guarantee for every destination.

docs.title: Credentials and per-user configuration
docs.text:
The optional system-keychain choice uses Secret Service for the Discogs token. Its availability in a build does not guarantee an unlocked, working credential service in every Linux session. Inspect errors and saved-location status instead of assuming a headless/container session has the same store as your interactive desktop. The token is excluded from normal configuration backups and is not displayed as returned secret text.

Use File → Open configuration folder to locate this user's actual settings. An AppImage does not automatically create a portable profile beside itself. Save configuration… saves supported settings, not pending metadata or music backups. Close the old app after finishing pending work before updating the executable/package. The update check opens release information; it does not perform a package-manager or AppImage replacement for you.

docs.title: Report a useful Linux problem
docs.text: Include the release filename, architecture, distribution/version, desktop session and exact error. State whether failure happens before the window, only with a file, or in file-manager/tray/credential integration. Package metadata, source and isolated model checks support these instructions; they do not claim native launch/write tests on every distribution or session.

docs.title: OpenTag on macOS
docs.text: Choose the build for your Mac, open music through Finder or OpenTag, and learn which shortcuts use Command versus the physical Control key. This page describes the desktop application; it does not turn a simulator preview into an iPhone/iPad app.

docs.title: Choose and install the Mac download
docs.text:
The examples below use the published v0.2.13 release. Check a newer release's own assets and notes before substituting its version. In About This Mac, distinguish Apple silicon from Intel.

Scroll the download table sideways on a narrow screen to read complete filenames.

Mac Download choices Apple silicon / arm64 OpenTag-v0.2.13-macos-arm64.dmg, OpenTag-v0.2.13-macos-arm64.app.tar.gz Intel / x64 OpenTag-v0.2.13-macos-x64.dmg, OpenTag-v0.2.13-macos-x64.app.tar.gz

These are separate processor builds, not one universal app. A source-code ZIP is not the desktop download. Use the DMG for a disk-image copy workflow, or extract the app archive to obtain OpenTag.app. Copy the application to Applications before opening your practice files; do not use the mounted image as a permanent home for the app.

Compare the downloaded package with the SHA256SUMS entry from that same release. For the Apple-silicon DMG, run this in its download folder:

shasum -a 256 'OpenTag-v0.2.13-macos-arm64.dmg'

Change the filename for the package you actually chose. Compare the whole hash, not just its beginning. A matching checksum detects a mismatched or damaged download; it does not identify a trusted publisher by itself.

v0.2.13 is ad-hoc signed and not Apple notarized. If macOS blocks a trusted, verified download as an unidentified/non-notarized app, Apple's app-specific opening instructions explain the System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway route after an opening attempt. Managed Macs can restrict that choice. Treat a malware or damaged-app alert according to Apple's guidance instead of assuming every alert means the same thing.

The release's packaging and version metadata do not establish a tested minimum-macOS matrix. Use the build for your processor and include the exact OS/version message if it cannot start. See installation for the shared download and recovery checklist.

docs.title: Open a copied album
docs.text:
1. Start the copied/installed OpenTag.app and choose File → Change directory… to open a copied album. Keep the original audio elsewhere.
  2. Select a track and inspect its tags before editing. Opening files does not itself save a new title or rename the file.
  3. For later additions, use File → Add directory… or Add files…. An ordinary folder/open-document request replaces the working list; finish pending edits before switching albums.

Finder Open With, dropping supported audio, playlist or folder items on OpenTag's Dock icon, and the ordinary open -a route feed the app's document opening queue. The packaged associations offer OpenTag as an alternate; they do not deliberately make it the default music player.

For an existing copied folder, this Terminal example uses the open-document route. Replace the example user/folder with your own path:

open -a OpenTag '/Users/you/Music/Practice Album'

That requests a replacement list, not /add. To pass explicit OpenTag switches, use the installed bundle executable as described in the command-line reference. Do not assume open --args delivers new arguments to an already running app. Inspect OpenTag's resulting file list and any pending-edit decision before proceeding.

Within the window, an ordinary file/folder drop replaces the list; holding Command while dropping adds to it. Native launch requests are queued for the current instance rather than being a headless batch-editing interface.

docs.title: Use the right modifier key
docs.text:
Most shared Primary shortcuts use Command on macOS: Command+S saves selected pending edits, for example. Some keys keep Control because macOS already uses the Command combination. Option is the Mac key named Alt in cross-platform instructions.

The table's “text field” means the cursor is typing in a field; “file list” means focus is outside text entry. Use visible menu commands when a system shortcut intercepts a key.

Chord Focus OpenTag result Command+T File list Reload tags Control+H File list Add directory Control+M File list First favorite directory Control+Q File list Toggle tag panel Option+T File list Extended tags Option+T Text field Text entry Control+Option+T Text field Extended tags Control+Tab File list Next pane

Command+Q remains the Mac quit command; it is not the tag-panel toggle. Command+H/M are not substitutes for Control+H/M in OpenTag. While typing, Option+letter can produce a character, so Control+Option activates the corresponding application Alt shortcut instead. Function keys may also require your keyboard's Fn key. See the complete shortcut reference for focus, helper menus and dialog-specific keys.

docs.title: Finder, paths and external drives
docs.text:
File → Open in Finder reveals selected files or the working folder. It is different from Play, which asks the system's default application to open the selected audio. Use Finder's information/properties controls for filesystem details; OpenTag's tag fields are metadata inside the audio.

In filename format strings, a literal backslash still separates folder components even on a Mac. For reviewed ARTIST = Juniper Vale, ALBUM = Harbour Lights, TRACK = 3/8, TITLE = Paper Boats:

%artist%\%album%\$num(%track%,2) - %title%

This describes Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/03 - Paper Boats beneath the source file's containing folder, with the original audio extension retained. It is a naming expression, not a Terminal command. Preview full paths before applying it. Tag-derived slashes are handled differently from literal folder boundaries; filename rules explain that distinction.

Case sensitivity depends on the actual volume. For a spelling-only rename, try one copy and inspect the result; do not assume another volume behaves the same way. An external drive must be mounted and writable for writes to succeed. Reading a tag successfully is not proof that a later write has permission. Use the actual operation error and keep the source copy.

docs.title: Window, credentials and configuration
docs.text:
OpenTag's Windows/Linux notification-area controls are unavailable on macOS. Minimized Mac windows use the Dock; there is no equivalent tray option to turn on in this build.

The Discogs token dialog can optionally use the system Keychain. Saving to Keychain is separate from ordinary options and from a configuration backup; the UI reports whether a token is set, rather than returning the secret. If a Keychain operation fails, read the error and inspect its saved-location status before repeating it. Do not paste the token into an issue report.

Use File → Open configuration folder for this user's actual settings location, and Save configuration… for a settings bundle. An app copied from an archive does not automatically get a portable, beside-the-app profile. Saving configuration does not save pending tags or back up music.

docs.title: If a Mac-specific operation fails
docs.text: Record the release filename, Mac processor, macOS version and exact error. Distinguish an app-opening/security problem, a file-access failure, a shortcut intercepted while typing and a remote-provider error. Try the visible command on one copied local file before expanding the selection. These instructions combine inspected release metadata with source/model checks; they are not a claim of installation or hardware testing on every Mac.
