docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Shortcuts depend on focus. When the cursor is in a text field, clipboard and undo keys usually edit that text. When the file list has focus, they can act on selected files or their tags. A modal dialog has its own keys and blocks most window commands until it closes.

In the tables, Primary means Ctrl on Windows/Linux and Command (⌘) on macOS. Control always means the physical Control key. Alt is Option (⌥) on a Mac, subject to the text-entry rule below. Function keys may require the keyboard's Fn key.

docs.title: Platform and focus rules
docs.text:
• On macOS, Option+letter can type a character. While typing, use Control+Option for an Alt application shortcut, such as Control+Option+T for Extended tags. Outside text fields, Option alone works.
  • Windows Ctrl+Alt and Linux AltGraph combinations are kept for text entry; they are not converter or action shortcuts.
  • macOS reserves shortcuts such as Command+Q, Command+H, Command+M, Command+Tab and Command+Space. The panel toggle, add/favorite directory, pane cycling and helper menu use the physical Control keys listed below.
  • Disabled menu commands remain unavailable through a shortcut. Save pending edits or select suitable local files when an operation asks for them.

These concrete cases illustrate the focus rule:

Press Focus and platform Expected behavior Alt+T Windows/Linux text field Extended tags Option+T macOS text field Text entry Control+Option+T macOS text field Extended tags Alt+5 Windows/Linux file list Tag → Tag Control+Option+5 macOS text field Tag → Tag Command+Shift+K macOS file list Numbering per folder Command+Shift+K macOS text field Text entry Control+Tab macOS file list Next pane Ctrl+Alt+T Windows/Linux text field Text entry

docs.title: Files, tags and selection
docs.text:
Shortcut Command and scope Primary+S Save selected files' pending tag changes Primary+R Remove tag types chosen in Options; while typing, consumed without removing tags Primary+T Reload tags from the selected files Primary+B Discard pending changes; it does not load configured default values Primary+Z Undo the recorded operation; text fields keep text undo Primary+Y or Primary+Shift+Z Redo, or repeat the last action when the menu offers Repeat Primary+C / X / V Copy/cut/paste tags outside text entry; text fields use their text clipboard Primary+A Select all listed files when not typing Primary+Shift+A Invert the file selection Primary+U Unselect all files Primary+N Select the file after the last selected row; also works from a tag-panel field and keeps focus there Primary+G Select files matching the active file's sort values Primary+Shift+G Select the next different group of sort values Primary+F Open Find for the file list F2 Edit the first selected file's filename column, or the first editable column when no filename column is available F3 Show/hide the filter F4 or Primary+Shift+T Open selected files in the default player; a configured default tool can replace the file-list double-click action F5 Refresh the loaded folders and file information

Primary+N clamps at the last file; it does not wrap to the first. Similar-file selection uses the active sort criteria, not an audio fingerprint. Selection is separate from checking a dialog's enabled fields.

docs.title: Remove, delete, copy and move
docs.text:
Windows/Linux macOS Result outside text entry Delete Delete/⌫ Remove rows from the list; keep the files on disk Ctrl+Delete Command+Delete/⌫ Send selected files to the system Recycle Bin/trash Ctrl+Shift+Delete Command+Shift+Delete/⌫ Permanently delete selected files without using trash Ctrl+Shift+C Command+Shift+C Copy files to another folder Ctrl+Shift+V Command+Shift+V Move files to another folder Alt+Enter Option+Enter Reveal selected files in the file manager

The key labelled Delete on many Mac keyboards sends Backspace. OpenTag accepts that key for these file-list operations. Confirm the command's wording: removing a row, trashing a file and permanently deleting it have different effects. File moves/deletions are not ordinary pending tag edits. For filesystem properties, reveal the file and use the file manager's properties/info command.

docs.title: Folders and windows
docs.text:
Shortcut Command Primary+D Change directory; where folder picking is unavailable, use Add files Control+H Add a directory Primary+Shift+D Load the upper directory Alt+Left / Right Back/forward through directory history, outside text entry Control+M Open the first favorite directory Primary+O Open Options Control+Q Show/hide the tag panel Control+Tab Focus the next available pane: tag panel, filter, file list Control+Shift+Tab Focus the previous available pane Primary+Num + Auto-size file-list columns to their contents

Hidden or unavailable panes are skipped during pane cycling. Control+Q does not mean Command+Q on a Mac. The latter belongs to the operating system. On macOS, Control+H and Control+M are directory commands outside text entry; while typing they are left to the field's normal editing behavior.

docs.title: Converters, actions, export and sources
docs.text:
Shortcut Command Alt+1 Tag → Filename Alt+2 Filename → Tag Alt+3 Filename → Filename Alt+4 Text File → Tag Alt+5 Tag → Tag Primary+K Auto-numbering Primary+Shift+K Auto-numbering with a counter reset per folder Alt+6 Action groups Alt+Shift+6 Quick actions Primary+E Export with the saved selection-dialog preference Primary+Shift+E Export per audio folder Primary+P Playlist for all loaded files Primary+Shift+P Playlist per folder for all loaded files Primary+L Local freedb Primary+I Reopen the last used tag source Primary+Shift+I Quick use of the last tag source; inspect its matching behavior first Primary+Alt+M Manage covers Primary+1 through 9, then 0 Run configured tools 1–10

On macOS, use Control+Option+1 through 6 while typing instead of Option alone. The cover-manager chord is explicitly Command+Option+M on a Mac. The playlist-per-folder command is separate from Generate playlists…; do not assume another application's shortcut opens that generator in OpenTag.

docs.title: Manual file order
docs.text:
With focus outside text entry, select the rows to move:

Shortcut Result Alt+Up / Down Move the selected rows one position Alt+Page Up / Down Move them to the beginning/end Alt+drag Move rows to the visible drop line

Manual ordering leaves the active sorted view and uses the displayed order as its starting point. Playlists and numbering can then use that list order. It does not rename or move the audio files on disk.

docs.title: Dialog keys
docs.text:
The same F-key can mean something different inside a dialog:

Area Keys and meaning Action groups Insert: add; F2: rename; F4: edit; Delete: remove; Space: enable/disable selected groups Action groups Primary+A: select all; Primary+Shift+A: invert; Primary+E/D: enable/disable all groups; Primary+S: save group order/state Actions and groups Alt+Up/Down and Alt+Page Up/Down reorder selected items Source review: fields F2 edits a value; Space toggles its enabled state; Primary+A / Primary+Shift+A select/invert fields; Primary+E/D enable/disable all Source review: tracks Alt+Up/Down and Alt+Page Up/Down change the file-to-source track order Toolbar customization F4 edits the selected item; Space shows/hides it; Primary+E/D shows/hides all; Alt+Up/Down or Alt+Page Up/Down reorders Export configurations F2 renames; F4 or Enter focuses the template; a double-click also edits the template

Changing a source-review field's selection is not the same as enabling it for import. Check enabled fields and track matching before applying a source result. See actions, export and Tag Sources menu for the corresponding workflows.

docs.title: Helpers and menus
docs.text:
Control+Space opens the helper menu beside a supported format-string input. On macOS, Control+Option+Space also works when the system claims Control+Space for switching input sources. Within those helpers, Shift+Delete removes a remembered format string. Shift+Enter in a supported tag-panel combo field adds its current text to the custom-value list; it does not save that value to audio files.

Use arrows to move through an open menu and Escape to close it. Action and installed web-source entries can have underlined access keys. Alt+A opens the Actions menu's mnemonic route outside text entry. Focus and a dialog's own keyboard rules take precedence over a window shortcut.

If a shortcut seems inactive, click the file list and retry a harmless command such as Find. Check modifier notation, Fn mode, pending edits and modal dialogs. The menu reference provides the equivalent visible commands.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
A placeholder is a name between percent signs. OpenTag replaces it with a value for each file: %title% with the title, %_bitrate% with the bitrate, %_folderpath% with the folder the file is in.

This page lists every placeholder OpenTag understands, grouped by what it tells you. For the rules of the language around them (optional sections, quoting, conditions), see Format strings.

Finding them while you type

You don't have to remember these names. Press the ► button next to any format string input, or Ctrl+Space (Control on every platform), and pick a placeholder from the menu.

docs.title: Two kinds of placeholders
docs.text:
Tag fields have plain names: %artist%, %album%, %mood%. They read the file's tag, and any field name works. A missing field gives empty text. See Placeholders: %field% for the details. Common field names include ARTIST, TITLE, ALBUM and TRACK.

Information placeholders start with an underscore: %_length%, %_covers%. OpenTag works them out from the file itself, its location, its audio stream or the current operation. You can read them but not write them.

The rest of this page lists the information placeholders. All of them:

  • are case-insensitive: %_BITRATE% and %_bitrate% are the same,
  • give empty text when the value can't be measured for a file (for example %_bitspersample% on an MP3), so you can test them with […] and $if,
  • are read-only: you can't set them as a field in Tag → Tag or the tag panel. To rename a file, use the _FILENAME and _DIRECTORY targets instead.

The example values are for track 2 of the guide's example album, stored at /Users/you/Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 on a Mac. On Windows the paths use \ and a drive letter.

docs.title: File name and location
docs.text:
Placeholder Gives Example %_path% The full path of the file /Users/you/Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 %_filename% The file name without extension 02 - Lanterns on the Water %_filename_ext% The file name with extension 02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 %_extension% The extension, without the dot mp3 %_folderpath% The folder, ending with a separator /Users/you/Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/ %_directory% The name of the folder the file is in Harbour Lights %_parent_directory% The name of the folder above that Juniper Vale %_volume% The name (label) of the disk the file is on Music Drive %_workingdir% The name of the folder you opened in OpenTag Music %_workingpath% The full path of that folder, ending with a separator /Users/you/Music/

Because %_folderpath% already ends with a separator, append a file name directly: %_folderpath%folder.jpg.

%_workingdir% and %_workingpath% are the folder you chose with File → Change directory… (or the first folder you opened). They are handy for paths relative to your library's root, and empty when you opened single files.

docs.title: Audio and technical information
docs.text: Placeholder Gives Example %_length% Playing time, m:ss, or h:mm:ss from one hour 4:04, 1:15:03 %_length_seconds% Playing time in whole seconds 244 %_bitrate% Average bitrate in kbit/s 192 %_samplerate% Sample rate in Hz 44100 %_bitspersample% Bit depth (lossless and PCM formats only) 16, 24 %_mode% Channels: the MPEG channel mode for MP3, otherwise Mono, Stereo or n channels Joint Stereo %_codec% The audio codec MPEG-1 Layer III, FLAC, AAC, ALAC, Vorbis, Opus, PCM, Monkey's Audio, Windows Media Audio %_vbr% MP3: VBR, CBR or ABR. Monkey's Audio: the compression level CBR, Extra High %_tool% The encoder that made the file (LAME version, Vorbis vendor) LAME3.100 %_filetype% The container format WAV

docs.title: Video (MP4 and Matroska files)
docs.text: Placeholder Gives Example %_video_codec% Video codec MPEG-4 Visual %_video_width%, %_video_height% Frame size in pixels 1920, 1080 %_video_bitrate% Video bitrate in kbit/s 4500 %_segment_title% Matroska only: the segment title Live in Bergen

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
When chapters are listed as separate rows, each chapter row has its own values:

Placeholder Gives Example %_subsong% The chapter number, counting from 0 0 for a file without chapters %_subsong_count% The number of chapters in the file 1 for a file without chapters

docs.title: MP4 dates
docs.text: Placeholder Gives Example %_mp4_creation_time%, %_mp4_modification_time% The dates stored inside an MP4/M4A file, as local date and time 1/2/24 3:04:05 AM %_mp4_creation_time_raw%, %_mp4_modification_time_raw% The same, as seconds since 1 January 1970 (for $fmtdate) 1704164645

docs.title: Tags inside the file
docs.text:
Placeholder Gives Example %_tag% Every tag type in the file, separated by spaces ID3v2.3 ID3v1 %_tag_read% The tag OpenTag is showing for this file ID3v2.3 %_tag_size% Size of the tags in bytes 4096 %_tag_size_prepended%, %_tag_size_appended% Tag bytes before and after the audio 4096, 128 %_id3v2_character_encoding% Text encodings used in the ID3v2 tag UTF-16 %_id3v2_unknown_frames% ID3v2 frames OpenTag keeps but doesn't interpret XABC

%_tag_size% and its variants exist for MP3, APE, FLAC, AAC, Musepack and WavPack files. The other two only exist for files with an ID3v2 tag.

docs.title: Cover art
docs.text:
These describe the first picture in the file.

Placeholder Gives Example %_covers% How many pictures the file has 1; 0 without covers %_cover_type% The picture type Front Cover %_cover_mimetype% The image format image/jpeg %_cover_description% The picture's description Album cover %_cover_size% Size in bytes 5843 %_cover_width%, %_cover_height% Size in pixels (JPEG and PNG only) 600, 600

%_covers% is the one to filter on. "%_covers%" EQUAL 0 shows every file without artwork.

docs.title: File properties
docs.text:
Placeholder Gives Example %_file_size% Size, rounded, with a unit (B, KB or MB) 5.6 MB %_file_size_bytes% Size in bytes 5878272 %_file_size_kb% Size in whole KiB 5740 %_file_size_mb% Size in MiB with two decimals 5.61 %_file_mod_date% Last modified, as a short local date 10/15/26 %_file_mod_datetime% Last modified, local date and time 10/15/26 4:12:09 PM %_file_mod_datetime_raw% Last modified, seconds since 1 January 1970 1792073529 %_file_create_date%, %_file_create_datetime%, %_file_create_datetime_raw% The same for the creation time

Dates use your system's date format. For a fixed format, pass the _raw value to $fmtdate: $fmtDate('yyyy-MM-dd',%_file_mod_datetime_raw%).

The creation-time placeholders are empty on file systems that don't record when a file was created (many Linux file systems).

docs.title: Information about the operation
docs.text:
Placeholder Gives Example %_counter% The file's position in the current operation: 1 for the first selected file, 2 for the next 2 %_date% Today's date, short local format 10/15/26 %_datetime% Now, local date and time 10/15/26 4:12:09 PM %_app% The program name and version OpenTag v0.1.0

%_counter% follows the order of the files in the file list, so sort the list first when you use it to number files. For track numbers, the Auto-numbering wizard is usually the better tool.

docs.title: Export only
docs.text:
These exist only inside export templates, because they describe the export as a whole or need extra work per file.

Placeholder Gives Example %_counter% The number of the current file in the loop 2 %_max_counter% The highest counter value of the loop 8 %_total_files% Number of exported files 8 %_total_size% Their total size, with a unit and your decimal mark 39.80 MB %_total_size_raw% Their total size in bytes 41733120 %_total_time% Their total playing time, hh:mm:ss, with a day count from one day (1d 02:03:04) 00:28:58 %_total_time2% The same, but hours keep counting past 24 00:28:58 %_total_time_raw% Their total playing time in seconds 1738 %_filename_rel% The file's path relative to the export file Harbour Lights/02 - Lanterns on the Water.mp3 %_folderpath_rel% Its folder relative to the export file Harbour Lights/ %_crc% CRC32 checksum of the file, 8 hexadecimal digits 4F2A91C0 %_md5% MD5 checksum of the file, 32 hexadecimal digits 9e107d9d372bb6826bd81d3542a419d6 %_md5audio% The audio checksum stored in FLAC and WavPack files, otherwise an MD5 of the audio without tags. Empty when unavailable

Checksums take time to compute on large selections, because OpenTag has to read every file completely.

docs.title: Playlists only
docs.text:
In the extended-info format string and file name of playlists:

Placeholder Gives Example %_playlist_filename% The playlist's file name without extension Harbour Lights %_playlist_filename_ext% With extension Harbour Lights.m3u8 %_playlist_folderpath% The playlist's folder, ending with a separator /Users/you/Music/Juniper Vale/Harbour Lights/

docs.title: Web source scripts only
docs.text: %_url%, %_coverurl%, %_preview% and %_current% exist only inside web source scripts, where they describe the page being parsed.

docs.title: Placeholders compared with Mp3tag
docs.text:
Coming from Mp3tag

OpenTag reads the same placeholder names as Mp3tag, so your format strings, columns and export templates keep working. OpenTag adds two: %_filetype% (the container format) and %_segment_title% (the Matroska segment title).

docs.title: Regular expressions
docs.text:
A regular expression (regex) describes a shape of text rather than exact text: “a number at the start”, “anything in brackets at the end”, “two words separated by a comma”. OpenTag uses them to find that shape in your tags and file names, and to rewrite it.

This page takes you from your first pattern to lookarounds, then documents the main places OpenTag accepts regular expressions. The web-source parser commands have their own reference. Each section builds on the one before. If you already know regular expressions from another program, skip to How OpenTag's regular expressions differ and the $regexp reference.

Try every example as you read

Select a file, open Convert → Tag → Tag… (Alt+5; Alt is ⌥ Option on a Mac), choose a field such as TITLE and type a $regexp(…) format string. The preview updates as you type, and nothing changes until you apply it. Start with the examples below on a copy of your files.

docs.title: Where you can use regular expressions
docs.text:
Where What it does Case $regexp(…) in any format string Replaces every match and returns the result Ignored by default; pass 0 as the fourth argument to respect it Replace with regular expression action Rewrites the values of a field, or the file name Case-sensitive comparison checkbox, off by default Filter: field MATCHES pattern Shows only files whose field matches Always ignored; write (?-i) to respect it Find, strategy Regular expression Lists matching filename/field values Case sensitive checkbox Web-source parser commands, such as SayRegexp and RegexpReplace Read or transform downloaded text and parser outputs Case-sensitive by default

Format strings, actions, filters and web-source parser commands use the shared Boost-compatible core. Find uses the browser’s Unicode JavaScript regular expressions. Their advanced syntax and line-break rules differ; a pattern accepted in one context is not guaranteed to work in another. The detailed replacement and core flag rules below apply to the shared core; Find’s specific behavior is described separately.

The examples use $regexp(text,pattern,replacement) and show the text, pattern and replacement in separate columns. You'd normally use a placeholder such as %title% as the text.

docs.title: 1. Plain text is a pattern too
docs.text:
The simplest regular expression is ordinary text. It finds that text wherever it occurs, and every occurrence is replaced:

Text Pattern Replacement Result Salt & Cedar & and Salt and Cedar Low Tide, Low Light Low High High Tide, High Light Paper Boats boats Planes Paper Planes Paper Boats Snow Rain Paper Boats

Two things to notice:

  • In $regexp, case is ignored unless you ask otherwise, so boats found Boats.
  • When nothing matches, you get the text back unchanged. That's convenient, but it also means a typo in a pattern fails silently. Check the preview.

Some characters have a special meaning in patterns: . ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \. To match one of them literally, put a backslash in front: \., \(, \?.

Text Pattern Replacement Result Fog Horn (Interlude) \(Interlude\) (empty) Fog Horn Who's There? \? (empty) Who's There

docs.title: 2. Character classes: one character from a set
docs.text:
A class matches one character from a set.

Pattern Matches one… Example match in Track 07: Low Tide . character of any kind T (the first character) \d digit 0–9 0 \w word character: letter, digit or _ T \s space, tab or line break the space after Track \D \W \S character that is not a digit / word character / space T / the space / T [aeiou] of the listed characters a [0-9a-f] in one of the ranges a [^0-9] not in the set (^ right after [) T [[:punct:]] punctuation (also [[:alpha:]], [[:upper:]], [[:digit:]]…) :

docs.title: Case classes, control characters and code points
docs.text:
Some escapes have different meanings in a pattern and a replacement. The following table describes their pattern meaning:

Pattern Matches \l A lowercase character \u An uppercase character \L A character that is not lowercase \U A character that is not uppercase \t A tab \n A newline/line-feed character \r A carriage-return character \r\n A Windows-style line ending, carriage return followed by line feed \xnn A character identified by a two-digit hexadecimal code point, such as \x41 for A \x{nnnn} A character identified by a braced hexadecimal code point, such as \x{732B} for 猫

Case-insensitive matching also affects case classes. Use (?-i) when distinguishing uppercase from lowercase is the purpose of the pattern:

Text Pattern Replacement Result aB1 (?-i)\l # #B1 aB1 (?-i)\u # a#1 aB1 (?-i)\L # a## aB1 (?-i)\U # #B# A \x41 # # 猫 \x{732B} # #

In a replacement, \u and \l instead change the next character's case, and \U / \L change a run of output until \E. See The replacement for that separate language.

Inside […], most special characters lose their meaning: [.?] matches a dot or a question mark. To include ], \ or ^ (at the start), escape them: [\]]. A - is literal at the start or end of the class: [_-].

Text Pattern Replacement Result paper_boats _ paper boats 06_the_keeper's_song [_.] 06 the keeper's song Track 07 \d # Track ## Salt & Cedar! [^\w\s] (empty) Salt Cedar

docs.title: 3. Repetition: how many times
docs.text:
A quantifier after a character or class says how often it may repeat.

Quantifier Means * 0 or more times + 1 or more times ? 0 or 1 time (optional) {3} exactly 3 times {2,} 2 or more times {1,3} between 1 and 3 times Text Pattern Replacement Result Track 07 \d+ # Track # Low··Tide··· (· is a space) \s{2,} Low Tide colour, color colou?r hue hue, hue 03 - Paper Boats \d+ - (empty) Paper Boats

docs.title: Greedy and lazy
docs.text:
Quantifiers are greedy: they take as much as they can and still let the rest of the pattern match. Add ? to make one lazy, taking as little as possible:

Text Pattern Replacement Result Juniper Vale - Salt - Cedar ^(.*) - .*$ $1 Juniper Vale - Salt Juniper Vale - Salt - Cedar ^(.*?) - .*$ $1 Juniper Vale (a) and (b) \(.*\) X X (a) and (b) \(.*?\) X X and X

The (…) and $1 in the first two rows are explained in section 5.

docs.title: 4. Anchors: where the match may be
docs.text:
Anchors match a position, not a character.

Anchor Position ^ Start of the text (and of every line in it) $ End of the text (and of every line in it) \A, \z Start and end of the whole text only \b A word boundary: between a word character and a non-word character \B Not a word boundary Text Pattern Replacement Result 07 Fog Horn 07 ^\d+ (empty) Fog Horn 07 07 Fog Horn 07 \d+$ (empty) 07 Fog Horn the other theme \bthe\b a a other theme ··Low Tide· ^\s+|\s+$ (empty) Low Tide

The last row uses |, which section 5 introduces: "spaces at the start, or spaces at the end". (The table shows it as |; you type a plain |.)

docs.title: 5. Groups, alternatives and capturing
docs.text:
Parentheses do three jobs:

  1. Grouping, so a quantifier applies to several characters: (ab)+.
  2. Alternatives with |: (Live|Demo|Remix) matches any one of those words.
  3. Capturing: the text a group matched is remembered and numbered from the left, starting at 1, so the replacement can reuse it.
Text Pattern Replacement Result Vale, Juniper ^(\w+), (\w+)$ $2 $1 Juniper Vale The Lanterns ^The (.+)$ $1, The Lanterns, The North Pier (Live) \((Live|Demo)\)$ [$1] North Pier [Live] 2024-05-01 ^(\d{4}).* $1 2024

Use (?:…) for a group that only groups and doesn't capture. Its contents don't get a number, which keeps your $1, $2 easier to count:

$regexp(%title%,'^(?:\d+[ ._-]+)?(.+)$','$1')

removes an optional leading track number: 03_Paper Boats and Paper Boats both become Paper Boats.

Inside the pattern itself, \1 means "the same text group 1 matched". That finds repeated words:

Text Pattern Replacement Result Low Low Tide \b(\w+) \1\b $1 Low Tide

docs.title: 6. The replacement
docs.text:
The replacement is text with a few codes in it:

Code Inserts $1 … $9, ${12} The text of that group. Use braces when a digit follows: ${1}0 \1 … \9 The same as $1 … $9 $& or $0 The whole match $` The text before the match $' The text after the match $$ A literal $ \U … \E Upper-case everything up to \E (or to the end) \L … \E Lower-case everything up to \E \u, \l Upper- or lower-case only the next character \t, \n A tab, a line break

With the text Juniper Vale and the pattern (\w+) (\w+):

Replacement Result $2, $1 Vale, Juniper \2, \1 Vale, Juniper [$&] [Juniper Vale] \U$1\E $2 JUNIPER Vale \L$0 juniper vale ${1}_$2 Juniper_Vale $$5 $5

Case codes can capitalise words, a job a regex alone can't do. Section 7 refines this example:

Text Pattern Replacement Result paper boats \b(\w) \u$1 Paper Boats the keeper's song \b(\w) \u$1 The Keeper'S Song

docs.title: 7. Lookaround: conditions without consuming
docs.text:
A lookaround checks what comes before or after a position without making it part of the match. That means it isn't replaced.

Syntax Means X(?=Y) X, if followed by Y X(?!Y) X, if not followed by Y (?<=Y)X X, if preceded by Y (?<!Y)X X, if not preceded by Y Text Pattern Replacement Result Track 12 of 15 \d+(?= of) [$&] Track [12] of 15 Track 12 of 15 (?<=of )\d+ [$&] Track 12 of [15] the keeper's song (?<![\w'])(\w) \u$1 The Keeper's Song photo.final.jpg \.(?=.*\.) _ photo_final.jpg

The third row fixes the problem from section 6. A letter only starts a word if neither a word character nor an apostrophe comes before it. The fourth row replaces every dot that has another dot somewhere after it, so only the last one (before the extension) survives.

A lookbehind must have a fixed length: (?<=of ) works, (?<=of\s+) doesn't.

docs.title: 8. Case and other modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers at the start of a pattern, or around part of it, change how it matches:

Modifier Effect (?i) Ignore case from here on (?-i) Respect case from here on (?i:…) Ignore case inside the group only (?-m) ^ and $ match only at the start and end of the whole text, not at line breaks (?-s) . no longer matches line breaks (?x) Ignore spaces in the pattern and allow # comments (for long patterns)

Modifiers win over the setting of the place you use the pattern:

Format string Result $regexp('Live At Home','live',x) x At Home $regexp('Live At Home','live',x,0) Live At Home $regexp('Live At Home','(?-i)live',x) Live At Home $regexp('Live At Home','(?i)LIVE',x,0) x At Home $regexp('Live at home','(?-i)(?i:AT) home',x) Live x

docs.title: $regexp(x,expr,repl[,c])
docs.text:
Replaces every match of a regular expression in a text.

Argument Meaning x The text to search, usually a placeholder such as %title% expr The regular expression repl The replacement, with the codes from section 6 c Optional. 0 respects case; leave it out (or use any other value) to ignore case

Returns x with every match replaced, or x unchanged when nothing matches.

Format string With these values Result $regexp(%title%,'\s*\(feat\. [^)]+\)',) TITLE = Paper Boats (feat. Mira Solberg) Paper Boats $regexp(%title%,'^.*\(feat\. ([^)]+)\).*$','$1') same Mira Solberg $regexp(%year%,'^(\d{4}).*$','$1') YEAR = 2024-05-01 2024 $regexp(%artist%,'^The (.+)$','$1, The') ARTIST = The Lanterns Lanterns, The $regexp(%title%,'abc',x) TITLE = ABC abc x x $regexp(%title%,'abc',x,0) TITLE = ABC abc ABC x

docs.title: Quote the pattern and the replacement
docs.text:
Inside a format string, $, %, [, ], ', , and ) have their own meaning (see Special characters), and regular expressions are full of them. Put the pattern and the replacement in single quotes to keep their syntax literal:

$regexp(%title%,'^(\d+)[ ._-]+(.+)$','$2 [$1]')

Without the quotes, OpenTag would read $2 as the start of a function and the first ) as the end of $regexp, and report an error. Inside quotes, write an apostrophe as '':

$regexp(%title%,'(?<![\w''])(\w)','\u$1')

To remove matches, leave the replacement argument empty after its comma:

$regexp(%title%,'\s*\(feat\. [^)]+\)',)

Do not use '' as an empty replacement: it means one literal apostrophe. Backslashes need no doubling: format strings don't treat \ specially.

Gotcha: no match means no change

$regexp(%title%,'^.*\(feat\. ([^)]+)\).*$','$1') returns the whole title for a song without “feat.”, because nothing matched. If you store the result in ARTIST, songs without a guest get their title as artist. Restrict the files first (filter title MATCHES "\(feat\."), or guard the expression:

$if($grtr($strstr($lower(%title%),'(feat. '),0),$regexp(%title%,'^.*\(feat\. ([^)]+)\).*$','$1'),%artist%)

The search checks a lowercase copy so FEAT. follows the same case-insensitive rule as the regex. The extraction still reads the original title, preserving the guest's spelling.

Gotcha: only the first value of a multi-value field

%artist% gives only the first artist, so $regexp(%artist%,…) only sees that one. To transform every value, use the Replace with regular expression action on the field.

docs.title: The Replace with regular expression action
docs.text:
The action rewrites a field in place. Its settings:

Setting Meaning Field The field to change. _ALL changes every field, _FILENAME the file name, _DIRECTORY the folder name Regular expression The pattern Replace matches with The replacement, with the codes from section 6 Case-sensitive comparison Off: case is ignored (the default). On: case must match

Differences from $regexp:

  • No quoting needed. The pattern and the replacement are plain text, not format strings. Type $1 as is, and % is just a percent sign.
  • Every value of a multi-value field is rewritten separately.

  • On _FILENAME the extension is part of the text. A pattern anchored with $ meets the end of .mp3, not the end of the name. To trim trailing spaces from a name, look ahead to the extension:

    Field Regular expression Replace matches with Low Tide .mp3 becomes _FILENAME \s+$ (empty) Low Tide .mp3 (no change) _FILENAME \s+(?=\.\w+$) (empty) Low Tide.mp3

Like every action, it can be undone with Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z after it has written the files.

docs.title: In the filter and Find
docs.text:
In the filter, MATCHES tests a field against a regular expression. The match always ignores case, so add (?-i) when case matters. Put the pattern in double quotes when it contains spaces or parentheses:

Filter Shows files where title MATCHES "\(live\)" the title contains (live) track MATCHES ^\d+$ the track has no total (7, not 7/12) title MATCHES "(?-i)^[^a-z]+$" the title has no lower-case letters (ALL CAPS) * MATCHES "\s{2,}" any field contains a double space artist MATCHES "^the " the artist starts with "The"

docs.title: Find uses JavaScript regular expressions
docs.text:
In Edit → Find… (Cmd+F / Ctrl+F), choose Regular expression to search filenames and individual tag values. Use Case sensitive to control letter case. Find compiles its pattern with JavaScript’s Unicode mode and an optional case-insensitive flag; it does not apply the shared core’s default multiline/dot-all behavior or replacement syntax.

For example, unscoped (?i) is accepted by the shared core but is invalid in Find. Type boats and use the checkbox instead:

Pattern Case sensitive Value Result boats Off Paper Boats Match boats On Paper Boats No match (?i)boats Off Paper Boats Invalid pattern

Find reports an invalid expression instead of treating it as no matches. It does not directly rewrite tags. Selecting a result changes the main selection, where configured tag-panel defaults or save-on-move settings can still act. Review the selection before applying an action.

docs.title: A pattern library
docs.text:
Copy, paste, adapt. Each row is ready to use in $regexp (with the quotes shown) or, without the quotes, in the action. Leave empty means no text after the last comma in $regexp, or an empty replacement box in the action.

Goal Pattern Replacement Before → After Remove a leading track number '^\d+[\s._-]*' Leave empty 03_Paper Boats → Paper Boats Underscores to spaces '_' ' ' the_keeper's_song → the keeper's song Collapse repeated spaces '\s{2,}' ' ' Low··Tide → Low Tide Trim spaces at both ends '^\s+|\s+$' Leave empty ·Low Tide· → Low Tide Remove a "(Remastered …)" suffix '\s*\((Remaster(ed)?|Live)[^)]*\)$' Leave empty North Pier (Remastered 2021) → North Pier Remove anything in square brackets '\s*\[[^\]]*\]' Leave empty Low Tide [Bonus] → Low Tide Remove "feat." from a title '\s*\(feat\. [^)]+\)' Leave empty Paper Boats (feat. Mira Solberg) → Paper Boats Swap "Last, First" '^([^,]+), (.+)$' '$2 $1' Vale, Juniper → Juniper Vale Move "The" to the end '^The (.+)$' '$1, The' The Lanterns → Lanterns, The Keep the year of a date '^(\d{4}).*$' '$1' 2024-05-01 → 2024 "&" to "and" '\s*&\s*' ' and ' Salt & Cedar → Salt and Cedar Capitalise each word '(?<![\w''])(\w)' '\u$1' the keeper's song → The Keeper's Song Upper-case a whole word '\b(dj)\b' '\U$1' dj nimbus → DJ nimbus

(· stands for a space, and | for a plain |.)

docs.title: How OpenTag's regular expressions differ
docs.text:
The shared core used by format strings, actions, filters and web-source parser commands accepts Boost’s Perl-compatible syntax. The following core rules do not describe Find’s JavaScript engine. If you come from another tool, watch for these:

  • Case is ignored by default in $regexp, the action and the filter. JavaScript, Python and most editors respect case by default.
  • Replacements are global. Every match is replaced, not just the first.
  • \d means only 0–9. Full-width and other non-ASCII digits don't count as digits.
  • ^ and $ also match at line breaks, and . matches line breaks. This only matters for multi-line values such as comments and lyrics. Use \A and \z, or (?-m) and (?-s), for the stricter behaviour.
  • \u and \l in a pattern are classes ("an upper-case letter", "a lower-case letter"), not Unicode escapes. Write a code point as \x{732B}. With case ignored, \u matches any letter. In a replacement, \u and \l change the case of the next character.
  • An empty pattern matches between every character: $regexp(ab,,_) gives _a_b_. The pattern argument is empty; '' would search for an apostrophe instead.
  • Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as emoji, count as two characters for . and {n}.
  • Case-insensitive matching of non-English letters follows your system's language settings.
  • Boost's extended conditional replacement syntax is not enabled. Use format-string conditions around $regexp when the output needs a decision.

docs.title: Tag mapping tables
docs.text:
A mapping connects the editable name ARTIST to native storage such as the ID3v2 frame TPE1 or MP4 atom ©ART. Use the field name in OpenTag; inspect the native identifier when troubleshooting another reader or an existing file.

New to this?

Read Field names for the meanings and special value syntax. A mapping changes where a value is stored; it does not calculate or translate that value.

docs.title: How to read these tables
docs.text:
The tables contain all 118 named fields from OpenTag's source-checked mapping vocabulary. — means no dedicated mapping in that cell. It does not always mean the field is forbidden: the custom-field fallback explains what is used instead. APE and Vorbis Comments store actual field names rather than using this fixed native-identifier table.

TXXX:description denotes an ID3 user-text frame with that description. UFID:owner denotes an owner-specific ID3 identifier. ----:namespace:name denotes an MP4 freeform atom. The © character is part of a four-character MP4 identifier, not decorative punctuation.

These are supported metadata representations, not guarantees that another player uses them or that changing the filename extension converts one format into another. See File formats for which tag family a file uses.

docs.title: ID3v2 and MP4

The ID3 columns describe the selected revision's dedicated mapping. A write in another revision can use custom text where no dedicated frame is defined. MP4 ARTIST writes ©ART and reads the alternative ©art spelling too. GENRE can read gnre as well as the text atom ©gen; ordinary writes use the text representation. Existing alternative/freeform storage can also be normalized on save unless the Advanced reuse options preserve an unchanged field.

docs.title: Matroska, ASF, and RIFF INFO
docs.text:
T=30, T=50, and similar Matroska entries are target type values. When no native name follows a target, use the field's own name. MKA entries describe the audio mapping; MKV entries describe the recommended video mapping when a video track is present and that Advanced option is enabled. A .mkv suffix alone does not select it.

SORT_WITH is nested under that level's TITLE. For example, album sorting is nested under the album-level TITLE rather than stored as an unrelated global text tag. PART_NUMBER at target 30 represents a track; target 50 represents a disc in audio mapping, or an episode in the recommended video mapping.

In recommended Matroska video mapping, target 50 PART_NUMBER is exposed as TVEPISODE, and target 60 PART_NUMBER as TVSEASON. The audio DISCNUMBER rule is not also applied to that episode value. Mapped native names stored at other, unrecognized levels may remain hidden and preserved. Track/edition/attachment-scoped metadata is not automatically merged into global editable fields; supported chapter-targeted tags belong to their chapter rows.

ASF WM/TrackNumber is the normal track mapping. OpenTag also reads legacy zero-based WM/Track as TRACK plus one when no modern value is present, and keeps an existing legacy attribute synchronized on a TRACK edit. This fallback is not a separate field shown in the table.

RIFF INFO holds one string per identifier. Multiple edited values are joined with ; there, so it cannot preserve separate values in the same way as a multi-value tag. A WAV file can also carry ID3v2 metadata alongside INFO.

docs.title: Custom-field fallback
docs.text:
Tag family A field without a dedicated mapping ID3v2 User text TXXX:FIELDNAME. Described comments/lyrics and owner-specific identifiers have their own syntax. MP4 Freeform ----:com.apple.iTunes:FIELDNAME. An explicit freeform namespace/name is also supported. Vorbis Comments The actual field name stored in the comment list. APE The actual field name stored in the APE item. ASF / Windows Media An attribute under its own name, unless it conflicts with another mapped native attribute. Matroska An unmapped name is written as a global target-30 SimpleTag; reserved native names cannot be used to bypass their mapped meaning. RIFF INFO No general long-name fallback. An unmapped four-character uppercase/digit identifier beginning with I, such as IENG, can identify an INFO field.

For example, ASF’s native Description belongs to COMMENT; trying to use a separate custom DESCRIPTION field can conflict with that mapping and be refused.

An empty fixed-table cell can therefore produce generic storage on an edit. This is different from claiming a dedicated standard mapping exists. Conversely, binary or unsupported native structures can be preserved without being exposed as a writable text field.

docs.title: Field-specific storage rules
docs.text:
The tables identify native locations. Several fields also impose value structure:

  • TRACK and DISCNUMBER share their MP4 atoms with TOTALTRACKS and TOTALDISCS; inconsistent simultaneous totals are rejected.
  • MOVEMENT and MOVEMENTTOTAL share ID3v2 MVIN.
  • COMPILATION, PODCAST, gapless and movement flags, MP4 store IDs, media types, ratings, credits, and lyrics have their own allowed value forms. See Structured values.
  • MUSICBRAINZ_TRACKID means recording ID; its ID3 storage is the http://musicbrainz.org UFID owner. MUSICBRAINZ_RELEASETRACKID is a different identifier.
  • YEAR and DATE are not interchangeable date transformations. A user-defined alias changes a name while leaving the text unchanged.

The source importers can supply BARCODE and CATALOGNUMBER from release data. Historical Mp3tag version annotations about introducing those fields do not describe OpenTag release availability.

docs.title: User-defined field names
docs.text:
Use File → Options… → Tags → Mapping for per-format Source → Target aliases. On read, the source name is shown as the target. On write, the target is translated back to each source mapped to it. Several sources can share one target; one source cannot map to several different targets. A Vorbis DATE → YEAR rule is an example of harmonizing names without changing the date text.

These aliases operate above the native identifier mappings. Enter OpenTag's readable field name as Source for ID3v2/MP4, rather than a frame or atom code. A custom alias does not replace the built-in mapping from TPE1 to ARTIST. Matroska is not a selectable tag type in that alias editor.

docs.title: Menu reference
docs.text:
Use menus to discover commands and check what a shortcut will do in the current context. A disabled item usually needs selected files, saved pending edits, a supported file type or an available platform capability. These pages follow the current desktop interface's English labels.

Menu Use it for File Save/reload tags, load folders or playlists, export reports and manage configuration Edit Undo, tag clipboard, selection, file transfers and deletion View Filter, tag panel, columns, sorting, toolbars and layout Convert Generate names or fields from existing data, import text and number tracks Actions Saved groups, Quick settings and explicit direct runs Tag Sources Search metadata providers, review results and manage installed sources Tools External tools and supported file-format utilities Help Documentation, shortcuts, issues, updates, releases and app information

docs.title: Choose the scope first
docs.text:
Some commands use selected files; others explicitly use all files. Playlist (all files) and Playlist (selected files) are different commands. A filter changes the visible list, and selection commands work with that view. Check the selection before writing or deleting.

A preview calculates a proposed result. Pending edits wait for Save tags. Other commands write when their own Apply or Export button is chosen. The linked workflow page identifies that command's write step.

docs.title: Other menus
docs.text:
Context and helper menus explain the commands offered by a file row, tag panel, cover window, Extended tags field and helper input. The helper button beside a supported format-string or field-name input opens a helper menu. Control+Space opens the focused input's supported helper. These helpers insert syntax or remembered values; they do not apply an action by themselves.

The tag panel's options menu controls visible fields, custom values and panel configuration. A dialog such as Actions or source review has its own selection, enabled-state and keyboard rules. See keyboard shortcuts before reusing an F-key in another area.

docs.title: Platform and version differences
docs.text:
File-manager labels become Open in Finder, Open in Explorer or Open in file manager. Command replaces many Ctrl shortcuts on a Mac, with physical Control exceptions in the keyboard reference. Mobile/provider-document workflows can lack directory picking or native file operations.

An entry documented for another application, such as a separate Exit item or a different playlist-generator shortcut, is not automatically part of OpenTag. Use the current visible labels and linked workflow instructions.

docs.title: Actions menu
docs.text:
Use Actions to apply a reusable sequence or run one action immediately. An action can change tags, paths or external files; inspect its settings on copied practice files before using a large selection.

New to this?

Build your first action group teaches the difference between saving a workflow and applying it. The action reference lists all current types.

docs.title: Menu entries
docs.text:
Entry Shortcut What it does Actions… Alt+6 Open the group library to create, edit, arrange, import, export, save or apply groups. Opening the library does not itself run a group. Actions (Quick)… Alt+Shift+6 Configure one action and choose Apply action to run it on the current selection, saving immediately. No enclosing group is required. Saved group name Its configured mnemonic, if any Run only that saved group on the current selection. Its checkbox state in the library does not prevent this explicit run.

Alt is ⌥ Option on macOS. On that platform, Option combinations used to type characters in a text field retain their text-entry behavior; use the menu when the shortcut is not appropriate to the current focus.

The library can be opened to organize groups even without a selected file. Applying a group or Quick action requires an eligible selection. Save pending edits first; provider documents can limit path-dependent actions. Read a disabled command's explanation instead of assuming it has already run.

docs.title: Quick settings are remembered
docs.text:
OpenTag remembers the last Quick action type and that type's last applied settings. Switching types can recall a different saved configuration. For example, returning to Replace can restore an earlier search/replacement instead of supplying empty controls. Check every field before applying.

This convenience is not a named, ordered workflow. To repeat several steps reliably, put them in a saved action group. The Quick dialog's Cancel closes without applying the current action.

docs.title: Checked groups and a direct menu run
docs.text:
In Actions…, Apply checked groups runs the checked groups in library order, and each group's actions in their displayed order. Selection highlight and the execution checkboxes have different jobs: highlighting chooses what to edit; checking chooses what a multi-group run executes.

A saved group's own menu item runs that group alone. For instance, if Clean spacing is unchecked and Build filenames is checked, choosing Clean spacing directly still runs Clean spacing. It does not also run Build filenames. Use the group library when both steps must run in order.

docs.title: Submenus and keyboard mnemonics
docs.text:
A # in a group name separates menu levels. An & marks the next letter as its mnemonic; && means a literal ampersand. For example, a saved name Cleanup#&Space titles appears under Cleanup as Space titles.

Press Alt+A to open the Actions menu, then the marked letters for the required level and group. Use distinct mnemonic letters within one level; the current implementation chooses the first matching group when names reuse the same letter. A submenu can also be opened with the pointer.

The stored full group name remains significant for references such as a custom toolbar item. A displayed menu label is not a format string and does not evaluate %artist% or scripting functions.

docs.title: If the result is unexpected
docs.text:
• Recheck which files are selected and whether another filter hid intended files before the action was started.
  • Check group/action order and the current Quick settings. A later action sees the earlier action's result.
  • Inspect the file errors and the available Edit → Undo operation. Export Cover records its created and replaced images for undo; reports, playlists and other external outputs have their own cleanup rules.
  • Save group edits with Save groups when the workflow must survive reopening the app; editing a group is separate from changing audio tags.

docs.title: Context menus and helper menus
docs.text:
A context menu offers commands for the place you opened it: a file-list row, the tag panel, a cover, an Extended tags field or a format-string input. Check that context and the current selection before choosing a command. Removing a name from a suggestion list, removing a tag field and removing a file from the file list have different results.

New to this?

Use your first tagging session to practise selection and saving. Multi-value fields explains how separate values affect the field and cover dialogs.

docs.title: Open and leave a menu
docs.text:
Right-click the relevant area. In a focused file-list row or cover window, Shift+F10 or the keyboard's Menu key opens its command menu. The cover also has a ⋯ button. Arrow keys move between enabled commands; Escape closes the popup. A text input generally keeps its normal text-editing context menu instead of opening the surrounding panel's commands.

The small ► beside a marked input opens a helper menu. With that input focused, Ctrl+Space opens its helper too, using physical Control on macOS. On a Mac, Ctrl+Alt+Space is another route when Control+Space is claimed by input-source switching. The helper's content depends on whether the input expects a field name, generating expression, matching pattern, regular expression or history value.

docs.title: File-list row menu
docs.text:
Right-clicking a row outside the existing selection selects that row alone. Right-clicking an already selected row keeps the selection. Thus a menu opened on one row can act on several selected files. Right-clicking a column header opens the column menu instead; see View.

Entry Task and scope Extended tags… Edit the selected files' full exposed field set. Copy as Text… Render selected metadata through the Copy as Text format, rather than copying whole audio files. Remove tag… Remove supported tag data under the current removal policy; inspect the confirmation and actual file errors. Tools → configured tool name Launch that external tool under its own selected-file/first-file settings. If no tools exist, Configure tools… opens their settings. Utils → Remove tag types… Choose which supported tag families to remove. This is not the helper's suggestion-list command. Utils → Strip chapters MP4… Remove supported MP4 chapter structures from eligible files. Utils → Remove unsupported fields… Run the format-specific cleanup on eligible selected files. Utils → Optimize… Run the supported format optimization after reviewing its prompt. Remove from list Hide the selected rows from the workspace; keep the audio files on disk. Play Open selected audio through the configured/default external playback route. Open in Finder, Open in Explorer, or the platform file-manager label Reveal the files in the platform's file manager.

Disabled commands retain an explanation, for example pending edits or an unsupported file/provider operation. Utility names are not universal repairs for every container. The current row menu does not duplicate every command from the top menus; use File, Edit or Convert when the task is not offered here.

docs.title: Tag-panel menu
docs.text:
Choose the tag panel's ⋯ or right-click its non-text background. Right-clicking a text input keeps the system edit menu; the cover window has the separate commands below.

Entry Effect Customize tag panel… Edit the field/control layout and defaults. Field values… Edit stored suggestions for tag-panel fields. Default values in input fields Apply the configured defaults to the selected files as pending edits; review and save them separately. A configured field's name Show or hide that control on the panel. Hiding a control does not delete its tag field. Display cover art Show or hide the cover section. Embedded images remain in files. Save configuration… Export the panel layout to a configuration file. This is not a backup of the selected files' tags. Load configuration… Read and persist a panel layout. Other ordinary panel settings remain separate. Import Mp3tag configuration…, where available Load supported panel settings into the customization dialog for review; OK saves the chosen layout. Position choices, where available Move the panel to an offered dock position. Hide tag panel Hide the whole panel. Use View → Show tag panel or Ctrl+Q to restore it; physical Control is used on macOS too.

Tag-panel options describes control types and default values. An imported layout may contain unsupported items; inspect the import report instead of assuming identical appearance across apps.

docs.title: Cover-window menu
docs.text:
The cover window summarizes embedded artwork across the selection. When all selected files have the same ordered covers, it shows one current image and previous/next controls. Different cover sets produce Covers vary, rather than pretending the first file's image belongs to every file.

Command Result Add cover… Choose an image to embed in the selected files. The chooser uses the resolved cover-art directory when available. Its fallback order is explained below. Remove cover For equal cover sets, remove the displayed occurrence. For varying cover sets, confirm removing all covers from the selection. Replace cover… Replace the displayed embedded image while retaining its position, picture type and description. It requires a common displayed cover. Extract cover… Save the displayed embedded image as an external image file. This does not remove it from the audio file. Adjust cover… Open the cover-adjustment action to change image format, quality or size. Manage covers… Review a whole cover set, including additions, replacements, reordering and removals. Its edits are written when confirmed in that dialog. Set cover type Choose a predefined picture role for the displayed cover, or for all distinct covers in a varying selection. Set cover description… Set the displayed cover's description, or all distinct descriptions in a varying selection. Empty text clears the description. Cut cover Copy the displayed image to the image clipboard, then remove its displayed occurrence from the selected files. Copy cover Copy the displayed embedded image to the image clipboard. Paste cover Embed an image supplied by the supported image clipboard. It is separate from pasting tag fields. Previous cover / Next cover Change which common embedded image is displayed; do not reorder the stored cover set. View larger… Open the displayed cover in a larger viewer; Enter or a double-click also opens it. Correct aspect ratio Keep the image's proportions in the display. Turning it off stretches the preview; it does not resize the embedded image.

For Add cover… and Replace cover…, OpenTag first evaluates the Cover art directory format and uses it if it resolves to a real folder. Otherwise it uses the selected file’s folder if that folder has a supported local image. Next it tries the current working folder, and falls back to the selected file’s folder when no valid working folder is available. A configured relative folder is resolved beside the audio file. This changes where the chooser starts, not which image is automatically embedded.

The menu offers 21 predefined picture roles: Other, File icon, Other file icon, Front Cover, Back Cover, Leaflet, Media, Lead artist, Artist, Conductor, Band or orchestra, Composer, Lyricist, Recording location, During recording, During performance, Screen capture, A bright colored fish, Illustration, Band logo and Publisher logo. Storage support depends on the audio/tag format. Choosing a role cannot make a format preserve distinctions it does not store.

The following availability examples assume an editable local selection and an available image clipboard. A common cover is already saved, and is the first of two images when navigation is relevant.

Cover state Add Remove Replace Extract Copy Next none Yes No No No No No same Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes varying Yes Yes No No No No

A folder image labeled Not embedded in the file is a preview fallback, not an embedded cover. Removing an embedded cover does not delete that separate image file. Import/embed the image explicitly if it must travel inside the audio file.

Cover clipboard/chooser operations depend on platform support. Save tags first when a displayed image is pasted but not written: Copy, Cut and Extract require the saved image. Review results and file errors after a change; a visible preview alone does not establish successful save-back.

docs.title: Extended tags: copy and paste fields
docs.text:
Right-click a field row outside its text value to open Cut field, Copy field and Paste field (or a named Paste ARTIST command). Copy/Cut need a valid field name and values that are the same in every selected file. A mixed field cannot be copied as if one value represented the whole selection.

The copied field retains separate values. Pasting finds an existing field with the same field identity and replaces its values, or adds a field row when it is absent. Cut field also marks the original row for removal in the dialog. These are dialog edits: commit/review them through the normal Extended tags workflow before treating them as written changes.

This field clipboard is distinct from Edit → Copy tags and the image clipboard. Right-clicking inside a value textarea keeps normal text editing; it does not silently copy the entire field.

docs.title: Field-name helper: suggestions, not tag deletion
docs.text:
The ► next to a field-name input can offer Choose field, including known fields and special targets valid for that action. Choose a field to replace the field-name input's current text. The following maintenance commands edit the stored field-name suggestion list:

Command What changes Remove field Remove the currently entered field name from the stored suggestions, when it belongs to that list. Remove all fields… After confirmation, clear the stored suggestion list. Reset fields… After confirmation, restore the built-in suggestion list.

None of these deletes metadata from the selected audio files. A removed name can still appear because it is already present in selected files, or because the current control offers it as a special target. To remove metadata, use a real field-removal operation such as the Remove Fields action.

docs.title: Format-string and pattern helpers
docs.text:
A generating-expression helper offers the current visible tag-panel fields first, then Extended fields, Information fields and Functions where supported. Choosing a field inserts its %field% placeholder at the caret, replacing selected text. Choosing a function inserts its signature; replace the argument markers with real inputs before using it. The first argument is selected after insertion so it can be overwritten immediately.

In these examples ▮ marks the caret, not a literal character to type:

Before Insert from helper After Track: ▮ %track% Track: %track% %artist% - ▮ %title% %artist% - %title% ▮ $num(x,y) $num(x,y)

A matching-pattern input, such as Filename → Tag, offers field placeholders and DUMMY (skip text). It does not offer generating functions or technical properties that cannot be written as captured tags. Regex inputs instead offer pattern fragments; replacement inputs offer capture references. A helper inserts syntax for that context; it does not validate every larger expression you build around it.

Export-aware inputs additionally offer export and playlist information. Those placeholders still require their real evaluation context. Inserting %_total_files% into an unrelated ordinary tag expression cannot create an export input set.

docs.title: History and favorite expressions
docs.text:
For inputs with remembered values, Manage history… opens an editor with Add…, Duplicate…, Edit…, Remove, move-up/down controls and a Use selected button. An entry has the expression, an optional name and description, and a Favorite flag. Favorites appear directly in the helper menu; choosing one replaces the entire input value, rather than inserting it at the caret.

For example, name %albumartist% - %album% Album label, add a description explaining its intended use, and mark it Favorite. The helper shows Album label; choosing it restores the stored expression. The name is a label, not extra text added to the result. A duplicated entry must have different expression text before it can be kept. Nonempty names must be distinct within that history list.

Edits to a history entry or its Favorite checkbox are stored as they are kept; Close leaves the list editor, and Use selected copies an entry into the original input. Changing the history does not run its expression on the audio selection. The list normally retains up to 25 entries by dropping the oldest nonfavorites first; an all-favorite list can exceed that soft limit. The histories belong to individual input contexts, not one global list of every format string.

Where Manage history… is unavailable, Remove from history removes the input's current remembered expression, while Remove all from history… clears that input's list after confirmation. Shift+Del removes the current value from an input's drop-down history. Removing history does not clear tags and does not rewrite an already exported report.

The filter helper also offers Auto-apply filter. Turning it on applies the current edited filter; with it off, use Enter to apply a pending query. See filtering for the file-list effect.

docs.title: Convert menu
docs.text:
Converters derive new tag values or filenames from existing information. Select the intended files and save pending edits first. The menu offers five conversion directions plus track/disc numbering; choose the direction by what you already have and what you want to create.

Item Shortcut Use it when Tag → Filename… Alt+1 Tags contain the artist, album or title needed for a new name/folder layout Filename → Tag… Alt+2 File/folder text contains the metadata you want to capture Filename → Filename… Alt+3 Parts of the old name need rearranging, optionally with scripting functions Text File → Tag… Alt+4 An external text table supplies tag values Tag → Tag… Alt+5 One field should be copied, combined or transformed from others Auto-numbering… Primary+K Selected files need track/disc counters and optional totals

Primary is Ctrl on Windows/Linux and Command on macOS. Option+digit works outside text entry on a Mac; while typing use Control+Option+digit so Option can continue entering characters normally.

docs.title: Read the direction before applying
docs.text:
For TITLE = Paper Boats and TRACK = 3/8, a Tag → Filename pattern $num(%track%,2) - %title% produces the stem 03 - Paper Boats, while keeping the audio extension. It does not change TITLE. Filename → Tag performs the opposite kind of task: %track% - %title% can capture 03 - Paper Boats.flac into fields. Those are different languages at the input boundary: a capture pattern names pieces to read, while a format string calculates output.

Tag → Tag can calculate %artist% - %title% into COMMENT, for example, without changing its source title. Text import can match rows by position or a filename key; inspect that matching mode before applying a table to several files. The linked converter pages give complete worked examples.

docs.title: Preview and write behavior
docs.text:
Use the dialog's preview before its Apply/rename step. In the current shortcut router, shifted Alt+digit chords do not invoke these five converters; use the explicit dialog controls to inspect the proposed result.

Filename changes and a converter's Apply operation can write immediately. Auto-numbering instead stages its proposed TRACK/DISCNUMBER edits as pending changes, then Save tags writes them. Primary+Shift+K opens numbering with per-folder reset requested; it does not immediately number or save the files. Do not infer the write step from the fact that two commands share this menu.

If a preview skips a nonmatching filename or reports an invalid expression, correct the input or pattern before applying. A successful calculation is not proof that every output path is writable or distinct. Check collisions, missing fields and the affected-file count, then inspect reported errors.

docs.title: Edit menu
docs.text: Edit contains tag clipboard, history, selection and file operations. First identify what has focus. Copying selected text is different from copying the tags of selected files; deleting a file is different from removing its row.

docs.title: History and tag clipboard
docs.text:
Item Result Undo Restore the last recorded operation; its label shows the operation/file count when available Redo / Repeat Redo an undone operation, or repeat the available last action/group; the current label identifies which Cut tags Copy tag/cover data and stage its removal from selected files Copy tags Copy selected tag values and available artwork data Copy as Text… Evaluate a format string for the selected files and copy a textual representation Paste tags Stage clipboard tag/cover data on selected targets Discard pending changes Remove unsaved changes without reading another file or applying panel defaults

Text-entry fields keep their normal text clipboard and undo behavior. Outside text entry, the app's tag clipboard can copy one file's tags to several targets or match multiple source entries to targets in order. Check the selection and ordering before pasting. Pasted artwork and cut-tag removals remain pending until Save tags; copying alone does not write anything.

For Copy as Text…, %artist% - %title% makes a readable artist/title line for each selected track. This is calculated text, not a new audio tag. Functions and placeholders follow the format-string reference.

History concerns operations actually recorded in the current desktop session. Check its label and any errors; do not assume every external change, file transfer, export or deletion can be reversed with tag-edit undo. If the menu says Repeat, it means another action execution, not restoration of a saved snapshot. Pending edits and available operations still constrain it.

docs.title: Selection and finding
docs.text:
Item Which files it selects Select all Every row in the current visible list Invert selection Visible rows currently unselected, while deselecting selected rows Unselect all No rows Select next file The row after the last selected row, clamping at the end Select similar files Rows whose active sort values match the active file Select next similar files The next different group of active sort values Find… Open the file-list search dialog

A filter limits what is visible. Select all after filtering therefore selects that visible result, not every file elsewhere on disk. Hiding a row with a filter does not automatically unselect it; check the selected count before a write. Similar-file selection uses sort criteria, not audio similarity or a duplicate-audio test.

For example, sort by album, select a Harbour Lights track, then choose Select similar files to select that album's matching sort group. Additional sort criteria can narrow the match. Choose the sort deliberately before using that result as the target of an action.

Select next file also works while editing a tag-panel field, keeping focus in the panel. Tags options can save pending edits when moving between selections. Changing selection alone is not otherwise a universal save command.

docs.title: Names, transfers and deletion
docs.text:
Item Effect Edit in file list Start editing the first selected filename column, or another editable column when no filename column is available Copy files to… Choose a destination and copy selected audio files Move files to… Choose a destination and move selected audio files Remove from list Remove rows; keep files on disk Delete files… Move selected files to the system Recycle Bin/trash when supported Delete files permanently… Delete without using the system trash Manage covers… Inspect and edit artwork for selected files

Read the deletion confirmation: Remove from list does not delete, while permanent deletion does not provide a trash restore path. File errors can leave only part of a requested copy, move or deletion completed; inspect the reported outcome before repeating it. These operations require supported local file access and are unavailable for provider selections where the operation cannot be performed.

Editing a filename cell changes a path; editing a metadata cell changes a field. Check the cell and the command's commit/preview behavior. For a batch rename from tags, use Tag → Filename instead of editing each row manually.

docs.title: Keyboard and context
docs.text: Primary+C/X/V, Z/Y and selection shortcuts follow the focus rules in keyboard shortcuts. F2 is Edit in file list when the list has focus, but can rename an action group or edit a source-review field in those dialogs. The cover area's context menu provides cover-specific commands; a tag clipboard operation can include artwork as well as text fields.

docs.title: File menu
docs.text: Use File to load audio, write or reload tags, make reports and manage the application configuration. Loading files into the list does not convert their audio. A command mentioning all files has a different scope from one using the current selection.

docs.title: Tags and copies
docs.text:
Item What it does Save tags Write pending field/cover changes to the selected files when save-back is supported Remove tag… Remove the tag families selected under Options, rather than deleting the audio Save a copy… Keep edited data through the supported provider-document copy workflow when available; check its format and cover limitations Reload tags Read selected files again from their current storage

For example, selecting two Juniper Vale tracks and changing ARTIST stages that value for both. Save tags writes the pending change. A field left at its keep-current-values state does not become an instruction to overwrite it. To replace or clear a field, make that edit explicitly and inspect the pending selection.

For a supported provider document, Save a copy… offers Edited copy with pending tag-field changes or Original backup from the last verified source. Pending artwork changes are not part of the copy request. The source and recovery copies are retained, and the written copy is checked before a successful result is reported.

Reload tags is useful after an external edit, but first resolve any pending changes you want to retain. It is different from Refresh, which revisits loaded folders as well. Remove tag… follows the read/write/remove policy in Tags → Mpeg and other format options; removing one tag family can leave another readable family in the same file.

docs.title: Playlists and reports
docs.text:
Item Input and result Playlist (all files) Create a playlist from the loaded list Playlist (selected files) Create one from the selection Playlist per folder (all files) Create playlists grouped by their audio folders Generate playlists… Open the dialog for format-based playlist generation Export… Run or edit a saved export configuration, depending on the selection-dialog preference Export CSV… Write a direct CSV export; use Export… for a configurable report template

Playlist paths and display titles are controlled separately from audio tags. Playlist per folder (all files) is the Primary+Shift+P command; it is not the same dialog as Generate playlists…. See Playlist options for path style, filename, encoding and BOM choices.

Export produces a report from selected files. The saved template controls text, loops and encoding. Primary+Shift+E requests per-directory export. An output report is a new text file, not a tag change waiting for Save tags.

docs.title: Load and navigate
docs.text:
Item What changes Change directory… Replace the loaded list with a chosen folder Add directory… Add a folder's supported files to the existing list Add files… Choose individual files Load playlist/cue sheet… Load the audio references in a playlist or cue sheet Upper directory Replace the view with the working folder's parent Previous directory / Next directory Move backward/forward through directory history Favorite directory Load the first configured favorite Favorite directories… Manage the ordered favorite-folder list Recent directories / Favorite directories Open an entry from the corresponding submenu when entries exist Clear list Remove loaded rows without deleting their files Open in Finder/Explorer/file manager Reveal selected files; without a selection, open the working folder when one is available Play Open selected files with their associated player

The Directories options control subfolder scanning and related behavior. Changing a directory can ask how to handle pending edits. A failed scan keeps the previous working directory. Adding a directory does not replace the working directory or silently save pending tags.

A loaded playlist determines an input order, but an active column sort can show a different order. Use View → Unsorted (load and playlist order) to inspect the load order. Loading a playlist does not rewrite the playlist or move its audio files. Cue-sheet chapter/track handling depends on the supported file/container workflow; it does not split the audio into new files.

See command line for opening paths from scripts or shortcuts. Where folder picking is unavailable, use Add files… and respect the current provider-document/save-back limitations.

docs.title: Configuration and closing
docs.text:
Item Result Options… Open application preferences Save configuration… Save a configuration archive for backup/transfer Load configuration… Choose and load a supported configuration archive Open configuration folder Open the folder containing the app's settings/configuration files

A configuration archive is not a backup of the audio library. Keep original media and any report outputs separately. Loading configuration changes app settings, actions, exports, layouts and remembered lists. After confirmation, loading discards pending edits and reloads the window. Inspect the selected archive and save edits you need first. The Discogs access token is not included in the configuration archive.

The current webview File menu has no separate Exit item. Close the window or quit through the operating system's app controls. Resolve pending edits when asked. General options can make minimizing use the notification area on supported platforms; a minimized window is not the same as an exited process.

Use the keyboard reference for platform-specific keys. Here, Primary means Ctrl on Windows/Linux and Command on macOS.

docs.title: Help menu
docs.text:
Use Help to find documentation, inspect keyboard shortcuts, report a problem, check released versions or identify the installed OpenTag version. These commands do not require selected audio files.

New to this?

Start with your first tagging session. Keep the app version from About OpenTag with any troubleshooting notes.

docs.title: Every current entry
docs.text:
Entry Result Documentation On desktop, open the published OpenTag user guide in the default browser. Its source remains in the OpenTag repository. Keyboard shortcuts Show the app's shortcut overview, assembled from current menu commands plus additional editing/navigation keys. Report an issue On desktop, open OpenTag's GitHub issue page in the default browser. Check for updates… Read the release list and show whether a newer applicable version is available. It does not download or install an update. Releases On desktop, open OpenTag's GitHub releases page for packages and release notes. About OpenTag Show OpenTag's version and MIT license identification. Close the dialog to return to the workspace.

On the inspected mobile path, external Help destinations report the URL to open in a browser instead of launching the desktop browser opener. Follow the message on that build. This is separate from whether the in-app shortcut or About dialog can be shown.

docs.title: Read the shortcut overview
docs.text:
Shortcuts use Command on macOS where the command is a primary-modifier shortcut, and Control on Windows/Linux. Some controls deliberately retain physical Control on every platform. The overview also contains commands that do not have a top-menu entry, such as moving within an action list or opening a format-string helper.

Find the command by task, then check its focus context. Copy while editing text copies text; Copy tags outside a text editor has a different purpose. The keyboard reference explains the platform and focus distinctions with examples.

docs.title: Check and obtain an update
docs.text:
1. Choose Help → Check for updates….
  2. Read the reported current/latest versions and whether the offered release is stable or a prerelease.
  3. Choose Open release page for an offered update, or View release notes when inspecting the latest known release.
  4. On that page, choose the package appropriate to the actual platform and review its installation/signing limitations before installing it yourself.

Options → Updates controls prerelease inclusion and automatic startup checks. A manual check still uses the prerelease preference. A failed check reports that the release list could not be read; it is not evidence that the installed version is current. Conversely, a successful release-list request does not test every tag source or network service.

There is no separate First Steps, donation, Mp3tag website or Mp3tag community command in this OpenTag menu. Use this guide's first-session link for the introductory task and OpenTag's own issue/release pages for support. A similarly named item in another application is not an OpenTag support route.

docs.title: Report a useful problem
docs.text: Record the OpenTag version from About OpenTag, the operating system, the command used and a short sequence that reproduces the result. Include the actual displayed error and the file/container type when relevant. Use a copied or minimal example where possible. A screenshot can explain a layout issue, while a copyable format string is more useful for a formula problem. Do not treat the issue form as a promise of an immediate response.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Your first tagging session
